content: Michael Burry says he won't buy Nvidia stock even if it falls further, as he's bracing for more bad news. "My spidey sense tingles that something is still wrong," the investor of "The Big Short" fame wrote in a Substack post on Sunday. Nvidia's founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned on Thursday following reports that he had extramarital affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and one of his direct reports. "I will not touch buying this stock at any price in the near term," Burry wrote. "I fear there are real problems with Nvidia that still will come to light." Nvidia stock was flat at roughly $162 in early trading on Monday, around a third below the all-time high of $243 it touched on October 6, less than six weeks ago. The company's market capitalization has tumbled from around $5.8 trillion at its peak to below $4 trillion. Burry — who pivoted from running a hedge fund to writing about his personal investments a year ago — said on Substack that he was concerned about Nvidia's purchase commitments, the future of the complex ecosystem it built, and its central role in the AI boom. Burry also said he was watching for "competitors and customers taking advantage" of Nvidia's troubles by negotiating lower prices and later purchases of chips. Those developments could shrink the company's profit margins and stop it from selling chips long before its customers have finished building the data centers to use them. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Elon Musk went further in an X post on Saturday, warning that many of Nvidia's deals were a "handshake with Jensen, not a written contract," and "at least some of those critical deals will be lost" without Huang at the helm. Jensen drove supply chain brilliantly at Nvidia, but many of those deals were a handshake with Jensen, not a written contract.                                   Without Jensen, at least some of those critical deals will be lost. Burry is best known for predicting and profiting from the crash of the mid-2000s housing bubble, after his prescient bet was chronicled in the book and movie "The Big Short." He wrote in a Friday post that he still owned put options on Nvidia stock that were scheduled to expire next February, and owned bearish puts on the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the Nasdaq 100, both of which count Nvidia as a major constituent. Burry has taken aim at Nvidia repeatedly over the past year, warning it's highly exposed to an AI slowdown as it has invested heavily in AI stocks, aggressively financed its customers' purchases of its chips, and essentially positioned itself as the lynchpin of the entire industry. Some Silicon Valley employees are about to see their financial circumstances switch from well-off to extremely wealthy. The year already saw the largest IPO ever, SpaceX, a record that could be broken later this month by Anthropic. For some employees, the windfalls could be life-changing but tied to a single company. Eric Franklin, a former Amazon employee who co-founded Prospero Wealth, a wealth advisory business focused on tech workers, said his firm has talked with several Anthropic employees who are "looking at $100 to $200 million outcomes." With wealth will come taxes, especially as employees try to diversify away from their biggest holdings: their employer. "If you think about the average Anthropic person or SpaceX person, their balance is their 401(k), maybe they've been doing their backdoor Roth IRA, and then they own Anthropic or SpaceX," said Thomas Kopelman, cofounder of AllStreet Wealth, who has managed the wealth of roughly 10 SpaceX employees. Selling those shares to diversify their investments could trigger enormous tax bills, especially for early employees who received shares at a fraction of their current value. In California, where profits from stock sales are taxed like regular income, those capital gains can face up to a 37.1% tax. Business Insider spoke with four financial advisors about the strategies tech workers can use to diversify their fortunes while minimizing their tax bills. Their advice ranged from simple psychological tricks to sophisticated investment strategies — and even buying car washes or shipping-container businesses. But the advisors agreed that before cashing out, employees should figure out how much money they actually need and build a plan around it. "You've won the game; you have all the wealth that you possibly could need," Koppelman said. "What do you want your lifestyle to look like and how much should we lock in day one?" From there, advisors can help a tech worker create a plan to minimize their tax costs and diversify their wealth. Timing is important to consider — employees and other insiders are usually restricted from selling their stock right when a company goes public. "It's almost never: 'Oh, well, let's use this one single product and boom, you're done," Franklin said, instead choosing different strategies for different timelines. Here are some of the tools tech workers are using to save on taxes as they look to stop being all in on their employers, from the simplest to the most complex. The simplest option is to change your mindset. If the only thing certain in life is death and taxes, you might as well come to terms with both. "The real challenge when you have these positions is you look at the value that's on your statement, and you think that's all your money," said Alex Shahidi, co-CIO of Evoke, a division of MAI Capital Management. "But in reality, there's a tax liability that's not written on your statement." Sophisticated strategies to try to defer and minimize those taxes introduce complexity which, "oftentimes creates unpleasant surprises in the future," he said. One approach for someone prioritizing simplicity, he said, is to sell some one year, some the next year, spreading it out over tax years. They could also focus on building a diversified portfolio, including assets such as gold, commodities, or other equities, to reduce their dependence on their employer's stock. One "completely psychological" technique is to wait until the stock appreciates enough to cover the expected tax bill and then sell it. "Then the market paid the tax for you," Shahidi said. "It actually works. Even very smart people are like, 'I just feel better about that.'" The first obvious tool for any tax-aware investor is direct indexing. Instead of holding an index fund that tracks, for example, the S&P 500, investors buy individual stocks that roughly mirror that index's performance. This allows them to roughly achieve the same returns as the index while using losses to offset gains in a process known as tax-loss harvesting. With smaller positions, this is usually where Prospero Wealth's Franklin will start. "That's a place where they can feel like they're getting something beyond what they would generally do themselves," he said. "It's something that's easy to explain." For wealthier clients, advisors may recommend direct indexing "on steroids," Franklin said, or long-short indexing, which introduces leverage and short selling to increase tax losses or to try to outperform an index intentionally. Long-short strategies have higher fees and can often be riskier than direct indexing. "The bigger the portfolio, the more long-short makes sense," Kopelman said. A popular way to access your stock value without immediately selling and paying taxes is to borrow against your shares. Investors could take out a loan against their shares, but rates aren't fixed and therefore create a lot of risk. Instead, advisors said there are other ways to borrow, with their help. Franklin gave the example of a client at a recently IPO'd tech company who decided to pledge a third of their position, $8 million, to a bank in exchange for instant liquidity of up to 90% of the shares' value. "You get the cash immediately, and then you can immediately diversify that and start doing tax-loss harvesting," Franklin said. This will allow you to generate much higher tax losses than you would if you were just investing with whatever cash you have on hand. Franklin's client was using what's called a variable pre-paid forward, a contract that allows you to delay selling your stock for 3 to 5 years while getting the money now. Of course, there's a risk that the stock price will have gone down in that time, and you could lose money when you repay it. A classic way to diversify a single stock is to use an exchange fund. An exchange fund allows investors to pool their appreciated shares with other investors' holdings, giving them exposure to a more diversified portfolio without immediately triggering capital gains taxes. The main caveat is that it comes with a seven-year lockup, fees, and sometimes a waitlist, depending on which stock you have. "You almost never can get into them by the position size that you want," Kopelman said. "It's an option, but it's one that I've never had a client do." Some of the advisors said they avoid exchange funds for this reason, though Eric Franklin said they can be a good tool for money you know you won't need until seven years in the future. From there, tax strategies can get even more esoteric. One option, said Gabriel Shahin, founder of Falcon Wealth Advisors, is investing in opportunity zone funds, which pool investment capital into low-income areas while allowing you to defer tax. "The problem is you're not going to get the same juice for investing in an op zone as you are in a tech company, let alone a private tech company," Shahin, whose firm manages $1.8 billion, said, meaning you really need to be focused on lowering tax for that to make sense. You can also buy a business, Shahin said, and use the paper losses from buying or operating the business to offset up to $512,000 in income, the current IRS limit for excess business losses that a married couple can claim. The tax code's bonus depreciation rules, which allow you to deduct up to 100% of the value of certain types of property, allow you to supercharge that with even more paper losses. There are a few catches: you need to pay with your time to pass participation rules, such as spending 500 hours a year on the activity. This also requires you to set up a separate LLC and do taxes on it, Shahin said. Shahin said investors adopting this strategy often buy shipping container businesses, car washes, or convenience stores. The most popular, he said, are solar businesses that allow you also to get solar tax credits. There are some "cool and gnarly" strategies out there, but they really require help from a professional, especially one with a tax focus like his own, Shahin said. "You can't afford to be cheap," Shahin said. "You think it's expensive to hire a professional? Try doing it yourself as an amateur." Jump to

Workers should be able to take paid time off to prepare for national emergencies, a House of Lords committee has recommended. In a report, the peers said a new "civic resilience leave" would enable employees to undertake training and emergency volunteering without losing income. It is one of a slew of recommendations from a 12-strong committee that has been examining how to make the UK better able to respond to crises including war, power cuts, cyber-attacks and natural disasters. It comes after the government launched a campaign calling on the British public to stock up on tinned food and bottled water to be prepared for emergencies. In a report published on Monday, peers on the national resilience committee will say the government's campaign, launched last month, was a "welcome step". But it will argue that Britain is still underprepared for potential disruption, adding that the public did not have the "full picture" about potential threats from Russia, China and Iran, including cyber attacks. It will recommend that all local councils should draw up registers of volunteers with "relevant skills and capabilities" to help out during crises, as well as lists of buildings in their area that could be used as emergency shelters. The government should also launch a national campaign for registered volunteers and civil reservists, it added, modelled on the programme launched by the NHS for "volunteer responders" during the Covid pandemic. It noted that the previous government floated the idea of a "civilian reservist cadre" to help out in times of crisis in its 2021 defence review, but this was dropped when the report was updated two years later. Although some employers offer time off to staff who volunteer, there is currently no legal entitlement to paid leave for those in roles such as coastguard rescue, firefighting, or the St John Ambulance. Army reservists can claim up to Â£400 a day, external from the government to cover lost pay if they are mobilised, but employers do not have to allow time off for training - although some choose to do so. In their report, the peers said a new right to paid time off could cover "approved" training and volunteering, without specifying exact roles. They did not recommend an exact leave entitlement, instead suggesting that Labour ministers should work with employers to design "proportionate arrangements" for workers. Elsewhere in their report, peers recommended the government should send booklets to every household with information about what to do in a crisis, modelled on those sent to homes in Sweden and Denmark. In its evidence to the inquiry, the government said it planned to provide information through its website - but peers rejected this approach, adding it risked "excluding some groups" and would not work during prolonged periods of disruption. The peers also recommended the development of a multilingual "public preparedness app" to access official guidance on preparing for emergencies. It should also allow users to automatically share their location with emergency authorities, similar to the 112 Suomi app in Finland, they added.   The Cabinet Office said it would "carefully review" the report, whilst insisting the government was already taking action to improve crisis resilience. It pointed to work already under way to update departments' secret defence plans, known as the "war book", and a major exercise scheduled for next year to test the the UK's resilience for war. The government also recently announced new measures to protect the UK's undersea internet cables, including powers for officials to inspect cable landing stations owned and operated by telecom companies. Warren Buffett's final weeks as Berkshire Hathaway chairman were fittingly free of fireworks. The low-key investor's conglomerate only made minor tweaks to its stock portfolio during the three months to September 30, a regulatory filing showed on Monday. Berkshire cut several smaller positions, including Capital One by 62%, VeriSign by 34%, Nucor by 15%, and Kroger by 10%. It once again trimmed its Bank of America stake by about 6% to around 456 million shares, worth close to $25 billion as of September 30. On the other hand, it boosted its Delta Air Lines stake by 12% to around 65 million shares, worth about $5.4 billion at September's close. It also bolstered its bet on homebuilder Lennar, increasing its volume of Class B shares by 86% and Class A shares by 99%. Those purchases propelled the total value of the position from $1.2 billion to $2.1 billion. The only new position was Bending Spoons, but the Italian tech conglomerate previously disclosed Berkshire invested in its IPO this summer, then took part in a private placement that raised its stake to about 4%. It's unclear whether Buffett, CEO Greg Abel, or investment manager Ted Weschler were behind the portfolio changes. Buffett said this summer that he initiated Berkshire's stake in Alphabet last year, a holding worth $36 billion at the end of September. The disclosure came hours after Buffett announced he was donating $5.5 billion of his Berkshire stock to four of his family's foundations, in line with his plan to gift his entire Berkshire fortune by 2034. Buffett, 96, championed kindness in a surprisingly short Thanksgiving message, telling his shareholders they'd "heard plenty" from him in the letter announcing his retirement as chairman in September. Berkshire investors were prepared for a pretty humdrum third-quarter portfolio update. The company's recent third-quarter earnings revealed that it bought $2.4 billion of stocks and sold $2.8 billion worth during the three-month period — tiny sums relative to its $335 billion stock portfolio. However, Berkshire did spend a record $9.6 billion on stock buybacks last quarter. Those purchases look well-timed so far, as Berkshire's share price has jumped 19% since the start of October, closing at record highs of around $593 a share. Buffett — who ran Berkshire for six decades before stepping down as CEO and chairman in the past year — struggled to find bargains during his final years in charge as both public and private company valuations soared. That made quiet quarters the norm, with Berkshire making few stock purchases or acquisitions. Jump to

At the dawn of the consumer digital camera age, manufacturers tested this new market with a wide array of interesting and unorthodox designs. This era only lasted a few years before they moved toward making models that resembled the 35mm cameras the consumers were used to. Sony’s Mavica offerings were particularly unusual, because they eschewed Flash storage for the then-ubiquitous 3.5″ floppy disk. Where there are files, there might be a need to share them, so [Bigcrimping] has created floppy3.5. It’s a NAS for digital Mavica disks.  Inside, along with the floppy drive, is an interesting dual-processor architecture. An RP2354 runs a Greaseweazle port and reads the floppy drive, to the extent that it can operate as a standalone Greaseweazle device through its USB port. An ESP32-S3 is hooked into the RP2354 via SPI and performs the tasks of decoding the raw floppy data, copying the resulting files to an SD card, and sharing the images over a web interface. There’s also a pleasingly retro display intended to look like a Walkman display of the same era. This is an interesting project, both for Mavica owners for whom it’s very cool indeed, and as a portable Greaseweazle peripheral in its own right. More than once, we’ve had a random old floppy for which this appliance would have been a huge time saver. As we said earlier this year, it’s now imperative that you copy that floppy! I have a sony mavica but no battery for it! It has a power in but it will not function without the battery.I work at a bus company. Lost and found items not picked up after 3 months are auctioned off amongst staff (proceeds go to charity) and someone lost a Mavica on the bus in 2024… With a shot battery, so it was not a day-to-day user My Mavica uses Sony Info-Lithium batteries and those are still available. Both as clones and 1st party spares. So you very likely can get a battery for it. The FD Mavica I have also uses memory sticks.  So not all of them skipped the flash. I still have the camera and last I checked it still worked (battery probably needs charged/replaced).  Only issue is the battery door is messed up a bit.  I remember working at a retailer that sold the old FD Mavicas. They had a great optical zoom but it was wasted on a device that only took, if memory serves, 0.333 megapixel photos? As for this device, is there something about it that gears its function specifically to disks from the Mavica cameras and not 3.5″ floppies in the broader sense? In photography, the size of the sensor matters. Because the bigger it is, the more light it can catch. That means that an older/lower-res (but bigger) sensor has fewer image noise. Generally speaking, I mean. I was hoping this would be in a form factor of a floppy and live its live inside Mavica without the need to shuffle floppies around. I wonder if anyone has ever done that. It’s probably harder to interface with the floppy read-write head than it is to skip the middle man and interface with the thing the floppy drive talks to. I know there was someone who modified diskettes to include a SD-card and a floppy drive to read them, but what I (and you) mean is more akin the wired (or bluetooth) cassettes you can put in your car stereo. That’s already a thing. It’s called FlashPath. I believe it even supports the mavica series directly.  Comment Name Email Website   Turn on JavaScript to leave a comment. Nvidia faces potential 30 percent value loss without Jensen Huang, say market analysts amid stock downturn. Save Share Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and other Silicon Valley insiders are calling on chipmaker Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang, who resigned last week from the company he cofounded. Musk is one of the 177,000 signatories to a petition titled “Stand With Jensen”, calling for the reinstatement of the executive, who resigned following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. “We are current and former NVIDIA employees, partners, shareholders, and supporters. We write with gratitude for Jensen Huang and with a clear demand to the Board: bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA’s best interests,” the letter published on the petition’s website said.      More privately, a group of Silicon Valley insiders is pushing to get Huang back in the role, with the Financial Times reporting that Huang is considering a comeback. The paper reported that an unnamed group of Silicon Valley insiders has put together a so-called war room and is lobbying the White House for support which is a move that may have been successful. “A lot of people are asking Jensen, they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” United States President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday. Trump’s reported trades this year suggest he held between $13m and $62m in Nvidia stock as of the end of August, the Washington Post reported on Monday, citing a review of his financial disclosures. But Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing Jensen back, the Reuters news agency reported citing three unnamed people. Much of Nvidia’s value is tied to Huang, with analysts estimating that the company could lose as much as 25 to 30 percent of its value without him. Nvidia’s stock was trending downward in early trading on Wall Street, with US markets opening down 2.3 percent on the day. Over the last five days, the stock has dropped 8.5 percent and is down more than 25.7 percent over the last month. The developments come as the White House moves to designate Nvidia, along with more than two dozen other companies, as “national champions” in the artificial intelligence industry, a new initiative intended to help the company secure more business overseas, according to reporting by The Wall Street Journal. They also come as the Trump administration issued a rule on Monday that it would restrict China’s access to chips made by companies including Nvidia, as Trump begins a trip to China where he will meet with President Xi Jinping. The restrictions are aimed at preventing Chinese companies from “circumventing” existing limits by using data centres in Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia and Thailand to train their AI models. “The rule is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the Department of Commerce said in a statement. The new rule comes as the Commerce Department is scrambling to demonstrate that it is cracking down on Chinese access to sensitive US technology, following reports that the agency under Secretary Howard Lutnick turned a blind eye to the smuggling of advanced Nvidia AI chips into China. This video can not be played Watch: The two sides of daily life in Shenzhen At 27, Huang Shihua is living the Chinese Dream. He works as an engineer for a leading humanoid robot company in Shenzhen. The sprawling south-eastern metropolis is touted by China as the origin story for a high-tech future powered by artificial intelligence, robotics and home-grown innovation. Drones soar across the sky to deliver your dinner, driverless taxis play relaxing music as you journey to your destination, and robots don't just hand you a cappuccino - they explain the origin of your coffee beans. "We have created a miracle in Shenzhen," Huang says, surrounded by humanoid robots making coffee and playing chess. "Many young people from across China, full of passion and dreams, have flocked here." Now they all spend their days figuring out ways to make robots smarter. Shenzhen, China's AI-powered "city of dreams", has long been a place of opportunity The Chinese call Shenzhen the "city of dreams". The moniker suits it: one of China's wealthiest, it is close to Hong Kong and the place where the country's explosive growth took off decades ago.  Its manufacturing inventory mirrors China's rise: cabbage patch dolls, then TVs, later iPhones, electric vehicles, drones and now the robots, which are drawing Huang and a new generation of Chinese ambition. The "miracles" these young engineers are chasing are central to Xi Jinping's bold vision for China. So where better to show it off than Shenzhen, which will be centre-stage when US President Donald Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and others arrive for a global economic summit this week. And yet there is another side to this flashy, coastal city, a side that they will not get to see. Drive away from towering skyscrapers towards Shajing and Songgang, once the source of much of the world's electronics, and you will run into the challenges confronting Xi's China. Young, ambitious developers  have turned Shenzhen into a "miracle", Huang says "Everyone feels life is hard," one construction worker tells us. "Lots of factories have relocated and workers lost their jobs." China remains exceptionally good at making things - and Shenzhen is proof of that. But the city also holds the evidence for what ails the world's second-largest economy. The property crisis is not over, denting confidence in the future. This is one of China's most expensive cities but even here, our taxi driver tells us, his house is now only worth a third of its original price. A weak property market and sluggish consumer spending mean many households are buying less. Factories are increasingly relying on exports while many manufacturers have cut production, downsized, automated or moved elsewhere in search of cheaper labour.  The result is a growing number of workers turning to temporary jobs in the gig economy, often with lower pay and fewer benefits. "Shenzhen is not a magic place," says one delivery driver in his 40s, unwilling to give his name. "Some say there is gold everywhere in Shenzhen, but it's not like that anymore. It's not a city where you can come and thrive. If you don't work hard, you won't have anything." The BBC spent several days in Shenzhen exploring these two very different sides of China's progress: on the one hand is the dazzling promise of AI, and on the other are the anxieties of workers who worry if there will be room for them in the future it creates. Delivery drones in Shenzhen have become a tourist attraction    Wednesday is sandwich and bubble tea day in the offices of DexForce Technologies. The elevator is packed with young engineers and developers headed to the right floor for the free carbs and sugar that will fuel their afternoon. They jostle past their creations en route: human-sized, yellow robots whose limbs fill every available corner. "I believe that in a decade, robots will be able to better serve humanity by taking on highly repetitive or even dangerous tasks," Huang says. That could be anything from serving coffee to working in mines, and they are being trained for all of that in this laboratory for the future, where machines flail, jerk or lurch into motion as they learn to behave. To him, "Shenzhen is another 'America'. Because, much like in the US, many young people have been able to realise their dreams and earn the wealth they desire." This is what Xi wants to hear as he pushes China to lead the world in advanced tech. Shenzhen has indeed long been a place for seeking opportunity but Huang and his colleagues want to do much more. They don't simply want to continue China's manfuacturing supremacy. They want to transform it. DexForce Technologies is brimming with robots - and faith in a tech-charged future Beyond making "our lives more convenient and comfortable", Huang sees AI as helping "the entire world become one family - a global village. AI has the potential to foster equality and the prospect of AI-driven equality is, to me, the most exciting possibility of all." Smiling enthusiastically, he explains how he hopes that robots can help emerging economies across Africa and South East Asia catch up by reshaping their production lines too. This tech-charged optimism, which is everywhere in the building, jars with the uncertainty elsewhere in Shenzhen, where robots are nowhere to be found. Yet. But that's just the first of the differences. In Huang's side of the city, tech and finance workers stroll to the office after a morning workout, sipping coffee that probably cost more than 30 yuan ($4.50; Â£3.40).  On the other side, scooters whizz through streets piled high with goods being shuttled between factories as vendors sell whole breakfast plates of spicy noodles for under 3 yuan. The two sides of Shenzhen are a contrast in more ways than one Outside one of the city's tallest skyscrapers, 50-year-old Ms Lu has a phone to her ear and a pen in her right hand while grabbing a bag with her left from a delivery driver. She shouts four key numbers at her co-worker: instructions for another Chinese woman who is waiting to take the delivery up the elevator to someone sitting at their desk. This is the lunchtime rush outside SEG plaza, home to 70 storeys of thousands of tenants. Lu used to be one of them. "I ran a small business on the second floor. I sold circuit boards," she says. "But it's getting so hard to do business these days and the rental fees got higher." Often likened to China's Silicon Valley, Shenzhen has seen rents soar with the influx of new capital, squeezing out smaller, more traditional businesses. At 50, Ms Lu couldn't find another job until the delivery drivers came to her with a plan. The wait for the elevator can take half an hour â wasted money for a driver trying to fill as many orders as possible. So Ms Lu became a new layer in the ever-evolving gig economy. "The delivery drivers bring food here to the building entrance. We pick it up and take it upstairs. The drivers pay us 2 yuan per order," she explains, always on the move. Delivery drivers earn between four to eight yuan per order, so Ms Lu gets a decent cut of their earnings. "The lunch peak time only lasts two or three hoursâ¦ if they use our service, they can get more orders done, and we can earn some money as well. But the market is bad. These days I only earn around 200 yuan per day." Ms Lu, standing in the middle, joined the delivery business after losing her job An estimated 200 million Chinese workers, roughly 40% of the urban labour force, now depend on some form of gig work. Many delivery drivers in Shenzhen tell us they chose temporary work because there are fewer opportunities at factories than before. "We need to adapt to the situation we find ourselves in," one driver told us, "rather than waiting for it to adapt to our needs." A group of them are waiting outside the gates of an e-cigarette factory to make industrial deliveries. Others nod in agreement. Another driver says he has little choice: "I have two children to raise and I can't stop working. I don't have time to think about anything else." Permanent jobs often require contributions to social security and pension, which reduces take-home pay. But gig work means more cash in hand and flexibile hours.  "Most workers prefer jobs with a fixed, shorter-term duration. It allows them the flexibility to resign and leave whenever they choose; they have no desire to become permanent employees," says job agent Li Xiaohe. Increasingly, he puts up boards on pavements advertising temporary factory jobs that pay around 22 yuan an hour for assembling small electronics.  Although agents also appear to be in a shrinking pool, with several former shop fronts shuttered: yet another sign of the downturn in traditional manufacturing. "Our business is perhaps not as optimistic as it once was," Li admits. "We can feel the effects of Shenzhen going through a transformation." Li, a labour agent who advertises temorary jobs, says his own business has been struggling That transformation is hard to miss. Drones buzz above the lush grounds of a purpose built "talent park" along the city's waterfront, dipping and darting as they deliver meals to a dedicated platform. Phones held high, tourists capture them landing with their lunch. "This is amazing. The technology is just great. I wish we had this back at home," exclaims one Canadian tourist. Our coffee order - for a five-yuan delivery - arrives in just over 15 minutes, the drone landing seamlessly so I can pick up my order. "I heard that many years ago, Shenzhen was a fishing village," says Anle, who is visiting from Vietnam. "Ha â no more fishing village," he laughs as he orders milk tea to be delivered by drone for him and his wife. For all the ingenuity on display, it feels more like a demonstration of what is possible rather than a mundane reality. The deliveries, which are only possible in certain locations, stop at 20:00 local time. The driverless cars, which need a separate app to order, are also a novelty â they even offer you a massage when you are on your way. At night, in the glow of a thousand dancing lights, the drones take on a different role. They fly above the park warning people to behave and not cause trouble. Shenzhen still draws millions of migrant workers from across China     Far from the glittering skyline, workers gather around plastic tables outside restaurants serving cheap hotpot and seafood skewers.  There are more expensive restaurants along the street, but they too have taken a hit. One owner told us business is down by more than 70% as workers are hesitant to splurge on dinner. Many of them have spent decades here, including 58-year-old construction worker Mr Wu. He arrived in Shenzhen from Sichuan in the 1990s not long after China opened the city up to foreign businesses. He was among millions of migrants from poorer provinces who came to work on production lines or build skyscrapers. They are still coming.  All the people we spoke to came from elsewhere. They often labour up to 14 hours a day and live in shared dormitories, sustained by the prospect of stable work and decent pay to send home to their families. Dormitories like these have houses workers over the decades For these workers, the Covid pandemic, when Chinese manufacturing hit a record low, appears to have been the first turning point.  "After Covid, our salary dropped by at least a third," Mr Wu recalls, after which wages never fully recovered. "I will continue to work," he adds. "As long as you keep working, you will have an income. More salary or not? It doesn't matter. As long as you keep working, you will have an income. If the economy slows down, we all slow down. If it grows, we all get better." For all these decades, Shenzhen lived up to its bargain: work hard and your life would improve.  But now, in a city that is being redefined by automation and AI, that old promise feels less secure. Following a record share price fall Tech giant Intel are being taken to court for allegedly "misleading" their investors about the sheer scale of the impact of generative AI-fuelled component price hikes on PC sales. The class action lawsuit in question claims that Intel's distribution and manufacturing partners have had to deal with "a massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", and that the gains from Intel's investments in AI datacenters aren't enough to make up for slowing sales of PCs to regular Josephines who just want fancy boxes they can play Deadlock on. All this follows Intel's last round of quarterly results, in which they announced a significant revenue fall; this triggered an Intel stock price drop from $92.07 per share on October 29th to $65.76 per share the next day, which this week's lawsuit characterises as "the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years". The lawyers in question are from Robbins LLP, who specialise in "shareholder, whistleblower, antitrust, & consumer litigation". In a press release, they say they've filed suit on behalf of anybody who bought Intel stock from July 23rd to October 29th this year. The suit claims that Intel neglected to tell investors that falling PC and component sales were having a "materially greater negative impact" on their third financial quarter 2026 Client Computing and Physical AI Groupresults than Intel had previously stated – to the tune of "hundreds of millions of dollars" in revenue shrinkage, compared to the previous quarter, with the situation still expected to "worsen". They also accuse the company of keeping schtum about the aforesaid "massive glut of unwanted PC inventory", together with the fact that "any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset by the negative effects on the Company’s business and financial results resulting from the PC market slowdown and the excess inventory buildup described above." Finally, they say Intel bosses have failed to disclose that they're struggling to procure an adequate supply of substrates – that is, materials used to create the base layer of chips, circuit boards and similar components. As such, the lawyers claim, Intel couldn't "ramp up production to meet data center CPU demand even if the Company chose to divert production resources because of a slowdown in PC-related sales." Once the Godzilla of personal computing, Intel haven't been having a brilliant few years. Back in 2024, they recorded a multi-billion dollar quarterly loss, pushing then-CEO Pat Gelsinger to resign. As regards sales of gaming PCs, they've fallen behind AMD, though they've reportedly taken some ground back recently as regards desktop CPUs. As regards graphics cards, they have long been dwarfed by Nvidia. Any Intel investor who wants a piece of that lawsuit has until January 12th 2027 to sign up as a lead plaintiff – that is, a court appointee who represents the interests of other class members. As regards us little people who don't buy stock in huge technology corporations, all this merely continues the weird existential crisis wrought upon 'traditional' gaming and computing hardware by the feckless quest to sell a better chatbot. Late last month, some 60,000 Microsoft employees were presented with a choice that could transform the trajectory of their careers: accept a buyout offer or remain at their jobs. Microsoft has said it expects fewer than 5% of eligible employees to accept the voluntary exit offer. The tech giant's move to downsize comes as many companies restructure or shrink their workforces via buyouts or voluntary retirement packages, sometimes citing AI as a rationale. Business Insider spoke to nine people who have previously accepted voluntary exit offers about their decision-making process and their top tips for people grappling with the same choice. They range in age from their 30s to their 60s and mentioned considerations ranging from finances and healthcare coverage to time, family, and identity. We reached out to their former employers for comment. Google and Microsoft declined to comment. Verizon confirmed former employment. Here's what nine people had to say about life after buyouts. Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience at the time: Principal group engineering manager, spent almost 25 years at Microsoft in various roles. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks. Jay Ongg wasn't thinking about retiring, but when Microsoft offered a voluntary retirement program in the spring, with employees' last day being in July, he began to think more about his future. It was a tough decision to make after more than two decades at Microsoft, where he said he worked on Xbox, Windows Mobile, Teams, and other products. It would mean saying goodbye to a large part of his identity. He decided to take the chance. "It was kind of scary, but I'm actually a pretty optimistic guy," Ongg said. Since then, he's been exercising more, experimenting with large language models to keep flexing his technical skills, and working on a personal finance AI assistant. His advice for workers debating whether to take a buyout is to take stock of your life, goals, and values. Think about yourself and your family. Whatever you decide, you need to feel good about it at the end of the day, he said. What are you trading off if you take it versus not?" Ongg said. "We all make decisions based on incomplete information, and there's no crime in doing that. We never have complete information." Company: Google Title and years of experience: Core engineering senior program manager, spent more than 5 years at the company and left when she was 36. Offer details: Google buyout for US employees in June 2025 Donnetta Kay Hagist didn't consider Google's voluntary exit offer until she got coffee with a colleague who revealed that he, a respected team leader, was accepting it. Shocked, she called her husband to tell him she, too, wanted to leave. "I believe that things happen for a reason, and this was the push I needed to bet on myself," Hagist said, adding that she wasn't scared to break out of the so-called "golden handcuffs." Given her husband's stable job, finances and healthcare were sorted — they calculated that she wouldn't need to land a new role until the spring. After her last day at Google in October 2025, Hagist spent a lot of time with her daughters, but quickly got nervous about the job market and started applying for new roles. A friend advised her to relax and take a well-deserved solo trip to Switzerland. She went on the vacation; she signed up for a Hyrox and a half-marathon; she spent more time on her relationships. In November, a mechanical services company, The Arcticom Group, reached out about a senior director role. She landed the job. Hagist said those considering a buyout should make sure their basic needs are met, and then ask themselves whether they're OK with their next three years mirroring their previous three years. "If you feel called to do something different, I encourage you to go explore it. The world is so big," she said. Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience: Lead e-discovery program manager, spent more than 12 years at the company and left when he was 58. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks. For Jonathan Monheit, Microsoft's voluntary retirement offer was a "winner winner, chicken dinner" moment. He and his wife already had plans to move from Seattle to Dallas, where they were building a new home. Monheit had gotten permission to work remotely through the end of 2026 and then planned to leave the company. He received Microsoft's buyout offer in the spring and realized he'd essentially be paid the same amount as if he'd worked through December. After his final day on July 2, Monheit and his wife drove to their new home, stopping at national parks throughout the 10-day journey. They spent the next few weeks settling in before jetting off to Singapore, Thailand, and Toronto. Now, around four months after leaving Microsoft, Monheit is starting to get a bit restless. "You're used to having things drive you every day. There are moments when I'm like, 'OK, what do I do now?' But in general, it's been healthy. I sleep better. I eat better," he said. He's started exploring new jobs. Ideally, Monheit said his next move is to become a consultant, helping companies approach e-discovery more efficiently. Company: Google Title and years of experience: Head of YouTube partner operations in EMEA, spent 17 years at the company and left when she was 41. Offer details: UK voluntary exit package in late 2025 Fernanda Monteiro was preparing to return to Google from maternity leave in February when an email arrived about a voluntary exit offer. She had initially dismissed it when it hit her inbox in December 2025, but then thought back to research she'd done about the identity transition that accompanies leaving Big Tech. She started thinking of the package as a springboard for a career pivot. Money was the most obvious question — abandoning her salary would mean rethinking finances, but at the same time, childcare in London is expensive. Monteiro could also feel burnout triggers creeping back in, so she started talking to former bosses, close friends, and family about the decision. "Closing my eyes and picturing myself going back to work and being a mother of two — I couldn't see myself in that position anymore. That gave me the answer," Monteiro said. She signed the buyout offer in late January and said she remained an employee until the end of April, though she never returned from maternity leave. She spent the first few weeks ticking off a checklist of corporate errands: scheduling medical appointments, sorting out login permissions, accessing personal documents. It was a bumpy emotional road, pocked with doubt and the exhaustion of a new baby. Now, Monteiro said she's confident in her choice. She has time to spend with her daughters as she builds a business as a career transition advisor, helping individuals and companies navigate transitions out of Big Tech. Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience at the time: Principal product manager, spent roughly 29 non-continuous years at Microsoft and left when he was 60. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks. Scott Thurlow started at Microsoft in the '90s, then worked for Expedia for a few years before boomeranging to Microsoft in 2007. He lived in Canada from 2014 to 2017 as Microsoft expanded into Vancouver. In 2023, he decided to pursue a doctorate alongside his job. By the time of Microsoft's Voluntary Retirement Program, or VRP, offer, Thurlow was mostly done with coursework and getting ready to begin the research portion on how organizations scale human oversight of AI. "There were two problems with staying around at Microsoft," he said. "Problem No. 1 is time, and problem No. 2 is imagine the conversation when I approach Google saying I want to understand how they're solving these problems if I'm also a Microsoft employee. I'm expecting they won't be entirely receptive to discussing things with me." He said the VRP, which he described as a "self-layoff," accelerated his departure from Microsoft by six months to a year. He left the company in July. Thurlow is hoping to wrap up his doctorate by summer of 2028. After that, he might consult, as he had already set up a practice in anticipation of consulting work, or he might work for someone else. His advice: If you're already working toward something else, a buyout could be a good opportunity. If you're unhappy with your workplace, consider taking it, too. He recommends having something to do after the buyout. "It can be a professional, it can be technical, it can be volunteering at social or charitable institutions," he said. "Just make sure you have something to invest yourself into so that you stay engaged with your life and your community." Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience: Principal site reliability engineering manager, spent more than 26 years as a full-time employee and left when he was 50. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks. Justin Long started preparing for life after Microsoft after witnessing rounds of layoffs in 2023 and 2025. He'd paid off his house, was saving more, and planned to become an individual contributor again instead of a manager. When the company offered him a voluntary retirement package earlier this year, he brought it up to his wife. "She was shocked because she knows how much I loved working there. But at the same time, it was getting less enjoyable," Long said. Long had aimed to retire at 55 but could stop working early with the package, especially because it offered years of healthcare. His wife got more comfortable with the idea after they met with the financial advisor who had been helping them plan for retirement. "All the right things fit into place. Not any one thing made me make the choice," Long said, adding that he could feel AI burnout building. Long rested for a week after his contract ended and then went on a trip to Hawaii with family, where he worked on his photography and scuba certification. For Long, this is true retirement — he'd only return to work if he started doing something new. He's started physical therapy for long-ignored shoulder pain; he's been cooking more, including banana oatmeal cookies from TikTok and split pea soup with Japanese sweet potatoes; he began volunteering for the King County Democrats. Long encouraged those grappling with a similar choice, especially at Microsoft, to consider their relationship to their jobs in a period of rapid transition. Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience at the time: Business strategy and sales program leader, spent nearly 26 years at Microsoft and left when he was 56. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks. Shawn Mrzena said he only planned to be in the tech industry for a decade. He ended up working at Microsoft for about 26 years. "I always say that Microsoft was my mini MBA. That's where I learned about business," he said. When Microsoft offered the VRP earlier this year, he had already planned to retire early or pivot to something new. He experienced several technological shifts during his career, and the rapid pace and demand of AI wasn't one he was excited about. "I just decided, 'You know what? I'm going to leave it to the next generation,'" he said. "This is not something I want to invest my energy and time into. I'm not waking up excited in the morning." Mrzena said he's busier now than when he had a job, but busy doing things he wants to do. "I'll purchase something that I'm interested in, like an instructional guide on building something, and I will spend my day fabricating, learning, building, arguing with AI or the book," he said. He is already exploring semi-retirement involving work in the trades. "I've always wanted to learn how to fabricate," he said. "So I still am looking at enrolling in our community college locally here and getting a welder certificate." For those debating a buyout, he said, you already know if it's time, especially if you are unhappy or hanging on by a thread: "This should be a quick decision. You know if you want to stay." Company: Microsoft Title and years of experience at the time: Principal group product manager for Microsoft Teams, spent more than 23 non-continuous years at the company and left when he was 56. Offer details: Employees who took the Voluntary Retirement Program were offered up to five years of health insurance coverage, with Microsoft paying for the first year; stock vesting; and base pay determined by seniority and tenure, capped at 39 weeks.  Mike RothKugel worked at Microsoft for over 20 years, with a few years at Google in the 2010s. For his last nine years at Microsoft, he worked on the Teams product group. He said he was planning on retiring in about two years when the VRP was offered earlier this year. After discussing it with his financial advisor, his thoughts turned to time. "I missed a lot of time with my kids growing up, and I was like, 'Hey, maybe I can get some of that time back right now, at least spend a little bit more time with them while they're still around, they're still in college, they're still on my payroll,'" he said. He said the VRP's healthcare offering — first year of healthcare paid for by Microsoft, followed by four years of COBRA at the person's expense — was a big factor. "That really helped put my mind at ease a bit," he said. "It'll still end before I'm eligible for Medicare or anything, but we'll cross that bridge when we get to it." Before the VRP, RothKugel's family bought a vacation house in Roche Harbor on San Juan Island, Washington. His kids are at college, so he spends his days with his wife and bulldog. He's been remodeling the San Juan home, taking calls for consulting and advisory work, and helping promote his sister's distillery, the Striped Pig in Charleston, South Carolina. "I've started to get a little bit of that itch of I really want to get back into work, but I'm avoiding that," he said. "I'm going to try to avoid that for as long as possible." Company: Verizon Title and years of experience: Senior client partner in business development, spent six years at the company and left when she was 54. Offer details: 3 weeks of pay per year of service, and continued healthcare for the number of weeks of separation pay, rounded up to the nearest whole number. When Bobbie Ziemer saw Verizon's voluntary exit offer in summer 2024, she knew what the severance money would go toward: the remaining college tuition for two of her kids and her nest egg. A self-identified "grinder," Ziemer said she'd never spent more than a few weeks without a job and assumed this time would be no different. After weighing whether she was OK with never working at Verizon again, as the package stipulated, Ziemer decided to stop working at the company in early September. Ziemer immediately started updating her résumé and reaching out to her network. Yet her optimism and funds dwindled as the job search dragged on, leading her to sign up for Medicaid and forgo luxuries like the hair salon. "It made me second-guess my talent, second-guess my experience, second-guess my value, second-guess my performance and achievements," Ziemer said. She landed a job in June but was recently laid off. Despite the challenges, Ziemer said she doesn't regret taking the buyout offer. Anyone considering a similar choice should take an honest look at their finances, she said, and prepare for more unemployment than they'd want. Ziemer suggests asking one question above all others: "Can you survive for up to a year if you don't get a job right away?" Jump to

The pain in AI stocks may stretch on for a while, one longtime strategist is warning. Jim Paulsen, the former chief investment strategist at The Leuthold Group, says he sees a deeper stock correction looming, even as the market aims to regain its footing after a brutal sell-off in Nvidia jolted investors this week. Paulsen is worried about a stark bifurcation between tech stocks and those in other sectors, with tech vastly outperforming most other areas of the market over the past several years. That gap will need to narrow before the bull market can be considered on solid footing, Paulsen told Business Insider in an interview, speculating there could be a reset that involves tech stocks tanking more than 20% as investors reset their expectations. A tech sell-off of that magnitude could drag the broader S&P 500 down by around 10% to 15%, he estimated, pointing to tech's outsize importance in the benchmark index. The upper end of Paulsen's forecast implies the S&P 500 dropping as low as 6,400, a level that hasn't been seen since stocks swooned in the first months of the US-Iran war. "We've had truly tech and telecom go up, and everything else is sort of debatable whether there's really been a bull market," Paulsen said. "My point is that the growth rate there is so phenomenal that even if it doesn't fall apart, it probably can't sustain those levels," he later added. Paulsen pointed to the growing gap between what he called the "new era" stocks in the market, his shorthand for the information technology sector, and "old era" stocks, a label that encompasses everything else. Over the last five years, growth in the S&P 500's tech sector has outpaced most other areas of the index, soaring 107% since November 2021. The one exception is energy, thanks largely to the spike in oil prices that followed the start of the Iran war. Paulsen said the split looks even more extreme than the bifurcation between tech stocks and other sectors at the peak of the dot-com bubble, and is unsustainable for a few reasons. Strategists, meanwhile, have been eyeing an earnings slowdown in 2027 as hyperscalers pull back on capex spending. Goldman Sachs estimated that S&P 500 earnings per share growth could drop from a pace of around 36% a year to 11%, falling below the historic average of around 15% annual EPS growth. If growth were to slow, the tech sector would likely be repriced rapidly, Paulsen said, pointing to how concentrated investors have been in tech. "If tech really hits the air pocket, it goes down radically," he said. The silver lining is that once the heat gets taken out of the tech sector, Paulsen sees the AI trade thriving again. The idea is that the US needs to let some steam out of the new-era economy in order for the Fed to lower rates, boosting the old-era side and allowing those stocks to recover. "Maybe the older economy does better for a while while the new era grows, but at a slower, more refreshing pace," he said of the market's long-term path. Stocks appear to be at a critical juncture, with the indexes whipsawing in recent weeks as investors panic about future data center construction and the crisis surrounding Nvidia's CEO. The two prominent fears spreading among investors have been that, 1), tighter regulation will put an end to new data centers in the US, and 2), that the AI trade will stumble without Nvidia founder Jensen Huang cheerleading the movement. See November 2026 CMS market share and website usage data from W3Techs, including WordPress, Shopify, Wix, and Squarespace, plus the latest platform trends. WordPress might remain the dominant force in content management systems (CMS) for now, but market share has dropped since its peak in 2022 to under 60%. According to W3Techs on Nov. 13, 2026, WordPress now has a CMS market share of 57.9%. Looking at historical data, WordPress dipped under 60% in 2016, 2017, and 2019, but this is the lowest drop since 2013. WordPress still remains a substantial lead over its nearest rival, Shopify, but is this an indication of a downturn for WordPress, or for the general usage of CMS? Shopify has continued its growth across all surveyed websites, with Wix and Squarespace also maintaining their growth trajectory. In fact, apart from Joomla and Drupal, which fell, and Webflow, which held flat, all other top CMS have increased market share, indicating WordPress is on a downturn to the benefit of other platforms. This report breaks down the current CMS landscape, compares the top platforms, and outlines the latest shifts in market share and usage. According to W3Techs, 67.7% of websites have a CMS, and Netcraft reports over 323 million domains From this, we can assume that the current market size for content management systems has risen to 218.8 million websites. *Approximations extrapolated from W3Techs and Netcraft data There are two different measures throughout this report: usage is a platform’s percentage of all surveyed websites, while market share is its percentage of websites with a known CMS. Data from W3Techs, Nov. 13, 2026. (WooCommerce and Elementor are not listed in the table above as they’re WordPress plugins and not standalone CMS platforms.)  *Graphs are separated due to the dominance of the WordPress market share. WordPress remains the most widely used CMS. Its usage across all surveyed websites rose from 23.3% in January 2015 to 43.2% in January 2022, before falling to 39.2% today. But its long-standing growth curve is now in a downturn. Its CMS market share has fallen by approximately 7.3 percentage points from the January 2022 figure of 65.2%. Since Jan. 1, 2026, it has declined from 60.2% to 57.9%, while all-website usage has dropped from 43.0% to 39.2%. Those figures do not show why individual sites changed platforms. For teams using WordPress, plugin compatibility, core updates, and security management remain practical considerations. Read more: Should You Still Use WordPress? As the second-most popular standalone CMS in W3Techs’ current listing, Shopify’s market share stands at 7.9%, and it is used by 5.4% of all websites surveyed. Both measures have increased from Jan. 1, 2026, when they stood at 7.0% and 5.0%, respectively. Market share is not a performance benchmark. For a separate, historical comparison of technical performance, see our 2025 Core Web Vitals CMS rankings. From an SEO and business perspective, Shopify’s growing footprint makes it a platform worth evaluating alongside the features, costs, and technical requirements of an online store. Wix now powers 4.2% of websites surveyed and holds 6.2% of the known-CMS market. Its market share has increased from 5.8% at the start of 2026, but its all-website usage remains at 4.2% at the displayed precision. Wix has benefited from its positioning beyond a lightweight website builder that consistently invests in branding and platform capabilities, making it a viable contender for mid-market adoption. Squarespace’s CMS market share has grown from 0.5% in January 2015 to 3.6% today, with 2.4% of all websites surveyed now using the platform. Its growth could be attributed to the increasing demand for low-maintenance, design-forward platforms that are easily accessible to small businesses and individuals. Read more: WordPress Vs. Squarespace – Which One Is Better? In contrast to all the other top CMS surveyed, Joomla and Drupal have continued to lose CMS market share, now accounting for 1.6% and 0.9%, respectively. At the start of 2026, those figures were 1.9% and 1.1%. Once platforms in favor with web developers and amateur coders, this shift likely reflects a broader trend where more user-friendly, SaaS-based platforms capture the attention of small businesses and non-technical users. Webflow, which last year looked like a growing contender, now holds at 1.2% of the known-CMS market, unchanged from Jan. 1, 2026. Its usage across all surveyed websites has slipped from 0.9% to 0.8%. Between Jan. 1 and Nov. 13, 2026, the proportion of websites using none of W3Techs’ monitored CMS platforms rose from 28.6% to 32.3%, an increase of approximately 3.7 percentage points. During the same period, WordPress usage fell from 43.0% to 39.2% of all surveyed websites. That reverses the earlier downward trend in the “no CMS” category. It is not proof that those sites are custom-coded or have abandoned a CMS, as the category means that no monitored CMS was detected. Since January 2024, Joomla’s CMS market share has fallen from 2.5% to 1.6%, while Drupal’s has declined from 1.6% to 0.9%. Over the longer period, Joomla has dropped from 8.6% in January 2015 and Drupal from 5.1% in the same month. They’ve slipped from the No. 2 and No. 3 spots to No. 5 and No. 10, overtaken by faster-growing platforms like Wix and Squarespace in 2022. Joomla, in particular, had strong momentum early on – briefly surpassed WordPress in search interest until around 2008, according to Google Trends – but it hasn’t kept pace with modern platform demands. Shopify is the platform with the most interest overtaking WordPress. Why did these popular content management systems decline so much? It’s most likely due to the strength of third-party support for WordPress with plugins and themes, making it much more accessible. But the rise of supported themes and plugins for Shopify is starting to gain on WordPress. The growth of website builders, such as Wix and Squarespace, indicates that small businesses want a more straightforward managed solution, and they have started to nibble on market share from the bottom. Although, it does not establish that users moved directly from Joomla or Drupal to those platforms. Over the period from November 2025 to November 2026, the CMS market share of: Growth has slowed sharply for Wix and Squarespace, while Shopify’s has accelerated from 4.6% to 16.2% and taken the lead against the others in a reversal from the last reported period (Wix was growing by 32.6%, Squarespace 9.7%, and Shopify by 4.6%). As mentioned above, SaaS web builders don’t require coding knowledge and offer an opportunity for a small business to get a web presence quickly. The rise of Shopify could be attributed to an influx to the platform from WooCommerce, as the WordPress alternative. WordPress is not known as a complicated platform to use, but it does require some coding knowledge and an understanding of how websites are built. On the other hand, a website builder is a much easier route to market, without the need to understand what is happening in the back end. Elementor is the most widely used WordPress page builder, installed on 18.2% of all websites with a known CMS and 12.3% of all sites surveyed (not shown below) – more than Wix and Squarespace combined – though it functions as a plugin within WordPress, not a standalone CMS. While not a CMS on its own, it is a major part of the WordPress ecosystem. Its figures overlap with WordPress and should not be added to WordPress’s market share or usage. W3Techs also compares platforms by overall popularity and traffic rank. The ranking bars measure a platform’s share among sites with a known CMS within each ranking tier, rather than its share of all websites. The WordPress, Joomla, and Drupal comparison above shows Drupal with a smaller overall footprint but a stronger presence among highly ranked sites. WordPress remains much more widely used overall. Wix and Squarespace have lower representation in the top-ranked groups than in the overall known-CMS sample. That is a traffic-ranking distinction, not a direct measure of business size or the quality of the software. Elementor gives site owners a visual way to build within WordPress. For businesses comparing drag-and-drop tools, the practical question remains how the builder fits their design, maintenance, and SEO requirements. WooCommerce has seen a decline to 11.4% of websites with a known CMS, while Shopify has increased to 7.9%. WooCommerce powers 7.7% of all websites surveyed, compared with Shopify’s 5.4%. As a WordPress-based ecommerce platform, it is included within the WordPress ecosystem rather than listed as a separate standalone CMS in the top 10 above. W3Techs’ separate ecommerce-system survey uses a different denominator: websites using an ecommerce system that W3Techs monitors. On that measure, WooCommerce has a 47.0% share and Shopify 32.7%. Those figures do not measure sales, revenue, or every online store worldwide. In comparison to other ecommerce CMS platforms, WooCommerce is still dominant right now. It has more market share than its competitors combined: Shopify (7.9%) + PrestaShop (0.7%) + OpenCart (0.4%). But it is losing ground, and this could be correlated to the decline of WordPress and users moving to other platforms. It will be interesting to see if Shopify overtakes in the next year.   The ranking comparison also shows why overall adoption is only part of the picture. Shopify has a stronger presence than WooCommerce in several of the higher-ranked groups, even though WooCommerce has the larger overall share of the known-CMS sample. Shopify surged during the pandemic, with market share growing by 52.9% from 2020 to 2021 and then 26.9% from 2021 to 2022, outpacing every other platform. After a dip in 2023, it recovered in 2024 and has reached 7.9% market share this year. As the market changes, platform choice affects site architecture, plugin availability, and technical SEO flexibility. WordPress continues to lead, but its gradual decline marks a turning point. SaaS competitors such as Shopify, Wix, and Squarespace are steadily gaining traction, offering streamlined platforms that appeal to most businesses. If more SMBs are switching to website builders, understanding the limitations and intricacies of these platforms for SEO could be a competitive advantage. CMS adoption determines how efficiently teams can build, secure, and optimize sites at scale. The one area I am most interested in is how AI and vibecoding might impact CMS platforms and if there will be a rise in websites without a CMS. Shopify now runs on 5.4% of all websites surveyed, not just sites with a CMS. With its increasing footprint, specializing in Shopify SEO could be a strategic move for an SEO professional. Wix and Squarespace remain important alternatives, too. Getting fluent in their ecosystems could help you serve businesses with different development and maintenance requirements. The reality is that WordPress remains the largest ecosystem in this survey, while other platforms give business leaders and SEO professionals an opportunity to diversify their expertise. Understanding the strengths and limitations of various CMS platforms can inform strategic decisions and align with evolving market demands. Intel, the US chip giant, is being sued by its shareholders who accuse the firm of hiding the severity of a slump in its personal computer (PC) sales that caused its share price to plunge almost 29% in one day. Billions of dollars was knocked off the value of the company after it forecast disappointing revenues ahead of its latest earnings report. Shareholders allege that Intel made "materially false and misleading" statements that failed to disclose the slowdown in PC sales and the impact of its data centre projects, according to a proposed class action lawsuit filed in San Jose, California. The BBC has contacted Intel for comment. In October, Intel firm announced its computer hardware sales had dropped sharply in the three months that ended in September.  That report undermined earlier suggestions from the chipmaker that demand had been improving, sending Intel shares plunging, according to the lawsuit. Shareholders claimed the "depressed demand for PC sales" caused "a dramatic slowdown" in quarterly earnings â a drop of 9%, or about $800m - to $8.1bn. The lawsuit, filed by legal firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd on behalf of owners of Intel common shares between 23 July and 29 October this year, was filed against the chipmaker, its chief executive Tan Lip-Bu and other company leaders. Intel has poured huge investments into manufacturing to meet the enormous demand for AI computing power. As more semiconductors are channelled towards data centres, chips for PCs and other electronics have become more expensive. Intel boss Tan had told analysts that the industry was facing an "unprecedented memory crunch", resulting in a shortage of chip supplies for PCs. "We need to address these challenges with urgency," Tan said in October. Intel shares have fallen sharply in the past month by 37.5%, though its share price is still up by 51% overall this year.
