For many Thanksgiving menus, stuffing is a must — but it can feel overwhelming trying to figure out which recipe and technique to use when making this classic side. To narrow down my options, I turned to recipes from celebrity chefs Ina Garten, Paula Deen, Ree Drummond, and Sunny Anderson. Here's how they stacked up, and which stuffing was my favorite.  Unlike the other recipes I tested, Garten's stuffing requires only one type of bread — baguettes — which made it easier to prepare. The recipe, found on the Food Network website, also includes celery, yellow onion,  Granny Smith apples, flat-leaf parsley, butter, rosemary, chicken stock, salt, and pepper. Toasted sliced, blanched almonds were optional. I also appreciated the addition of fresh herbs, but was unsure how I'd like the apples and almonds combined with the savory onions and celery.  This recipe yields a huge portion, so I cut it in half. Overall, the process was pretty simple. While my cubed bread was drying in the oven at 300 degrees Fahrenheit for about 10 minutes, I sautéed the veggies, apples, and herbs in a saucepan with butter. Once the mixture was combined, I poured it over the bread cubes, along with the vegetable stock.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  This recipe calls for cooking the filling inside a turkey cavity for two-and-a-half hours at 350 degrees Fahrenheit. I wasn't making a turkey for this taste test, so I baked the stuffing at the same temperature in a shallow dish for an hour instead.  The final dish was pretty crispy and golden on top, but its center looked less appetizing.  The texture was OK, and the insides definitely seemed soggy. I probably could've avoided this by adding a little less broth than instructed.  Next time, I'd definitely omit the nuts. I used slivered almonds, and their crunchiness, size, and shape threw off the dish's overall texture. The crusty, breaded exterior was delicious and added all of the crunch this dish needed.  I could definitely taste the rosemary, and I actually enjoyed the apples, which added a slight sweetness to the stuffing that balanced the other savory flavors. In true Deen fashion, this stuffing recipe from the chef's website calls for a full stick of butter.  Other ingredients include white bread, cornbread, saltine crackers, celery, onion, chicken stock, eggs, salt, and pepper. Sage and poultry seasoning were optional.  I was also unsure about the mixture of carbs here — saltine crackers, white bread, and cornbread, which I made from scratch using Deen's recipe. For the carbs, I started by making cornbread — a quick and easy process that resulted in a savory, slightly dense dish. In the meantime, I dried my white-bread slices in the oven. I then sautéed the veggies with the stick of butter and mixed all of the prepared ingredients in a bowl.  When adding the vegetable stock, I stopped after about five cups because the mixture already looked far too soggy. I was shocked that the recipe asked for seven cups. Still concerned about the texture, I poured out more broth before adding five eggs to the mix. I then transferred everything into a shallow, glass baking dish. It took about an hour in the oven for the mix to really crisp up. The top of the stuffing was slightly golden, but it didn't get as crispy as the other recipes I tested.  When I took a bite, I found the interior was far too soggy — there was definitely too much broth, and the crackers turned mushy after absorbing the liquid.  The flavor was OK — very savory and buttery — but the super-soggy texture was not appetizing. If I made this again, I'd swap some of the crackers for more bread and use significantly less broth.   The Pioneer Woman's recipe calls for a lot of bread — three different types — including cornbread, French bread, and Italian bread. Since I already had the ingredients for Deen's cornbread, I made it for this dish as well.  The stuffing recipe also asks for butter, onion, celery, chicken broth, parsley, rosemary, basil, thyme, salt, pepper, and (optional) turmeric.  I omitted thyme from this recipe and others as a personal preference.  In general, this recipe had a similar process to the other two, from making the cornbread and dehydrating the other carbs to sautéeing the veggies. I noticed a little too late that I was supposed to let the bread dry for one to two days. Instead, I threw it in the oven at 300 degrees Fahrenheit for 15 minutes, and it still firmed up really well.  The recipe instructed me to add six cups of broth to the sautéed vegetables, then ladle this mixture onto the tossed bread cubes until they were soaked to my liking. I preferred this approach because it was easier to control and prevent the stuffing from getting soggy.  My stuffing took about 40 minutes in the oven — not the 20 to 30 minutes the recipe called for — but the extra time helped it achieve a crisp, golden top. Although the stuffing was toasty on top, it still looked soggy inside. However, upon tasting it, the dish's flavor and texture weren't bad at all. The center was slightly soggy but not overwhelmingly so, and the extra-crispy top helped balance the texture.  My only issue with this recipe was that it had way too much celery. I'm not a fan of it in general, but I can tolerate it in moderate amounts — still, almost every bite tasted strongly of it.  That said, the savory, herby bites with minimal celery were delicious.  Anderson's simple and quick recipe combines store-bought stuffing mix with sautéed veggies, broth, and herbs to make it taste homemade.  The recipe, which I also found on the Food Network website, features boxed stuffing mix, butter, celery, onions, parsley, thyme, sage, garlic, salt, pepper, and turkey or chicken stock. Anderson's recipe also featured four add-on combinations to give the dish more flavor — sausage and bell peppers, oysters and hard-boiled eggs, walnuts and apples, and sautéed fennel bulb and dried apricots. I opted for that last combo. This recipe was quick to put together. For the base, I just dumped the stuffing mix into a bowl and added freshly chopped parsley.  I got to work mincing the garlic and chopping the onion, celery, fennel bulb, sage, and dried apricots. Then I cooked the veggies, sage, garlic, salt, and pepper in a pan until the mix started to soften. After combining the sautéed mixture with the boxed stuffing and vegetable broth, I added the dried apricots and pressed everything into a glass baking dish.  I covered the whole thing with foil and let it bake for 45 minutes at 350 degrees Fahrenheit. Then, I removed the foil and cooked it for an additional 15 minutes at 400 degrees. I was worried this recipe would turn out too soggy since it's meant to be a wet dressing, but it actually baked up really well. It came out of the oven with a soft, almost creamy center and an extra-crispy exterior.  The sautéed veggies created a very savory flavor profile, and I couldn't even taste the celery. I was a little unsure about the apricots, but they added a touch of sweetness and melt-in-your-mouth texture.  If I had to choose a favorite, I'd go with Anderson's unique stuffing. I was surprised by how much I enjoyed the fennel-and-apricot combination — it added an interesting twist to the dish but still felt traditional. Plus, this recipe was the quickest and easiest to make. I also loved the flavor of Garten's herby stuffing with rosemary and apple, but next time, I'd leave out the almonds and use less broth. Deen's recipe had an enjoyable savory, buttery flavor, but it needed far less liquid to fix the texture. I think adding more bread would also help.  For Drummond's stuffing, I'd use slightly less broth to improve the texture and way less celery to help the flavor of the sautéed veggies and fresh herbs shine. Sam Altman shrugged off the idea that OpenAI could become the Lyft to Anthropic's Uber. "That is not a worry," Altman said on Monday during a live interview at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World event. Altman's response to the question about OpenAI's chief rival generated audible laughter in the room. In 2019, Lyft went public before Uber, and its shares outperformed its ride-share rival's on their respective first days of trading. But Uber got the last laugh and today is worth roughly 22 times Lyft by market cap. Altman said that the narrative about investor demand is different than what he's seeing. He said that "there is a lot of skepticism from journalists" but that investors remain "pretty bullish." "I get that you have to write something every day, and there's got to be all this, you know, this fight and that one, and this winner, and this loser, and what's happening here and there — but the macro trend and the value being created, I'm not at all worried about there not being a huge amount," he said. The OpenAI chief reiterated his view that the ChatGPT maker will eventually go public. Anthropic publicly released its S-1 on October 26 and is expected to debut on Nasdaq later this week. That doesn't mean that being a public company will be easy, Altman said. "I think there are real downsides to being public," he said. "And it's a very volatile time in our industry with high-stakes, consequential decisions to make around safety and how society is going to interact with this technology. And there are doubtless things that are easier as a private company." Altman said it's "directionally a good thing" that more investors want exposure to the AI boom. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar recently said that bringing the company public is in line with OpenAI's mission to bring super intelligence to everyone. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Your teenager's first smartphone is something they'll remember for a long time. Everything about it, from unboxing the package to turning it on for the first time, can be a special moment. But when buying your teenager their first Android smartphone, more expensive doesn't necessarily mean better. Usually, parents give teenagers their first phone so they can stay in touch during the day, talk to their friends, or perform basic tasks like sharing notes, making video calls, and using social media. As such, getting a budget Android phone for your teenager's first smartphone could be an excellent choice. That said, the budget Android segment is the most crowded, making it tough to identify the best phones. While affordability is a major criterion, your teenager would also want excellent durability, adequate storage, and solid performance. This means having a bright and smooth display, at least a full day's battery life, decent cameras, good gaming performance, and excellent software support. We've made the selection easier by combing the market and identifying the five best budget Android smartphones to serve as your teenager's first. Our picks are all from reputable brands, are relatively recent releases, and, most importantly, are easily available for purchase in the United States. The Samsung Galaxy A17 5G was priced at $200 until earlier this year, when Samsung bumped its price by $50. Still, at $244.99 on Amazon, it's a top-tier budget Android option, especially if you want to give your teenager a phone that will last them a long time. That's because the Galaxy A17 comes with one of the longest software support guarantees, providing six years of OS and regular security updates until 2031. Combined with a bright 6.7-inch AMOLED screen and a fingerprint scanner built into the power button, it's no wonder Android Central calls it the "best cheap Android phone for your kids' first phone." While it only comes with 4 GB of RAM and 128 GB of storage, there's a microSD slot and the option to use some of your storage as RAM. The Galaxy A17 is no performance beast, but it "manages to push through everyday tasks without issue," according to PCMag. Like other Samsung Galaxy phones, it also comes with built-in parental controls. Parents can use Google Family Link to remotely monitor a child's screen time, set app usage limits, restrict access to certain apps, etc. The cameras are also more than decent for the price. The Galaxy A17 features a triple-camera setup (50 MP, 5 MP, 2 MP) at the back, which CNET found could "capture all the action without too much blurring," while Phone Arena noted an "overall pleasing look." It also rocks a large 5,000 mAh battery that can easily last your teen a full day. Unfortunately, there's no wireless charging, unlike the Moto G phones on this list. It also doesn't get the Galaxy AI features, though Gemini and Circle to Search with Google are available. Priced at $499.99 for the 8 GB RAM / 128 GB storage version, the Moto G Stylus 2026 is one of the very few budget smartphones to come with a built-in stylus. That makes it a great choice for teenagers who'd like greater precision when doing creative work, such as editing videos, or playing games. There's also a 256 GB variant for $100 more, but you can skip it and expand the phone's storage using the microSD slot, which, along with its 3.5 mm audio jack, is another rarity these days. The phone features a large 6.7-inch AMOLED display with a 120 Hz refresh rate and 5,000 nits of peak brightness, making it better for outdoor use than the likes of the Google Pixel 10a and the iPhone 17e. While its benchmark scores are not up to par, Phone Arena says it still "boasts enough oomph to get you through a full day of everyday tasks like browsing the web, web streaming, and light gaming." Moreover, it comes with Gemini, Copilot, and Perplexity pre-installed, and your kids will also appreciate its AI features, such as the handwriting calculator and Sketch to Image. Battery life is a particularly strong aspect of the Moto G Stylus 2026. It features a large 5,200 mAh battery and lasted "nearly two days on a full battery with regular use" in PCMag's testing. Furthermore, it supports fast charging at 68 W wired and 15 W wireless. As for your kid's security, the phone includes an on-screen fingerprint reader and face unlock, but it only promises two major Android OS updates. That's underwhelming when rival budget Android phones that can last up to five years. Launched in 2025, the Samsung Galaxy A36 remains a solid budget Android pick thanks to its well-rounded package and an above-par six years of OS and security updates, which further increases its value for money. In fact, the Galaxy A36 was the first A-series smartphone to get such a long upgrade window, up from four years previously. It's available on Amazon for $339.98. For the price, you get 8 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage, along with a large 6.7-inch display that's both smooth and bright. It can run just about any app your kid wants to install from the Google Play Store, and Tom's Guide had "no trouble at all" running everyday tasks and even playing games like Modern Combat. GSMArena called it "a solid performer in its price range," remarking that it does a good job with "most day-to-day tasks and light games." Although PCMag experts recommend using wireless earbuds when listening to music on the A36, its call quality is excellent. Its cameras are the same as last year's A35, but they still deliver the "classic Samsung look" and support 4K / 30fps video recording. It comes with a 5,000 mAh battery that PCMag found lasted more than 16 hours when continuously streaming a 1,080p video. Plus, it charges at 45 W, which is the same as the flagship Galaxy S26+. It's also a great choice if your teenager likes AI features. The A36 was the first A-series phone to get Circle to Search, and it also rocks an Object Eraser in the Gallery app and an AI Select tool that lets you interact with text, images, and videos on the screen. The Nothing Phone (4a) Pro is our top recommendation if you want to give your teenager a mid-range Android phone with flagship-level performance and features, plus a design style so unique it's bound to stand out in your kid's hands, should they like that kind of attention. It doesn't feature a fully transparent back like its smaller siblings, the Phone (4a) and Phone (4b), and swaps out the Phone (3a) Pro's surrounding Glyph LEDs for a dedicated circular Glyph interface dial. At the time of writing, the 8 GB / 128 GB version is available for $499 on Amazon, while the 12 GB / 256 GB variant is priced at $599.  PCMag calls it a "midrange heavy-hitter." Its Snapdragon 7 Gen 4 processor makes it significantly more powerful than the similarly priced Moto G Stylus 2026, Samsung Galaxy A56, and Google Pixel 9a. According to TechRadar, it "didn't seem to break much of a sweat," and its gaming performance is "pretty unimpeachable." You get a super-large 6.83-inch AMOLED display with a 144 Hz refresh rate, along with a near-stock Android experience, Google's built-in parental controls, and a dedicated physical AI key.  As for the camera, its 50 MP telephoto lens is a rarity at this price, and the overall picture quality is among the best in this segment. Tom's Guide found it equal or superior to the flagship Google Pixel 10. Moreover, its 5,080 mAh battery will easily last your teenager an entire day, while 50 W wired charging means they can top it up quickly. Lastly, the (4a) Pro comes with Android 16 and promises up to three major OS updates. Other security features include an on-screen fingerprint sensor and the option to require a lock screen password before shutting down the phone. The Moto G Power 2025 costs just $199.99 and is therefore the best option if you're after a super-cheap yet modern and capable Android phone for your teenager. Despite its low price, its rounded corners, thin bezels, and vegan leather back make it "look like a premium phone," according to PCMag. With a 6.8-inch Full HD+ LCD display panel and a 120 Hz refresh rate, the Moto G Power 2025 is also a solid choice for users looking for a snappy and responsive big-screen phone on a budget.  CNET had "no trouble watching YouTube, browsing websites, and taking video calls." Moreover, its 5,000 mAh battery will get your child "through a full day of regular use without issue," per Android Central. It also supports 30 W wired and 15 W wireless charging. Combined with an IP68/IP69 water and dust resistance rating, it's ideal for teenagers who want a phone that can support them through their long university days.  Moto G Power's cameras are about what you'd expect from a phone this cheap. Its two rear lenses, a 50 MP main camera and an 8 MP ultrawide camera, along with a 16 MP selfie camera, produce photos that look "passable during the day" and in good lighting, according to Phone Arena. It comes with Android 15 out of the box and includes built-in parental controls powered by Google Family Link. However, it only promises two OS updates. Lastly, while there's only 128 GB of storage, like the Moto G Stylus phones, you can expand the storage by up to 1 TB using a microSD card. Our top priority while selecting phones for this guide was budget-friendly Android smartphones. As such, we first had to decide on a price range. All the phones on this list are under $500, with options under $350, $250, and even $200, so there's something for all price segments within the budget category. Next, we only picked phones from reputable Android brands, including Samsung, Motorola, and Nothing. We also made sure not to sacrifice performance for affordability. We considered the features teenagers would typically want from their first smartphone. That included looking into the phones' screen quality, storage, chipset and real-world performance, camera, battery life, and more. We also went beyond the spec sheets and looked at what expert independent tech outlets, such as PCMag, Android Central, CNET, TechRadar, Phone Arena, and Tom's Guide, had to say about them after extensive hands-on testing. You'll also see that all our picks are either the latest launches in their respective series or no more than one generation old. This adds more value to their software support guarantees, as you'll be upgrading from a relatively recent Android version. Lastly, we made sure our smartphone picks are easy to purchase, with availability through either Amazon or the companies' official websites.

Intel has been sued by shareholders who accuse the company of misleading investors about the severity of the PC market downturn and its impact on the company's financial performance before its shares plunged by nearly 29% in late October, reports Reuters.       The proposed class action lawsuit led by the Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System pension fund was filed on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California. The lawsuit alleges that Intel failed to inform investors in a timely manner about the extent to which slow demand for consumer processors and excessive inventories would affect its sales. In particular, the plaintiffs argue that the negative impact of the PC market downturn on Intel's business was greater than the benefits the company enjoyed from the unprecedented buildout of AI data center infrastructure and other AI-related opportunities. "Intel made statements that were materially false and/or misleading when made because they failed to disclose the following adverse facts pertaining to Intel’s business," the lawsuit reads. While Intel, like many other major technology companies, has invested heavily in its manufacturing capabilities, supply constraints have prevented the chipmaker from fully capitalizing on strong demand for data center processors. Meanwhile, a severe shortage of memory has driven up DRAM prices and, consequently, the cost of PCs, which has affected demand for consumer systems. As a result, Intel could not sell enough CPUs in the third quarter, which dramatically affected the company's stock price in October. Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan expressed disappointment with the supply constraints, the extraordinary situation in the memory market, and the subsequent weakness of the PC business during the company's earnings call. Yet, the plaintiff believes that the company should have warned about the turmoil situation on the client PC market earlier. In fact, back in the early 2000s, when Intel was led by Craig Barrett, the company routinely issued mid-quarter business updates to inform investors about changes in its financial outlook. In fact, in September 2004, Intel used such an update to cut its third-quarter revenue and gross margin projections due to weaker-than-expected demand for its processors and inventory adjustments by its customers, which were very similar circumstances that the company faced in the third quarter of 2026. A similar update could have alerted Intel's shareholders to the challenges the chipmaker faced well ahead of its quarterly earnings release. Unfortunately, Intel abandoned the practice of mid-quarter updates in January 2006 under Paul Otellini, though it occasionally revised its guidance between quarterly earnings releases thereafter, particularly during the global financial crisis of 2008 – 2010. Intel's shareholders also allege that the company had a financial incentive to withhold information about the state of its business as it raised $23 billion through a stock offering at $95 per share in mid-August, roughly halfway through its third quarter. Intel secured the additional capital as it planned to expand its semiconductor production capacity. Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox. Intel’s stock price dropped by 28.6% on October 30, erasing around $140 billion of the company's market capitalization, after the chipmaker issued Q4 revenue and earnings projections that fell short of expectations and warned that the PC market downturn would persist. Meanwhile, despite the massive sell-off, Intel's shares have gained 62% since the beginning of the year. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages on behalf of Intel investors who purchased the company's shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner are also named as defendants. Executive Editor and lead writer for BI Today Grand Theft Anthropic. GTA VI(PO). Grandthropic. Call it whatever you want. Just don't call it boring. Grand Theft Auto VI's release and Anthropic's market debut arrive this Thursday. Not since "Barbenheimer" — when "Oppenheimer" and "Barbie" premiered the same weekend — have we had two cultural and business phenomena collide on the same day. I'll start with Anthropic, since that's the easier sell. A valuation as high as $1.4 trillion with as much as $90 billion raised makes it a behemoth (and potentially record-breaking) IPO. It's also the first major test of investor appetite for a company focused solely on AI. Then there's GTA. The last installment — GTA V — surpassed $1 billion in sales within the first three days of its release in 2013. It remains a top-selling game to this day, with almost 235 million units sold overall. GTA VI is already off to a hot start. Presale estimates have reached 12.13 million units, totaling $1.18 billion in revenue, according to SensorTower data. The impact also extends to companies' PTO calendars. (Or your favorite newsletter writer; I'll be out next week.) Workforce management tech company UKG said time-off requests for the week of GTA 6's release are up roughly 20% compared to the same week in previous years. Some companies are even leaning into it. 'Grandthropic' comes with some incredibly high stakes. For Anthropic, the fate of the wider AI trade rests on its shoulders. And that was before one of the industry's mascots — Jensen Huang — blew up spectacularly. This isn't an offshoot of the AI ecosystem, like a chipmaker or data center, or a company leveraging AI atop a mature business. Anthropic is as pure-play of an AI company as you'll ever find. Which raises the question: If investors don't support Anthropic, why have any confidence in the wider AI trade? I argued that point on my Instagram. For GTA 6, it's tough to compare it to the rest of the video game industry because its incredible success makes it an outlier. But with the threats posed by artificial intelligence and high hardware costs, GTA's success could serve as the anchor that keeps gamers engaged, bridging to other games. Jovian Zayne didn't think she was overdoing it. She was pregnant with her daughter and pushing hard for a new client when a health scare put her in the hospital. "I don't think I recognized that I was pushing myself as hard as I was because it didn't feel like it," Zayne told Business Insider. "It felt normal." After leaving the hospital, Zayne immediately knew what she had to do. She had to drop the client. Even though she was frustrated with her body back then, she never saw walking away from the client as a failure. Zayne said her faith had a lot to do with that: She trusted God would have the right opportunity waiting for her. "If I'm not well trying to work with this person and this environment, or this client, this is not who I'm meant to be with," she said. That time in her life became part of "Soft Landings for Hard Days: Wisdom, Companionship, and Guidance to Encourage Your Spirit released last month. The book began as journal entries and prayers, plus the notes of encouragement she saved when things were at their worst. It's built around five "invitations" (be gentle with yourself, feel your feelings, believe you are worthy, honor the seasons of your life, and appreciate life's goodness), and it works partly like a workbook for those in the middle of transition, such as a layoff or thinking about a professional pivot. Zayne's executive coaching in tech, finance and healthcare shaped the book, too. She thinks companies have gotten "less human-centered, particularly in the last five years." With the constant push for efficiency, she said, it's hard for anyone to feel like the person behind the work counts for much. "I tell leaders now, you will either run into disappointment, dissatisfaction, disease, or depression by ignoring yourself in all of this transition," she said. The other option, as she sees it, is centering your humanity and then questioning the bigger systems that keep shrinking how people get to show up at work.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Since I'm in the middle of a career transition, I wanted to know what that actually looks like. For anyone else in that spot, whether they were laid off, are planning a pivot or just have a feeling it's time to go, here's her advice. Zayne said start with questions: 1. "What do I want to do? 2. How do I want to apply the skills that I've gained over time? According to Zayne, getting an honest answer starts with giving yourself permission to be candid. "So you're not judging your answers, but you're curious about them," she added. Skip that part and you'll end up in what she calls self-abandonment. "So often, we're lying to ourselves, which makes a hard day even harder," she said. "You will not land softly in that." She also suggests that ambitious people get picky about their circle during a transition. Mentors, sponsors, coaches, and advocates count along with a therapist if you need one. "Curate the people well to hold you honest," she said. Zayne is practicing her own advice right now while on a book tour to promote, "Soft Landings for Hard Days." She's seeing a lot of friends as she travels for the book, but said only a few people have "intimate access" to her right now. If you're entering a new field, Zayne recommends first deciding where you want to show up and how you want to be perceived — then giving yourself time to adjust. It also helps to break a big change into smaller pieces and take it slow. "We have a lot of gripped hands to imaginary timelines, of when something has to happen or how it has to happen," Zayne said. "When we force-feed our life to ourselves, we choke." Zayne knows how this feels. When she wrote her book, which took about six years, she pulled back from people and group chats to sustain her new writing habits. For someone who prides herself on checking in on people, that was tough for Zayne. Her executive coaching business slowed down as well, since she couldn't chase new clients like before. It didn't bother her, however, because in her mind the book was its own business development. And when the workplace itself is the problem, Zayne doesn't want people taking it out on themselves. Instead, direct your critiques on the workplace, the culture, the systems, or the people instead of internalizing them. "Be hard on those systems, be soft on yourself," she said. Jump to

Don't call it a Sam Altman comeback. As calls grow among Nvidia employees, investors, and Silicon Valley leaders for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as Nvidia CEO, some observers are comparing it to Altman's ouster and subsequent reinstatement as OpenAI's CEO in 2023. Huang and Altman left abruptly after their respective boards raised concerns. Each company appointed insiders as interim CEOs. And both leaders have attracted widespread support: More than 700 OpenAI employees demanded Altman's return, while a petition calling for Huang's reinstatement has garnered over 100,000 signatures, including from Nvidia employees. The parallels only go so far. One key difference: Nvidia is a public company, so it has to meet tougher reporting requirements and answer to shareholders in ways that OpenAI, a private company, does not. Crucially, the reasons given for each leader's departure are also different — and could make a Huang comeback more complicated than Altman's. OpenAI said almost exactly three years ago that Altman was not "consistently candid in his communications with the board." Huang's Nvidia exit is mired in his admission of being unfaithful to his wife and questions over whether he was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort." "In short, one board had a disagreement; the other has open questions of fact that only an investigation can answer," David Astorino, a senior partner at leadership advisory firm RHR, told Business Insider. Huang resigned on Thursday after reports that he had at least two extramarital affairs, including one with a direct report and one with a woman who US officials believe was passing information to Beijing, according to reporting from The New York Times.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Nvidia's stock has taken a beating in the days since the scandal started; it's down another 4% today. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, called the Altman comparison "an imperfect analogy." "Jensen's situation involves internal and external factors that OpenAI's did not," he said, adding that Huang's situation was closer to Apple's firing in 1985 of Steve Jobs, who returned to Apple a decade later to lead its historic comeback. "The lesson is the same: Founders cannot be replaced," he said. On Monday, the Jensen defenders had a blow to their comeback hopes. Nvidia's board of directors is not considering reinstating Huang as CEO, a person familiar with the matter confirmed to Business Insider. That follows fierce speculation among investors and on prediction platforms. Gene Munster, a managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management, put the odds of a Jensen return at 51%, up from 10% on Friday, he said in an X post on Sunday. He said the "bring back Jensen" movement was gaining momentum and that Huang's resignation, rather than a formal firing, could give Nvidia's board "air cover" to bring him back. Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives, took the opposite view, arguing that legal, board, Washington, and China-related scrutiny had permanently changed Huang's standing. "The old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good," Ives wrote in an X post on Sunday. "We see no chance Jensen comes back to Nvidia as CEO." Meanwhile, prediction platform Kalshi said in an X post on Sunday that Huang's odds had doubled to 21%, while Polymarket put his chances of rejoining Nvidia at 7% by November 30, 12% by year-end, and 38% by the end of 2027. Astorino said Huang's return was "unlikely in the near term." "If they reinstated the CEO before the investigation ends, that would likely be a difficult decision to defend," he said. Dan Kaplan, managing partner and co-head of global HR practice at ZRG Partners, told Business Insider that Nvidia's board must protect the company Huang built, rather than the founder himself, and that employee and investor loyalty cannot substitute for the investigation's findings. He also poured cold water on the Altman-Huang comparisons. "The circumstances are different, and you can't simply replay the Altman comeback, no matter how much Silicon Valley loves a good comeback story," Kaplan said. Jump to

Chief Correspondent covering media and technology Sam Altman came back. Can Jensen Huang do it, too? After all, it was just three years ago when the leader of an enormously important AI company was pushed out by his board, then returned days later after an outcry from employees and Silicon Valley power players. But Huang in 2026 is not Altman in 2023. That doesn't mean we won't see the same story played out. It does mean it seems less likely: Right now, Nvidia's position is that it's not happening. To understand why, we need a brief recap: The story began with China: in 2025, The New York Times reported that federal officials were investigating whether Singapore-based Megaspeed was diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese companies. Last month, the Times reported that officials suspected Megaspeed executive Alice Huang of being a "Chinese intelligence asset" and that she had a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang. The Nvidia CEO and his company dismissed the concerns. Then it metastasized into a story about Huang's conduct. He acknowledged being unfaithful, and Nvidia said it would investigate whether he had been targeted by foreign intelligence, while expressing support for him. Days later, after the Times alerted Nvidia to a story about Huang's relationship with a direct report, the board met. Huang resigned the next morning. Since then, reports have described disagreement in Washington over Alice Huang's role, and long-running suspicions of Jensen Huang among China hawks including Marco Rubio. Some of that tension is now public, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling out Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over Nvidia policy. And yes, that's the short version of the recap. But it's important to go over it. Because in some narratives — especially the ones promoted by Jensen Huang's vocal supporters — the story is really about Nvidia's foes working to remove a leader they don't like for political reasons. Perhaps it is! But that's why the timeline is important to underline. Maybe Nvidia's board would have pushed Huang to resign if the issue was solely about his relationship to Alice Huang, and/or the way Nvidia chips have been used by China.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Last week's newsflow, though, suggests that it was news of the affair with Jensen Huang's employee that pushed the board to ultimately act. So there's a version of a story where Nvidia's board may not have pushed out its visionary leader if the only issue was China. Disclosure of the second affair (Reuters has subsequently reported yet another affair with another Nvidia employee) is what did it. All of which makes bringing Huang back more complicated than Altman's story. In Altman's case, OpenAI's board was unable to clearly tell a story about why, exactly, they fired Altman. In Huang's case, Nvidia's board can point to multiple instances where Huang reportedly violated his own company's rules. It can also argue that Huang misled his own company about his behavior, as multiple outlets have reported. Those are all fireable offenses in most of corporate America, regardless of national security debates. In the inevitable shareholder lawsuits that will follow Huang's departure (one has already been filed), board members will be criticized for not uncovering Huang's acts on their own. They will be able to say, credibly, that once the acts came to light, they acted, which led to Huang's ouster. But bringing Huang back once those facts are known will generate much more risk for the board: Board members couldn't simply say that Huang was the victim of a political plot. They'd have to explain why they thought his transgressions weren't harming the company. And if Nvidia stock fell for any reason after Huang came back, they would face blowback for that, too. What about the fact Huang has boosters throughout Silicon Valley, and in the White House? Donald Trump had reportedly told Huang not to resign last week, and on Monday said he "wouldn't mind" if Huang came back. Perhaps if this were a couple of years ago, after Trump's victory in what was described as a vibe-shift election, Nvidia officials and board members might agree to follow Trump's lead. And they might have expected some kind of political or legal shield for their actions — like the kind that Apple and Google got from the Trump administration when they agreed to keep hosting TikTok in America, contrary to US law. But this time around it's not really clear what the White House position actually is on Huang and Nvidia. Trump has spoken glowingly about Huang and Nvidia, but that's different than pushing a private company to reinstate a disgraced CEO. Meanwhile, the Democrats have won their own supposed vibe shift election, and have promised to spend the next couple years investigating both Trump and his private sector allies. Bringing Huang back at Trump's behest makes Nvidia and its board even bigger targets. That alone may be enough to keep him out of the company for good. Jump to

Tech > Mobile > Phones Xiaomi's bonkers dual-screen phone is here and I've been testing its camera. Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe Editor at Large; Lead Photographer, Europe November 16, 2026, 12:48 pm ET Xiaomi is taking the wraps off its phone in Paris tomorrow, but I’ve had the phone for the past few weeks and have been putting the camera to the test in my beautiful home of Edinburgh, Scotland, and in Paris, France. While it’s too early for me to share my full thoughts on the phone and its cameras (keep your eyes peeled tomorrow for that), I did want to share some of my favorite photos I’ve taken with the phone so far. The images seen here are taken with the phone’s various built-in camera modes, largely the black and white mode, as I love the dramatic, filmic look it produces. They’re presented either as-shot or with minimal exposure adjustments using the phone’s built-in editing tools. Stay tuned for much more information on this phone and its wild second display on the back. Taken using one of the phone’s built-in color styles, I love the vibrancy in this shot. The reds really pop, while the wider angle of the main camera emphasizes the tunnel effect of the alleyway, drawing the eye to the person and their dog. More from CNET I may be spoiling the rest of the images here by saying that this is my absolute favorite shot I’ve taken, but there we go. I took this using one of the dedicated black-and-white modes, and I think the tones here are perfect. Excellent dynamic range and contrast, and just the right amount of film grain. I positioned the figure between the buildings and had the phone almost on the floor to turn the rain-soaked tiles into a reflective surface to add some drama to this scene. I then applied a wide cinematic crop in post to give it that extra edge. Lovely stuff. Most of my favorite photos with the phone were taken using the black-and-white mode. It’s no surprise; I shoot in black and white very often on my Leica Q3 43, and I used the monochrome mode for my favorite shots with Xiaomi’s Leitzphone earlier in the year. The phone captures excellent black-and-white photos at night, too. And by exposing for the bright highlights in this scene, I was able to create this stark, moody image of my handsome orange cat, Toulouse. Is he the best cat you’ve ever seen? Of course he is. Back in color, this UFO that had presumably crash-landed in this Parisian market looks great in this filmic color mode. The oranges and reds pop against the other tones in this scene. While this quick street portrait is similarly punchy. I used manual mode here, taking full control over the white balance and exposure settings to achieve the tones I wanted. It’s a great-looking shot with excellent dynamic range. Xiaomi’s phone doesn’t appear to go too hard with its software processing either, meaning that even fine details look quite natural. Other Android phone-makers could take note. As with the photo of Toulouse the cat, I exposed for the highlights here, forcing the rest of the scene under this bridge into shadow. As a result, it looks moody and dramatic but crucially it also looks exactly as I hoped it would. Many phones would try to artificially lift the shadows here, which would ruin the vibe I was going for. I took this with the phone’s telephoto zoom lens, aiming to focus more on the digger as the subject and use the water for reflection. I love how this shot looks, especially in black and white, as the cloud detail behind it is especially noticeable. While here I used the full wide angle of the main camera in order to create a lot of negative space around the figures, emphasizing the size of the building around them. That building was Le Grande Arche in Paris and despite it being a miserably cold, wet and cloudy day I think the phone has captured a satisfyingly stark scene here.  I don’t like flying, so I distracted myself on the flight out to Paris by taking photos of things with the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, including this man having a look out of the window. And this shot of my plane’s wing somewhere above the UK. Again, in black and white. When it looks this good, why would I choose anything else? And while we’re still in black and white, a particularly friendly pigeon. Hi, friend! And to round us off, this dude in shades looking at a menu.  I’m genuinely really thrilled with so many of the shots I’ve taken with this phone. The black-and-white mode in particular is spectacular, and I’m looking forward to taking more shots with it. Stick around for more details on the phone — including the full review — coming soon.  		© 2026 CNET, a Ziff Davis company. All rights reserved.

Software hasn’t been working too well lately, has it? This weekend we saw the double-whammy of a 2 day global Microsoft outage, then an FAA ground-stop that halted all flights in the United States. Can you believe it’s only been four weeks since the PHP2Shell vulnerability? A critical exploit in PHP, powering an estimated 70% of the world’s websites, with sites taken completely offline as engineers frantically patched their systems. And then there was the eMudhra fiasco, where thousands of SSL certificates - the way we secure HTTPS websites and internet traffic - were compromised by a private key so weak, it was almost comical. It’s like 2026 has been a year of hacks, outages, vulnerabilities and IT panics. What exactly is going on here? You might be tempted to blame AI, and you wouldn’t be completely wrong. Artificial intelligence models are definitely a part of this. Even if companies like Microsoft don’t divulge whether broken systems were built with AI, we do know that hackers and researchers can now use AI technology to find complicated exploits in a matter of hours. I work with AI heavily in my job. It’s tremendously powerful. It’s also corrosive if used unwisely. But AI is both a cause and a symptom of the problem here. What we are seeing is software breaking down at a systemic level. This problem is insidious because it is not only the software itself that is broken, but the entire way we’ve come to build it. Look at the recent crises in software reliability and you’ll notice they don’t share immediate causes - that we know of - yet they look uncannily similar to each other. The Microsoft outage likely emerged from a network configuration failure that stopped MS datacenters communicating with each other. Exactly what happened next remains confidential, but it seems to have triggered a cascading failure where no service could be restored into a valid state long enough to bear traffic. Reddit and Bluesky speculated that even MSFT engineers had no real handle on the complexity of this outage. Microsoft have faced increasing criticism for the (un)reliability of their Azure platform. Back in March, ex-MSFT engineer Axel Rischin published this scathing criticism: Microsoft rushed Azure out of the gates under intense competitive pressure. Corners were cut. Fundamental principles of reliability and operational simplicity were quietly abandoned. Instead of going back to the drawing board to tackle the growing technical debt, Microsoft relied on quick fixes: layers of automation running mitigation scripts, a growing team of on-call staff, and, when automation was not enough, manual repairs. His article depicts a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where nobody can make sense of the whole picture. On October 21st, security research firm Wiz proudly shared an exploit that could execute arbitrary code on any PHP website. Called PHP2Shell, Wiz trumpeted the power of AI tools to achieve exploits far beyond the skills of human attackers. It turns out the PHP runtime had hidden several complex memory bookkeeping bugs for over a decade. PHP is used extensively in e-commerce and most famously in WordPress, which was once the go-to for cheaply building simple websites. The PHP2Shell writeup depicts an internet dependent on a long chain of dependencies, hiding vulnerabilities too complex for any human to identify. Most people outside of tech won’t have heard of this, but back in May we faced a crisis when an attacker compromised some important packages in the JavaScript ecosystem (NPM). These packages used GitHub Actions to perform Continuous Integration (CI) - automated tests, releases, etc. - and had a crucial misconfiguration where anyone who forked their projects could insert compromised code back upstream. When the next upstream CI build ran, it would retrieve libraries from a cache. The JavaScript package manager, NPM, allows these libraries to include scripts. They’re intended for housekeeping tasks, but here, they were used to hijack the projects’ secret tokens. The JavaScript ecosystem has long been criticised for poor security. NPM projects are complicated chains of dependencies calling dependencies calling dependencies. Any dependency may carry scripts. Any dependency author was just one slip away from allowing their code to be compromised - all they had to do was copy-paste the wrong code. In other words: a highly complex system made of low quality parts, where a single error can compromise everything. It wasn’t always like this. Only 12 years ago, tech was a different industry. Building software was hard. Computer programs comprise millions of tiny instructions, and turning these into a workable system is like constructing a watch by hand, with hundreds of interacting components. Except, unlike a watch, each computer program must do something completely new and different. It was the most fun I’d had as an adult. It was as much an art as a science. You had to be able to hold everything in your head at once: visualise how all the tiny parts could be orchestrated into a cohesive whole. I recommend anyone the adventure of writing a computer program by hand. But, it was less fun if you were a manager. Not many people can write computer programs well, and it’s very hard to scale human beings. Getting them to communicate without misunderstandings is hard. Many projects failed. You can find programmers who know how to manage the complexity, but they want to be paid lots of money. Different movements attempted to solve the core problem. Some people thought that software development practices could help, like if you turned programming into highly structured templates of “best practices”. Or if you used management styles like SCRUM. But they only ever helped so much. About ten years ago, two small revolutions happened in our industry, whilst the rest of the world paid little attention. They were cloud computing, and open source libraries. Cloud computing was about substituting your hardware and infrastructure with virtualised infra you could rent from someone like Amazon Web Services. You could click a button in AWS and it was like a server just popped into existence by magic. Companies loved Cloud because it allowed them to remove sysadmins and ops people from the equation. You didn’t have to wait for someone to actually go to a site and install a rack in a datacenter. The promise was that your software could move as fast as code and not long after, a movement called DevOps essentially ended up merging developers and ops. And then, we had the Open Source boom. It was always possible to reuse code from other places - programmers sharing snippets on forums or sites like StackOverflow - but when tools like NPM hit the scene in 2014, it really felt like a gamechanger. You could just add a line to your package.json, hit npm install and - whoosh - now you could reuse code written by any stranger on the internet. Teams loved NPM (and PyPi, Maven…) because now they didn’t have to solve any hard problems if someone else had solved it first. All of the little components in a program - the cogs and wheels in my watchmaker analogy - were once crafted by hand. Now you could get cogs and wheels and whole mechanisms, for free, forever. This meant that the programmers could focus less on the details. Instead of figuring out the nitty gritty of, say, writing the code needed to check someone’s password, you could just ask NPM and friends to take care of it. Open source was great because you had a small number of passionate, unpaid developers, building code that everyone else depended on. You could make millions of dollars from their code, and you didn’t even have to be particularly nice to them. (People weren’t) But the cost was that everyone stopped knowing the details. You had to give away control. If an NPM package is compromised, or the author has an agenda, you’re in trouble. Because there were fewer details to take care of, tech professionals began to lose their specialisms. You didn’t need a team of ops people, a team of backend developers, a team of mobile developers, a team of testers. You could flatten them into generalists. This changed the balance of power between workers and management. Imagine a building site where there is a plumber, a builder, and an electrician. If any one of them threatens to quit, you have a problem, because you need each of them to get the project done. Whereas if you can make everyone a mix of plumber-builder-electrician, they lose that leverage. Whether you think that power imbalance is a bad thing may depend on your politics. But it had a slow effect of taking influence away from the people close to the work. They’re the ones able to raise the alarm when things start going wrong. By 2016-17, there were signs that the superstructure of open source had weak points. The left-pad incident was an early warning of where we were going. In the tangled web of the JavaScript ecosystem, with its myriad dependencies, one library author took down his packages in a legal conflict, and ended up breaking almost everyone else’s projects. But largely we managed to make do. Even after the hiring and firing cycle of the post-pandemic era, and near misses like the XZ Utils backdoor, technology managed mostly to remain stable - thanks to armies of diligent developers and ops folk across the globe. …And, yes, then AI. A lot has been written about how AI systems are inherently non-deterministic, a kind of slot machine that only creates simulacra of work. Acting like a stochastic parrot, this argument goes, AI generated code will always be prone to hallucinations and bugs. And there’s truth to that. But I think the danger in the present moment is the opposite. It’s not so much that the model outputs are crap and unreliable. They’re actually pretty good at doing what you ask them to do (though I suspect that mostly works because Anthropic and co heavily subsidise compute). I think the real AI threat is decoherence. Kristen Maevyn wrote an essay named The Decoherence Trap which talks about a problem where the individual parts of a system may look fine in isolation, but don’t make sense as part of a larger system. Decoherence: the accumulation of locally valid but mutually incompatible or redundant models within a system, such that the cost of change is dominated by translating among those models and preventing unintended side-effects. Software engineers, as I’ve seen them working over the last year, have all but turned over all their work to AI agents. It started with small tasks like writing tests, functions, and individual components. But now it’s everything - not only the components, but the design, the orchestration, the whole concept. Programming was the activity of translating ideas and intents from the messy human world into code so crystalline, so precise and pedantic, that even a computer could execute it. It was fundamentally the act of distilling complexity into order, making something real out of nothing. This activity is rapidly dying. It no longer happens in most tech companies. Most SWEs now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent - they just can’t keep on top of the complexity. Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels - we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole. Kristen writes: Decoherence grows relative to the rate of change of a system, and it increases faster the more decoherent a system is, resulting in runaway exponential growth. It is not a new phenomenon, and humans have always countered it through carefully finding ways to do more with less, unifying disparate patterns and models into a cohesive whole. However, the widespread use of AI is currently producing it at a rate that is unsustainable. A form of learned helplessness has emerged, along with a paradoxical false confidence, caused by the ways LLMs provide the illusion of work without actually forcing us to think through the details. This de-skilling of software engineers only shifts the balance of power even further away from developers - who can no longer raise the alarm. At its worst, AI turns tech workers into “meat proxies” who spend their days massaging prompts and letting Claude figure out if the work is actually complete. It’s not just programmers. It’s the whole chain, top to bottom. Everyone is using AI, especially in big tech. Claude generates code because the engineer wrote a prompt. The prompt comes from a ticket that was written with Claude. The project manager wrote the ticket based on a summary of a document, that was written by, and then summarised back, by Claude. The document uses statistics from a calculation, by Claude. The business is panicking about the stock market, and the stock market prioritises short term trends over long term engineering. Does this sound accurate? It’s a caricature, but not by a lot. I believe that tech companies risk losing their “organisational cognition” - their ability to think and respond as a coherent unit. This is the real threat: a scenario where nothing in the system is done with intent, and nobody in the system has control. We generate complexity faster than we can tame it. Look at the problems I’ve outlined. They are about systems of excessive complexity, made of parts that need to work perfectly or else everything falls apart. These parts are being individually corroded by corner-cutting, cost-cutting, overcomplication, over-reliance on uncompensated work and - I fear - helplessness amongst the people who build digital infrastructure. This is a threat to all of us. The tech industry is now critical to everyday life. It’s the software that controls your flights, your banking, your petrol pumps, your TV, your payroll. It’s what allows you to navigate roads and find your friends. It’s how you date and how you eat. It’s how you’re reading this. Society has extended trust, too much trust, into technical systems that are now demonstrating systemic deterioration. I do not think society, government, or institutions are prepared for a world where the incidents and outages of 2026 become commonplace. They too are extending the chain of dependencies, assumptions, complexity and unwarranted trust. Each layer, each link in the chain is a new point of attack that can subvert everything on top of it. The internet is at a breaking point. The software we build is not legible enough to bear the responsibility the world is giving it. We are telling ourselves the AI revolution is succeeding, precisely because of the rate at which we are generating complexity. The actual load-bearing parts of the ecosystem - open source, engineering-led judgement - are crumbling away. I think we are only at the beginning of a very painful phase. This is not a blip, and it’s not an aberration - it’s the new normal. © 2026 Jimmy Breck-McKye. Built with Astro.

Tesla's Cybercab comes with some pretty important T&Cs. Elon Musk's EV giant said on Friday that select customers were now being invited to buy Tesla's steering-wheel-less robotaxi for their own personal use. For the lucky few who have received an invite, the Cybercab starts at $29,990, with an "autonomy subscription" of $299 a month. Opting out of that subscription will turn the Cybercab into a shiny gold lawn ornament. The autonomous EV "will not operate" without an autonomy subscription, according to Tesla's Cybercab order and subscription agreements, which were uploaded to Tesla's website over the weekend.  Those who get the green light to order a Cybercab will also only be able to drive it within the limits of Tesla's Robotaxi ride-hailing service. Right now, that includes parts of Austin, Dallas, and three other cities in Texas, as well as Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. But owners will not be able to add their Cybercabs to the service and make money from them, a key part of the robotaxi pitch Musk has been making for nearly a decade. That's not the only catch. Like other limited-edition vehicles Tesla has released, Cybercab owners are barred from reselling their robotaxis without the company's permission. Those who do face a $50,000 penalty, and Tesla might also remotely brick your vehicle. More unusually, the Cybercab's order agreement says that Tesla can repurchase the vehicle "at any time," at a fair market value determined by the company. A replacement is not guaranteed, and owners have to pay the cost of shipping their Cybercab back to Tesla.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  Other details buried in the fine print include a ban on modifications, including wraps and tinted windows. Would-be Cybercab owners should also be aware that Tesla will be collecting their data.  That includes personally identifying data such as location data and "cabin camera image data" recorded by a camera above the rear-view mirror, per the autonomy subscription agreement, which states that the data will be used to provide ride support and improve the product. It's unclear whether Cybercab owners can opt out. The Cybercab is not the first Tesla vehicle to come with major strings attached. Early adopters of the company's Cybertruck pickup also faced a $50,000 penalty if they tried to resell it within a year, and Tesla told customers who spent $250,000 to reserve the rocket-powered Roadster last month that it "cannot guarantee" the flying EV will ever be delivered. The subscription-only model of the Cybercab, however, is the latest sign that Tesla is pivoting toward a business model closer to a tech company than an automaker. Musk announced this month that Tesla would discontinue the Cybertruck, after the company sunset the Model S and X earlier this year. The billionaire CEO has said that in the future, most of Tesla's revenue will come from robotaxis, autonomous driving subscriptions, and the company's Optimus humanoid robot. Early invitees to order the Cybercab, which Tesla estimates will begin deliveries in December, include YouTuber Marques Brownlee. The tech reviewer once bet that if Tesla delivered a sub-$30,000 Cybercab by the end of 2026, he'd shave his head. In a series of X posts over the weekend, Brownlee said that his hair was safe as the Cybercab was not publicly available, before posting a screenshot of a confirmed order after some goading from Musk.  He added that the fact that the Cybercab is geofenced to a small number of locations meant Tesla has so far not delivered on Musk's promises of personal robotaxis. "It's a paperweight if I take this thing home," Brownlee said. Jump to

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Kunal Bahl, the 43-year-old cofounder of the Indian digital commerce holding company AceVector Limited and investment firm Titan Capital. It has been edited for length and clarity. Entrepreneurship was always on the cards for me. An H-1B rejection just fast-tracked it. I grew up in New Delhi, and then I went to the University of Pennsylvania in the US for a program that blended an engineering and business degree. While I was in college, a bunch of big things happened in the tech sphere: Google went public, and Facebook became viral. By 2006, which is when I graduated, it was all the rage. The internet economy was taking off. I had a lot of business ideas, but it became clear that I could not start a company because of my visa status. I was on an F-1 visa, and I first needed to find an employer who could sponsor my H-1B, then lay out a pathway into Silicon Valley. From there, I'd try to start my own company. I interned at Microsoft during my junior year and returned in October 2006 in a full-time role after graduating. While waiting for my H-1B visa selection, I was counting down the days until my Optional Practical Training, a temporary yearlong work authorization after graduation, would expire. I remember vividly that, in June or July of 2007, I got an email that said my H-1B petition had been rejected. For a moment, I didn't understand. It was unfathomable to me that, if I worked at a company like Microsoft, my H-1B visa would not be approved.                                    Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.                                  I checked with the Microsoft team. Looking at their faces, I gathered that there was a finality to the rejection. The company was very nice about the situation, suggesting that I work in the Microsoft India office and try again for the H-1B after a year. At no point had I considered moving back to India. But I gathered myself up and decided that if I go back to my country, I'd work for myself, not for Microsoft. I no longer had the baggage of having to figure out this H-1B situation. I felt liberated because I didn't have to worry about visas or green cards. So I called up my best friend from high school, Rohit Bansal, who was working in a financial institution at the time. We used to sit next to each other in class and talk about starting a business together. I asked if he wanted to do something together. He said, "Great, let's do it." Our company was incorporated on September 12, 2007, a few days before I touched down in India. India has a hot startup ecosystem now. That cannot be said of the India of 2007. The country had very few internet users and smartphones, and digital payments were few and far between. Things were pretty dull, to be honest. I was not returning to the promised land or a burgeoning startup ecosystem. Even launching a startup was frowned upon. People would ask, "You guys have a good education, so why didn't you get a job? Does nobody want to hire you?" We started as a physical coupon book business, because Indians love a good value. But getting funding was a challenge. Angel investors weren't common then. We had both saved up a bit from our year working corporate jobs and pooled our savings — about $60,000 in total. That became our seed capital. We stayed with our families for food and accommodation, and worked out of a small office in the basement of a residential building in Delhi's furniture market. We had neighbors complain about people going in and out of the building late, because Rohit and I would work 20 hours a day to get our business off the ground. Our company pivoted from being an online couponing platform like Groupon to one of India's first e-commerce platforms, called Snapdeal. Now we have two publicly listed companies that we spun off from the original coupon book business. We wanted to give back to the startup ecosystem in India, as well. In 2011, once we had built up some capital, we started investing in early-stage startups and formed Titan Capital. Over the last 15 years, we've invested in more than 320 startups, many of which have gone public. I'm now also a judge on Shark Tank India. In hindsight, my not getting the H-1B visa was serendipitous, though it hurt at the time. It was part of a larger plan: I had to return to India and help the next generation of founders. It was easy for me to pack up my bags and come back because I wasn't married and didn't have children. And I know it's far more difficult for those who have dependents living with them in the US, like children or parents. So I do empathize with workers facing immigration struggles in the US. That said, India has changed drastically since the time we started our company. India now has a billion internet users. There's ubiquitous smartphone penetration. There are so many coworking spaces for startup founders. There is a high talent density. There is a robust funding ecosystem. The startup tech scene is front of mind for the government. There is no better time to come back to India. Jump to

Author of the Legal AI Insider newsletter I’m heading to Scottsdale for the TLTF Summit, an invite-only gathering of law firm leaders, general counsels, and startup builders, with one question: Is winter coming for legal tech? Mentioned in this issue: Victor Wang, Eilla, Crunchbase, Harvey, Legora, Anthropic, Davis Polk, Nikki Shaver, Leah, Latham & Watkins, Crosby, Norm, Atticus, Finch, Theo Ai, Irys, Eve, Jay Madheswaran, Emily Heyward, Red Antler, Laurel, and Ryan Alshak.  Agenda A LinkedIn post from commercial lawyer Victor Wang caught my attention last week. Wang cited data from startup Eilla suggesting that funding for legal-tech startups fell 39% year over year after stripping out the blockbuster rounds for Harvey and Legora. I decided to check Eilla’s math against Crunchbase, a database I use regularly. Crunchbase shows that legal-tech startups raised a record $4.6 billion in 2025. Harvey and Legora’s rounds alone accounted for just over $1 billion, or 23% of that total. So far this year, startups in the space have raised $3.8 billion, per Crunchbase. The two giants took a bigger share. Their rounds account for $1.95 billion, or 51% of all funding. So, how does Eilla’s thesis hold up? Crunchbase suggests the gap may be even wider. Funding for everyone else totals $1.89 billion so far this year, compared with $3.59 billion in all of 2025 — a difference of roughly 47%. One important caveat: This compares a year-to-date figure with a full-year total. Still, the concentration of capital is hard to miss — and the drop-off hard to ignore. Two plausible explanations: The category is maturing. Investors may see Harvey and Legora as the runaway leaders in the race for law firms and corporate legal departments. Those who can get in may prefer to write larger checks to the two companies rather than spread their bets across younger startups. Investors may also be waiting to see how the model labs change the game. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft are all moving deeper into the legal market. That could make investors wary of startups that look like thin wrappers around the same underlying models. I’ll be looking for other explanations at the TLTF Summit. Tell me your theories. Now that I’ve said it, you can’t unsee it: An astonishing number of startups building for lawyers have human names. There’s Harvey, named partly for “Suits” superlawyer Harvey Specter. Legora was once Leya, not to be confused with contracts startup Leah. Crosby and Norm sound like two guys from the Rat Pack. Legal tech has room for not one but two companies named Atticus, plus a Finch. For an industry obsessed with automating human work, its startups seem awfully attached to names you’d find on a Park Slope preschool roster. Looking at you, Theo Ai and Irys. For centuries, law firms have been putting people’s names on the door, trading on the reputations of the lawyers behind them. The startups may be following suit. Eve makes software for plaintiff-side firms that help everyday people take on insurers and corporations. Cofounder Jay Madheswaran says the company takes its name from EVE, the sleek robot who steals WALL-E’s heart in the Pixar movie, not the biblical first woman. “EVE plays a very heroic role and we felt that was appropriate,” he said. “Also, we’re big fans of palindromes.” Emily Heyward has another theory. Her branding agency, Red Antler, worked with Laurel, a startup that helps lawyers track their billable hours, when it rebranded from Time by Ping. Human names took off during consumer tech’s heyday, as startups like Casper and Oscar were trying to persuade people to do unfamiliar things online, like buy a mattress or shop for health insurance. Now, legal tech is asking lawyers to trust machines with work once done by people. Heyward thinks a friendly name can help make that leap feel a little less daunting. “It’s like a business you could grab a beer with,” she said. For Ryan Alshak, cofounder of Laurel, the name checked a few boxes. It has roots in ancient Greece, where laurel wreaths symbolized victory and honor. He also liked that it began and ended with the same letter, “to symbolize that time is both finite and infinite,” he said. The name turned out to be more personal than he imagined. Earlier this year, Alshak got curious about the meaning of his late mother’s name. Randa, he discovered, is an Arabic name associated with a fragrant tree: the bay laurel. “Sometimes the name chooses us,” he said.
