Arcentry journal Sometimes, repetition is good. Service Oriented Architectures give teams the freedom to work the way they work best. You are Lisa. You work at Megabank. Your team builds the account management part of the website - transaction lists with filters and queries, charts for account levels, and statement exports in .csv and .pdf. Youâve built a sleek backend in Go and a frontend in Svelte, all running on a Kubernetes cluster that you manage. Your buddy Steve, two floors up, builds the investment banking part of the customer portal. Portfolio lists with filters and queries, charts for market prices, and order exports in CSV and PDF. They used Node for WebSocket connections, Erlang for the processing side, and React for a smoother frontend experience. Hanna, on floor five, handles credit cards. Her team has developed a nice customer portal featuring a list of credit card charges that can be filtered and queried. Pretty charts allow you to track debt levels over time. And, for extra convenience, you can export your charges in CSV and PDF. Hannaâs team implemented all this in PHP running on Apache servers, with a frontend in Angular.  All three teams adhered to the corporate branding guidelines, so their products look and feel reasonably similar. They also work fairly well and were shipped on time. But - great news! Megabank has hired some new top talent. Mike comes from the mythical lands of tech and management consultancy. Heâll be the super senior VP of platform at Megabank. It takes Mike just two days to realise that work at Megabank is highly inefficient. Each team has reimplemented the same functionality over and over again. They are also relying on their own stacks, so transferring people between teams is much harder. Sure, they shipped quality products on time - but with Mikeâs process improvement expertise, imagine how much more they could be doingâ¦ Mike creates a fourth team-the platform team. That team has two tasks: Soon, the platform team goes to work. They decide that backend functionality will be implemented in Go from here on, frontends in React, and everything will be hosted on Kubernetes. As far as platform teams go, this is a very modern and common-sense decision. The other teams start learning these technologies. Some already have some experience; others have to learn from scratch - but those are just temporary teething pains. Soon, everyone will have adjusted to the new reality and efficiency will skyrocket. Except maybe for the investment banking team. They really need their Erlang architecture for decentralized networking - after all, they process fast-moving market data, order execution, and the like. It also turns out that Go is overkill for the credit card guys. They just need a simple model-view-controller architecture like PHP provides. Having pointers to memory addresses and managing concurrency via goroutines rather than just writing linear PHP that Apache runs in parallel is really much more than they bargained for. But at least on the frontend side, a lot of time will be saved. The new list components and charts are well designed and can just be dropped into a customer portal, saving lots of development time. Except for the investment banking team - they need candlestick charts that were supported by their chart library but havenât made it into the generic charting component yet. They raise a ticket with the platform team, but it gets deprioritised since the CSV and PDF exports have to be implemented first. The credit card team is also really struggling with porting their backend to Go. They ask if they could use the transaction list from the platform team but send the same data format from their existing PHP implementation. The platform team doesnât want to be seen as the obstacle, so they agree. But writing documentation for the internal data structure of the transaction list component hasnât been planned for - after all, it was never meant to be available externally. And really, the focus right now is on building the PDF and CSV exports. Unfortunately, this year, none of the teams will be shipping much. But Mike made an amazing presentation called âMegabank platform vision 2028 â a road to global efficiencyâ. So his bonus will be fine. This story has played out too many times. You were probably part of it at some point. And it makes sense on its face. The inefficiencies are real. But-they are necessary. Different requirements need different solutions. Different people know different things. Standardisation and abstraction seem like good solutions on their face but are hard to implement in practice. Minor differences multiply into large, unwieldy problems. The solution is often the opposite of what good software design teaches. Do Repeat Yourself. At least, allow for some level of repetition. But more importantly, create clear boundaries within which teams can be flexible, and clear interfaces and protocols to interact and combine their services. This idea is as old as the internet - and is often called Service-Oriented Architecture, or SOA for short. Think of service-oriented architecture like going to a street food market. Each vendor has a little booth with a menu of available options. If you want to order something, you know you need to talk to the vendor, request your option, and pay using a shared currency or card. Thatâs the common interface. How the vendor prepares the food, where they source their ingredients from, which kitchen appliances they use - all of that is not your concern. You interact with the common interface. For our three teams, that means that each can continue using their stack and approach and ship at their own cadence. But Mike also had a point with his platform team. There are things that are necessary for a user experience to not feel disjointed. And there are capabilities, such as DevOps, that are best handled centrally. So, rather than prescribing an exact technology stack and building shared components, Mike shifts the platform teamâs responsibility. It now: With these changes, efficiency rises back up. Not because the teams stopped rebuilding the same thing, but because they’ve stopped getting in each other’s way. Some code is duplicated. Some problems are solved three different ways. And that’s fine. Minimizing the amount of code written or the number of technologies used isnât a goal in itself - but building good products, shipping them on time, and allowing teams to work effectively together is. Lesbians and other queer women have made Saint James Libations a go-to spot in the little over a year that it’s been open. But this isn’t just any lesbian bar. There’s exposed brick on the walls and Lauryn Hill is playing on vinyl while friends, lovers and temporary strangers are throwing back glasses of wine in lieu of tequila shots. “We just wanted to create something really beautiful, especially for our age and our demographic, which is 30-plus, where it’s not just all parties,” said Lola Memberr. Memberr and her partner, Akila K. Stewar,t are the Black lesbian couple behind the space. “In the queer community we love to party and stuff, but we wanted to do something a little bit more third space-y, more of a focus on wine, focus on hospitality.” A look at the event calendar at Saint James Libations shows that there’s always something going on, from its jazz nights to its “WLW” — or women loving women – parties on Saturdays to its happy hour with $2 oysters and discounted glasses of wine. And while the vibe at Saint James is unique, it is a part of a larger trend of wine bars, clubs and other upscale cocktail spaces that are specifically designed with the LGBTQ+ community in mind. It’s a cultural phenomenon that seems largely feasible in only a small handful of U.S. cities, according to Stephanie Bonvissuto, a women and gender studies professor at Hunter College. “Let’s remember what a third space is, right? It’s not a working space, it’s not a home space but it’s a space for communities to come together to share ideas, to build community,” Bonvissuto said. “So New York City has a longstanding history of literally — and figuratively — making room for that.” It wasn’t that long ago where it didn’t seem as if there was any room at all. The number of lesbian bars across the U.S. had slowly dwindled from roughly 200 in the 1980s to less than 20 in 2020, a year that saw businesses of all kinds shutter their doors en masse. By 2021, there were only three spaces dedicated to queer women left in New York City: Ginger’s Bar, in Park Slope, and Cubbyhole and Henrietta Hudson, less than a mile away from each other in the West Village. But at least a dozen new spaces operated by queer women have opened across the U.S. in the last half decade, with a particular resurgence of post-pandemic spaces for queer women in New York City. The city now boasts three different queer women-owned sports bars — Blazer’s, Athene Keke’s and Wilka’s. There’s Ligaw, a speakeasy in the Lower East Side operated by a couple, and a self-proclaimed “dyke bar for the queers” known as The Bush in Bushwick to name a few that have set up shop in recent years. It’s partly fueled by what Bonvissuto, who is a queer trans woman, refers to as a politically fraught period in which the rolling back of federal protections for LGBTQ+ people is heightening the urgency to find some semblance of community. “I think that there is a strong correlation between politically repressive times and this desire for community space, the desire to see ourselves, to be around people who are speaking our language, right?” Bonvissuto said. “Part of culture is a shared vernacular, and we want to see that, hear that and be a part of that.” The proverbial renaissance of third spaces is providing an array of options for LGBTQ+ patrons, and allowing some establishments to tap into a particular market. Both the pair behind Saint James Libations — and others spearheading spaces for queer people who love wine — described a similar profile of a typical patron: an older queer woman who is often in search of a more sophisticated night out. After her favorite cafe-slash-bar in Ocean Hill closed, Gia Ramos was on the hunt for a space where she could be surrounded by other queer people. That’s when she heard about a Black lesbian owned wine lounge-slash-bookstore opening up in Bedford Stuyvesant. This piqued the curiosity of Ramos, 28, who said that wine has been her de facto drink of choice as someone who was not a heavy drinker. Within months, she became a regular at Gladys Books & Wine, often swinging by multiple times a week. “I love music, but sometimes you just want to be able to vibe, and I feel like that’s what wine bars kind of represent,” Ramos said. “It still kind of gives a vibe, but not too much anxiety.” When Tiffany Dockery first opened Gladys, she envisioned a space that would cater to the “Black auntie aesthetic.” “The design of the space was meant for Black women to walk in and think of that auntie who might have moved away to the big city and created a life all on her own,” she said. And while she originally envisioned catering to a clientele of Black queer women in their late 30s to mid 40s, she's been surprised to even see some people in their twenties who have also flocked to the space as well. “After COVID, I think a lot of us went through this reckoning with our relationship with alcohol because that’s what you did during COVID,” she said. “But now I don’t really want to have a strong drink, but I still want to have something in my hand. I think wine lends itself to a more elevated culinary experience.” Like Saint James Libations, Gladys Books & Wine hosts events geared toward putting people in a room where they have no choice but to talk to each other, ranging from speed-dating events, wine tasting events and book discussions. Its aim is to make it very clear who the bar is interested in attracting. “I’m very strong about us not just being lesbian-owned but a lesbian space,” Dockery said. “I think they’re a part of our history and I think we need them to continue the larger social project of liberating ourselves, which is not just at the core of being a lesbian, but also being queer.” For Megan Utter, 32, starting a wine club gave her the opportunity to create the third space that she wanted to see. It all started when she posted about wanting to start a wine club on Lex, an app that acts as a figurative bulletin board for people wanting to post missed connections, reselling tickets sold-out queer events or needing to borrow power tools. The response was encouraging enough for Utter to host the first event in which thirty people showed up. Chardonnay’s premise was simple. Each month, Utter works with a wine bar to host a pop-up event for queer people — although its audience leans towards lesbian women and other sapphic wine lovers — and can essentially take over any given space to create a pop-up queer wine bar. A Chardonngay party. The city is now home to more events like this, many of which not only subtly cater to an older crowd, but explicitly market to one. There’s Officially Exes, through which parties and ticketed dinners are advertised for members of the lesbian and sapphic community ages 28 and up, as well as Old Bae, which charges an extra cover for anyone under 30 at its takeover of the Bush, a popular lesbian bar. “I just feel like the nature of wine bars is where I feel the most comfortable because they're very approachable,” Utter said. “I love a party, but it's just hard to walk up to someone and be like, ‘Hey! What’s your name?’ And I feel like in wine bars it's quiet enough where you can, like, sit in a corner and get to know someone.” She said half of attendees come alone and often leave with a new friend, or two. Utter said she’s been able to build nearly her entire friend group through the wine club. A friend of hers recently started dating someone she had met at one of the Chardonngay events. Melanie Johnson, 34, said she found out about Chardonngay two years ago while scrolling through the comments on a TikTok video about meeting other queer people in the city. Johnson said she had already been exposed to wine tasting events while studying abroad in college, so plopping herself into a seat surrounded by other strangers wasn’t unfamiliar. It was at the third event that Johnson said she met a couple other queer attendees who invited her to go to a couple events for Pride afterward. Those same people have formed the basis of a friend group she’s been able to sustain since then. She’s been to roughly half a dozen Chardonngay events since — and it has continued to fuel her social calendar. She’s even run into a couple familiar faces — which has prompted a couple “I didn’t know you were also queer?!” or a “Wait! What are you also doing here?” moments. “This year I met another girl and we've hung out a ton this summer since meeting, and I can already tell we're gonna be good friends,” Johnson said. “So it's the gift that keeps on giving, for sure.” Back at Saint James Libations, Stewart and Memberr are already reminiscing on the completion of an opening year. “What's kept us driving and kept us going is just the immense amount of love and support that we've been given from the community,” Stewart said. She said that patrons often tell her and Memberr that they look forward to ending up at their wine bar to cap off every single week. It’s a sentiment that makes a lot of sense to the pair. “I think now I just wanna hang out, listen to good music, and just be in a space where I don't feel that I'm too old to be in, that I belong there,” Memberr said. "And I think one thing we do in the queer community is we know how to party. We know how to create culture.” Tagged Giulia Heyward is a breaking news reporter on the Day-Of desk. In its Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping guide, Google says Universal Cart can keep track of all your wishlisted items and alert you when there's a Black Friday price drop. It can also keep an eye on out-of-stock items and let you know when they're back in stock. These alerts have been available since Universal Cart launched in the US about a month ago. It allows you to save products you find in Google Search, AI Mode, or the Gemini app, and they'll be in the same cart when you come back to shop online. Route previews reveal delays, weather, tolls and parking tips so you can plan around disruptions before you leave. Sanuj Bhatia / MakeUseOf  If you've ever kept a sold-out item's webpage open for days in the hope that the Buy Now button would appear again, Universal Cart might have just what you need. Although Google's not the only one providing such services. Safari's Notify Me feature already offers pretty much the same thing to iOS users. Adding products to the cart can trigger email alerts or push notifications through the Google app. Android users are automatically opted in to push alerts, while folks on iOS need to allow notifications for the app in Settings. You can manage the two types of alerts separately, so you can leave cart emails on and turn off push notifications if you'd rather check deals from your inbox. Moreover, the cart can show you relevant promo codes when you're finalizing your purchase. You also have the option to check out with Google Pay (if supported) or finish your purchase on the retailer's website. Before finalizing a purchase, it's good practice to check price changes with Google to make sure you're actually getting a legitimate Black Friday deal. To see how good the new price actually is, open the product listing on Google and look for Price Insights. It allows you to compare offers from different stores and see how the current price stacks up against what the item usually costs. You can even use these features when you're shopping in a physical store. If something catches your eye on a shelf, Google Lens can help you find the exact product online, even if you don't know what it's called. By Stephanie Chalmers The majority of Australia's central bank board judged a fifth hike in interest rates this year was needed this month, as inflation risks were still skewed to the upside and financial conditions might not be as restrictive as required. Minutes of the RBA's November 2-3 board meeting released this morning showed six of the nine members assessed policy tightening this year were not "clearly sufficient" to address inflation risks given the potential rise in the neutral rate and how sticky inflation has been. "In particular, they judged the risks of unintentionally leaving monetary policy insufficiently restrictive currently to outweigh the probability associated with unintentionally setting monetary policy too tight," the minutes showed. "These members cited the length of time inflation had been - and was projected to remain - above target ... They also cited various tentative signs of residual economic resilience." Thus, a fifth rate rise was warranted to provide "greater assurance" that inflation would come down, it noted. The three members who voted against a hike were concerned that the economy might be near the point of entering a materially sharper downturn as unemployment climbed and housing prices fell, and wanted more time to assess the impact of the rate hikes so far. The RBA has raised interest rates five times this year to an 18-year high of 4.85% to fight inflation. The policy tightening has been felt most acutely in the housing market, which is on track for its biggest downturn in four decades. Unemployment also hit a five-year high of 4.7%. The split decision had markets wagering that interest rates have likely peaked in Australia. Rate cuts are coming into view, with about 22 basis points of easing priced in by the end of next year. Low fares and free snacks used to be all it took to win over fliers.  These days, however, airlines are chasing the travelers willing to spend extra — and JetBlue wants a bigger piece of the pie. The airline unveiled its new domestic first-class cabin, dubbed "BlueFirst," at a media event in New York last Wednesday. Launching in December, it's JetBlue's latest effort to capitalize on the booming demand for premium travel as it shifts from its low-cost roots. BlueFirst is quintessentially JetBlue — and, I think, a sweet spot in the market: chic and playful, with distinctive touches like its "Mixologist Mode," that allows you to mix your own cocktail. Still, it lacks some of the more over-the-top bells and whistles found in the Big 3's newest first-class seats. While I'm excited for JetBlue's evolution, choosing it means accepting some of the airline's less glamorous trade-offs. JetBlue has long lagged major US airlines in on-time performance — and it chose Amazon Leo, not Starlink, for its next-generation WiFi.  A spokesperson said reliability is a "top priority," and JetBlue recognizes that "a consistent, reliable experience is an essential part of delivering the service our customers expect." Still, I think frequent flyers and people looking for a nice new premium option will like what JetBlue has on tap. About a month ahead of BlueFirst's inaugural flight from Boston to Fort Lauderdale on December 8, JetBlue Airways invited a small group of media to tour the new cabin. The cabin was small — just three rows deep — but I found the classic JetBlue branding and modern finishes distinguished it from competitors. JetBlue said the cabin size will vary by aircraft. "It's premium, but is certainly not pretentious," JetBlue's SVP of marketing and brand, Stephanie Evans Greene, said of the design. I was eager to try JetBlue's new "Mixology Mode," which lets customers use the seatback screen to concoct a drink order with up to four ingredients and send it to the flight attendants. The tool is organized into categories, from soft drinks and mixers to alcohol and preset cocktails. I chose the Brothers Bond bourbon whiskey with a Diet Pepsi since JetBlue doesn't serve Coke products. My drink was delivered on a coaster, made by local New York artist Danielle Rose Fisher, which I thought was a nice touch. The ingredients weren't pre-mixed, which I prefer because it lets me control the strength of each sip. In my opinion, phone stands are a must in first class; they make doomscrolling on a cross-country flight much more comfortable. On BlueFirst, the phone stand is on the tray table. Delta, American, and United all offer device holders in some first-class cabins, but not across their entire fleets. There's also plenty of places to charge your phone or tablet, including USB-C, USB-A, and a universal power outlet. Poking around the seat, I found large storage bins in the middle armrests; the tray tables were in the outer ones. I could store things like a water bottle, chargers, and a book. The seatback pocket would fit my laptop. I thought there was plenty of nooks to stay organized, and the dedicated overhead bin space would be helpful, too. When the flight attendant delivered my drink, she pulled out the second mini-table built into the seat — I probably would've missed it otherwise. The Big 3 offer versions of this feature, too, and I'm glad JetBlue didn't leave it out. I don't want to spar with my seatmate over table space. It's standard for first class to get a hot or cold meal on flights over a certain distance. On JetBlue, the minimum is 899 miles. Because JetBlue's Airbus planes don't have a microwave, they've developed bento boxes that can be served cold. They come with an entrée, a side, and a dessert. I tried several options, including the tortellini pasta salad, the smoked salmon and herb cream cheese crepe, the carrot cake, the sesame tofu noodles, and the quinoa cinnamon crunch. I also tried snacks like popcorn and sour candy and the pinot noir red wine. I thought everything was tasty and fresh — the carrot cake wasn't too sweet and the noodles weren't oversauced — and I liked the variety of food for different routes. Granted, I had these on the ground and not on the plane. I'm curious to see how the taste holds up at 35,000 feet. One thing I noticed about JetBlue's small BlueFirst cabin was that it lacked privacy dividers between seats or a curtain separating it from the rest of the plane. Often, the Big 3 will curtain off first class from economy to distinguish the service. Delta and United have gone a step further in their newest cabins by adding dividers or wings for added privacy. Blake Rittenberg, JetBlue's senior manager for product development, said the setup is intentional: "We're an egalitarian airline; we like to have everybody feel part of this," he said. "It's the same reason we don't have the curtain in Mint." The third row of BlueFirst does have small flaps between each set of seats to provide some privacy from the people behind — to me, that's a logical middle ground. BlueFirst comes with a number of perks beyond the seat itself, like priority boarding and free checked luggage, but it does not guarantee access to JetBlue's new airport lounge network, BlueHouse. There are locations in New York-JFK and Boston that can be accessed by JetBlue Premier credit cardholders, Mosaic 4 members — JetBlue's highest loyalty tier — and those flying in Mint business class to Europe, the Caribbean, or coast to coast. Those with BlueFirst tickets alone will be turned away unless they also have the right credit card or status. A spokesperson told me: "This approach allows customers to choose the products and benefits that best suit their travel needs." This isn't unusual; the Big 3 have similar restrictions, though United and American allow lounge access to first-class passengers on certain international regional routes, such as to Canada, Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean. Basic premium — or the unbundling of premium tickets to cut fares — has taken hold across airlines, aiming to make premium more attainable. United, Delta, and JetBlue all offer it. For JetBlue, "BlueFirst Base" strips away advanced seat selection, a second free checked bag, free cancellations or changes, and same-day switches. Looking at the Boston-Fort Lauderdale route through March, some "Base" fares, pictured, are as low as $650 round-trip, with "Flex" fares often over $1,000. The basic economy fare on the pictured trip is about $390. JetBlue said pricing will fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. I'm among those who like the idea of basic premium, and a $650 price tag would be worth the three-hour trek for me — especially if economy is only a few hundred dollars cheaper. Jump to

Michael Irwin's latest project relied more on his woodworking and people skills than his deep knowledge of coding. The principal software engineer for Docker, a platform that helps developers adopt models, tools and agents securely, handmade a wooden base to serve as a gaming controller, attached red, blue, and green buttons with wires, and took it to a conference last week. It corresponded to a game coded by AI, and Irwin used the gimmick to draw people to his booth where he engaged them in talks about AI agents. The game is a frill that Irwin wouldn't have taken the time to make before AI accelerated coding. "It's been a dream of mine for a long time, and it's just now more accessible than it's ever been," he says. Gone are the days when software engineers spent most of their time in solitude, coding remotely and rarely attending meetings. Their remit has expanded beyond the keyboard, and the boundaries of technical work have blurred. Companies, including Amazon, increasingly expect engineers to connect personally with customers. People outside engineering teams at many companies have taken up generating code and using AI at work; a fifth of OpenAI's Codex users were non-developers as of June. Bosses expect developers to manage teams of agents and communicate complex technical work in simple terms, all while acting as designers, architects, and big picture conceptual thinkers rather than cogs in a coding machine. "The micro level is mostly able to be passed off," Irwin says. "It takes a different mindset." "This new way of working, it might not suit the typical engineer personality," says Sam Dhar, an engineer at Galileo, an AI startup Cisco acquired earlier this year. But it relies on the expertise and judgement that engineers have always had to build over their careers. Still, there's pressure for developers to make that mindset shift in a condensed timeline or risk being laid off and replaced by someone who can charm their way through an interview rather than ace a take-home coding test. Hit swiftly and broadly by automation, developers are a bellwether for white-collar work. They sit at the frontier of AI's transformation of work, which will either swallow jobs or create new ones, depending on who you ask. "It's only happening to engineering first," Dhar says. "It's potentially going to manifest in a way where all work is done in some respects with AI, where the accountability still resides with the humans who are reviewing and fixing and asking the right questions." Reports of the coding apocalypse are greatly exaggerated, so far. More people work in the field than ever: About 1.9 million people worked in software development, testing, and quality assurance in the US as of last year, up from about 1.5 million in 2020, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. The bureau projects the industry will grow by 10% over the next decade. A developer in 2020 would hardly recognize the demands of the job today. Vibe coding forever changed software engineering last year. Big companies like Microsoft said Google AI had written large swaths of their latest code, and engineers began spending more time reviewing lines of AI-generated code than they did typing it. Experienced developers finished projects faster, and companies scaled back on hiring junior engineers. 2026, the father of vibe coding said, would be the year of "agentic engineering." Amazon Web Service recently used agents to generate 100% of the code for a new emulator tool. Software engineers have moved away from writing code and on to concepts. They still need deep technical expertise to evaluate AI's work, but they also need business sense. "You have to really understand a lot more about why we're doing whatever it is we're doing, and ask a lot of the right questions," says Paul Elliott, vice president of product and engineering at software testing company Chromatic. That requires more conversations across the company. For all the left-brain, right-brain debate and stereotypes of developers working remotely with headphones on, engineers are making the leap to become more forward-facing. "It's definitely a trainable skill," Elliott says. Marc Brooker, vice president and distinguished engineer at Amazon Web Services, says engineers on his team now spend more time with customers and prospects, talking to decision-makers and developers at other companies. Training for these scenarios is less formal and more often involves shadowing calls with engineers who have more public-facing experience. "The outcome of that is so that the engineers can go back to their teams and their organizations and turn what they learned into really great product decisions, really great technical decisions," Brooker says. Dylan Wight, founding software engineer at Flagler Health, an AI-native operating system for musculoskeletal care, says that his days now consist of reviewing code issues raised by agents and determining if they're practical problems or oversensitive flags. Wight also has multiple meetings weekly with the system's users in the healthcare industry, which he welcomes. He has a side "that's more entrepreneurial and likes talking to users and understanding their needs," he says. "If people wanted to just think about code, I think it would get harder, because that part is mostly done." The wall between engineer and product manager is breaking down. Product managers previously owned many of those client conversations, volleying between business needs and the technical expertise of developer teams. Now, AI companies increasingly use the term "member of technical staff" to describe their workers. Anthropic released a report about its workforce last month, showing that technical workers spent 16% more time in meetings now compared to a year ago. At the same time, more workers are shipping code, and engineers are gaining a stronger presence: The ratio of engineers to product managers has jumped to 17 to one. "Engineers are definitely taking on more product level autonomy, but product managers are also taking on more technical work," says Frank Fusco, CEO of software company Silicon Society. "I think the definitions of those jobs are changing." Forward-deployed engineers, who work inside another company's systems, have become increasingly popular in the AI era, as they work with clients on solutions, combining technical knowledge with that problem-solving ethos. Companies increasingly demand technical candidates who can work in the office, a shift after years of allowing them to work independently and remotely. Michelle Volberg, CEO of software recruiting company Twill, says that last year about half of the roles her company worked to fill were remote. Now, some 95% of jobs require hybrid or full-time in-office work. That mirrors larger trends in white-collar work as employers have gained power in a tight labor market, but perhaps also a desire to have engineers communicating across the company more frequently. In early 2024, 63% of tech jobs postings had in-office requirements, according to data from recruiting and staffing company Robert Half. That figure now hovers at 84% this fall. The proportion of job posts for remote tech roles declined from 10% in early 2023 to just 3%. "A lot of these managers are bringing engineering on site now to have this collaborative approach," says Kareem Osman, tech industry expert at Robert Half. Some hiring managers now require candidates to have those public speaking skills, Volberg says. She searches for developers active on social media like YouTube and LinkedIn who already talk or post publicly about what they're building. "It also comes down to the soft skills of, 'can you talk to the CEO and the founder about what the business needs directly as an engineer and then translate that into something that you're going to go to your desk and build?'" she says. Data from CompTIA, a nonprofit trade association for the US IT industry, shows that 47% of open software engineer roles in early 2020 listed communication skills in job descriptions, but now nearly 60% of jobs seek candidates with such skills. For some, the soft skills are there and just need some refining. Chuck Hardy, director of product and engineering at Akeneo, says the company pulled engineering teams into customer conversations before the AI boom. He looks for people with critical thinking skills and judgment, and when hiring, gives them sample questions and spends time role-playing with candidates before they go to a panel interview. "We're not there to test you or to trick you," Hardy says. "We're there to create an environment where you can figure out how to demonstrate your best self in a short period of time." For experienced engineers, the AI boom offers an opportunity to step up to more autonomous work, while relying on their expertise to evaluate AI. But for younger engineers, the opportunity to develop expertise in the intricacies of code is vanishing. A potential career ladder collapse looms. At Anthropic, the proportion of junior technical hires declined from 27% in March of 2025 to 9% this May. About 7 to 8% of computer engineering and computer science majors who graduated in the past few years are unemployed, according to the latest data from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York — a proportion on par with performing arts majors. With demand for engineers projected to grow, the vanishing training ground could lead not just to eventual worker shortages but to a shrinking number of people with the practice and savvy to spot issues in AI-generated code. AI can turn anyone into an amateur, letting novice cooks spin up recipes, rusty writers refine their grammar, and those with limited drawing skills design templates. It has democratized coding for people who have never done more than customize an early-aughts blog. A debate brews about whether generalists or specialized experts will emerge as winners. Right now, the transformation of software engineers hints that it's both: a keen, technical eye to search for flaws and vulnerabilities in code, paired with communication skills and creative thinking, makes a candidate highly valuable. That balance could change as AI advances. But it indicates a future when the bounds of white-collar job titles and their tasks could continue to bend and blend. Week 10 was one where the lows felt higher than the highs. Drake Maye went down and took the whole Patriots offense with him. Carson Beck started his first game and the impact may have cratered the entire Arizona offense going forward, and Jonathan Taylor just might not escape generic RB1 hell. Let’s discuss.  Tyson followed up a 4/30 debut with a triumph of modern target volume, managing 11/80 on 3 targets as no Saints player other than him managed more than five. The 80 is the key here – I don’t think that Tyson needs to go skyrocketing up into the WR2 range based on this. The Saints just aren’t playing like that kind of offense right now. But I do think it at least inches into the realm of possibility down the stretch. We all knew that first-round pick Tyson would get a chance to do this sort of thing, and though the Saints didn’t win this game, they did establish that they’re willing to use him quite a bit. I’m not quite buying the idea that he is now the offense’s No. 1 option and that all Chris Olave shares are headed to the dumpster, but I do think he’s going to crowd out some of the other ancillary targets in this offense. I take no pleasure in noting that RB2 was already down bad enough with four teams on bye to have time-share backs as easy No. 2 runners. The Texans lost Woody Marks to a concussion halfway through Sunday’s disastrous loss to the Browns and will now be in line to be Houston’s No. 1 back on Thursday night assuming David Montgomery can’t get off the mat. I’m going to level with you here: I don’t think Demercado is good. I also don’t think the Texans can run the ball well. But this remains to some extent a volume game, and Demercado could be the No. 1 back against a Colts defense that has been dastardly for most of the season. He’s not someone to blow the whole FAAB wad on, but Demercado could give you a big game on Thursday before fading back into anonymity. The Tennessee Titans offense has been … cooking(?) since the bye. They’ve now scored at least 20 points in each of their last four games, and they’re playing the Cowboys next week. I already know that you don’t believe me that this is happening, and I understand and accept that. You can skip on to the next capsule to read about someone who matters. Well, you’re still here for some reason. Ayomanor has played at least 50 snaps in each of the last three games, he’s found 22 targets over those three games and turned in his first useful box score of the season with 79 scoreless yards against the Jaguars. At the same time, the Titans defense has absolutely collapsed, allowing 40 to the Bengals and Jaguars after the Jeffrey Simmons and Amani Hooker trades. This team has become a points funnel all of the sudden. And, again, they’re playing the Cowboys next week. I’m not telling you Ayomanor is a superstar waiting to be born. But there are six teams on bye next week, and you’re going to need to make some weird roster decisions. Ayomanor might just be a good enough WR3 to get you through something next week against Dallas’ barely-there defense. Kansas City’s hilarious beatdown of the Falcons culminated in Downs notching 4/53/1, the touchdown being just his second of the season. However, the additional funny context here is that Downs played just 10 offensive snaps in his first game as a Chief. Mahomes steps up and drops a dime to Josh Downs for a TD!KCvsATL on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/dwTMy1qZYC We’ve been burned by Downs before, of course, but with Eternal Non-Entity Xavier Worthy in front of him, it’s easy to understand that Downs is going to eventually feast on a larger play volume. Is it going to be a Rashee Rice volume? That I’m not yet sure of. But I am pretty sure that Downs is going to do well enough that fantasy managers will be happy. Going forward, it’s going to feel easy to pencil Downs in as a WR3. There’s also going to be plenty of runway to grow. The Colts part of his season never happened. Please stop asking about it.  (If you’re looking for Emmett Johnson praise, you’re late, I did that after Week 8.)  Drake Maye went down with an ankle injury early in the first quarter, effectively sabotaging the offense. A.J. Brown left with his own injury near the end of the game. Neither player returned, and Patriots coach Mike Vrabel deferred to testing. The early news on Maye from PFT was not exactly encouraging. New England is on bye, of course, which helps the odds that Maye won’t miss much time. But if he does miss time – and we’ve seen enough hints that this might happen – this offense looked dead in the water with Tommy DeVito under center. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. For some time the Blu-ray supplanted DVDs as the go-to format for movie watching. It provided a higher quality image than standard definition DVDs as well as eventual support for 4K resolution. However, Blu-ray players have increased in price over the last decade, and many people have moved away from owning their own physical media library. With the rise of streaming services, content has been available in a more convenient package, though Blu-ray has started to regain some footing as customers grow more and more tired of increasing subscription costs. There are more reasons for keeping Blu-ray access around than movie watching. The format can be used to back up and archive not just media files, but any file type found on a PC. You can even use Blu-ray discs to preserve your retro games library, which makes them a great alternative to hard drives and SSDs, particularly for archiving purposes. And even though many Blu-ray players remain quite expensive, PC users can simply purchase an external Blu-ray drive instead. Depending on its feature set, a Blu-ray drive can be capable of burning Blu-rays, DVDs, and CDs, as well as digitizing older such formats into digital files. Of course, they can also be used simply to watch movies and listen to music. While these devices can be quite expensive too, if you're willing to part with a few high-end features, there are more affordable Blu-ray drives out there, under $200. Here's five that are available and actually worth buying. At around $170, the ASUS SBW-06D5H-U is on the higher end of our pricing spectrum, but it's one of the most capable options available. It's a top choice among both experts and customers. Computing for Geeks has selected it as the best slim USB-C drive to pair with conversion software MakeMKV, though the drive is compatible with all kinds of software and both PC and Mac platforms. It's particularly fast, as ASUS has included USB 3.2 connectivity. The drive also supports USB-A connectivity and comes with a cable for each. In addition to being able to burn Blu-ray discs, DVDs, and CDs, this drive can burn to M-Disc, a format made to last for hundreds of years without degradation. It can burn Blu-rays at 6x speed, DVDs at 8x speed, and CDs at 24x speed. It's also capable of burning rewritable Blu-rays, which isn't a feature that's easy to find among more affordable Blu-ray drives. These drives often need accompanying software as well, and the ASUS SBW-06D5H-U comes with bundled disc-burning software called CyberLink Power2Go 8. The ASUS SBW-06D5H-U is also popular at Amazon, where it's creeping up on nearly 700 customer reviews, averaging a 4.4-star overall rating. The Dainty Blu-ray drive can connect to a PC over either its built-in USB-A or USB-C cable connectors. The connections can be used in tandem to ensure the drive receives a stable power supply while in operation. Insufficient power is a common complaint among budget Blu-ray drives, as it can cause interruption while the drive's in use. Oftentimes it may seem like the drive has failed, when in reality it simply isn't drawing enough power from the device it's connected to. This drive is compatible with Blu-ray discs, CDs, DVDs, and dual-layer DVDs, via Windows, macOS, and Linux-powered devices. While it can handle CDs and DVDs right out of the box, like most other external Blu-ray drives, third-party software is required for Blu-ray playback and writing. One free compatible option is VLC Player, which is also an essential TV app. Regularly priced at just $90, the Dainty Blu-ray drive is a bargain compared to models from the bigger names in the space. Among Amazon customers, the Dainty Blu-ray drive has received an overall rating of 4.0 stars.  While most budget external Blu-ray drives are focused primarily on getting the proper hardware into an affordable package, the Archgon Blu-ray drive comes with some modern styling to it. It is designed to be incredibly slim and sleek, using a unibody aluminum casing that looks like something Apple might make. It is, however, compatible with Windows PCs or Macs, and connects using included USB-C and USB-A cables. As far as the inner hardware goes, this external Blu-ray drive uses a high performance LG optical drive with outstanding read and write speeds.  Wirecutter named this drive the fastest in terms of ripping speeds among several they've tested. It's also rated highly by purchasers at Amazon, where it has received on overall rating of 4.2 stars and is priced at $147. Wirecutter noted that it tested slower when ripping DVDs, but that seems a small drawback to a Blu-ray drive with support for 4K resolution that's priced as well as this one, relative to the competition. The Buffalo MediaStation 6x portable is another popular Blu-ray drive, and another that Computing for Geeks speaks well of. For desktop use, the MediaStation 6x can burn Blu-rays, DVDs, CDs, and M-Discs. Regularly priced in the $190 range, this is another drive that's on the higher end of affordability, but just like the ASUS SBW-06D5H-U, it comes with CyberLink Power2Go software included. The drive will work for PC, Mac, and Linux users, with Windows 8, 10, and 11 supported on PCs. Another major draw for this drive is the company behind it. The Blu-ray drive market is packed with generic manufacturers, and while it can be a relief when names like ASUS pop up with available models, Buffalo has been around since the 1970s and makes many of its products, including the MediaStation 6x, in Japan. In addition to support for burning regular Blu-rays, the MediaStation 6x also includes support for writing to BDXL high capacity Blu-ray discs. Between the M-Disc format and the BDXL format, users have plenty of options for backing up massive media libraries as well as for simply watching Blu-ray movies. The drive has USB 3.2 connectivity through either the USB-A port or USB-C adapter.  PC users with limited built-in connection ports may want to look at the Godbpnymu 8-in-1 Blu-ray drive. Through numerous built-in ports, it's capable of being part of a multi-peripheral setup of external devices. With the inclusion of two USB-A ports and two USB-C ports, devices like a wired mouse or keyboard can be connected. The drive even includes an SD or TF card slot. For use as an archiving device, the drive can burn dual-layer Blu-ray discs at 6x speed and supports M-Discs as well. The Godbpnymu Blu-ray drive is also capable of playing Blu-ray discs through third-party software such as PowerDVD or Leawo, as well as CDs and DVDs. It's made to be taken on the go as well, coming with a carrying case and four CD sleeves. This Blu-ray drive has managed a 4.0-star overall rating among 1,400 Amazon purchasers, and while some users report quality control issues with the drive, at $68, it's one of the most affordable Blu-ray drives out there, and is listed as an Amazon Best Seller.  When affordability is the top priority in a Blu-ray drive, not all non-negotiable features are going to be part of the package. More affordable Blu-ray drives often lack things like 4K compatibility, but that's also what keeps them under the $200 price range. Using that as our pricing framework, we sought Blu-ray drives that provide the most bang for the buck within it, placing priority on drives whose feature sets made them most worth buying. While we have some hands-on experience with these kinds of devices through our own Blu-ray collections, we also looked for expert reviews and recommendations across the internet. Input from Wirecutter and Computing for Geeks informed our selections, as did hands-on feedback from customers at Amazon. When selecting Blu-ray drives from off-brand manufacturers, we turned to products with a large number of reviews to ensure that our selections lived up to the manufacturer's claims.

President Donald Trump said Monday morning that he "would not mind" if Jensen Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia and claimed that he doesn't know whether Alice Huang, the woman Huang allegedly had an affair with, is an intelligence asset for China. Before departing from the White House for a high-stakes trip to Asia, including meetings with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, Trump addressed the scandal that prompted Huang to resign from the company he co-founded in 1993 and turned into an artificial intelligence giant. Asked specifically by ABC News senior political correspondent Rachel Scott if he trusted U.S. intelligence reports that Alice Huang was a suspected intelligence asset for China, Trump responded, "I don't know that she is a spy." "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't know," Trump said. Trump had been briefed twice over the past year on Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang by intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, a U.S. official and sources briefed on the matter told ABC News. The president did not take any action at the time, the sources said. Trump was first briefed on U.S. intelligence that Jensen Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be working for Chinese intelligence in the fall of 2025, the sources told ABC News. On May 12, 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio shared intelligence with Trump on Air Force One showing Huang was in a relationship with a woman believed to be an intelligence asset for China, the U.S. official and sources said. Trump was briefed by Rubio shortly before Huang was set to join Trump on the trip to China, the U.S. official and sources said. Jensen Huang's stunning resignation was announced on Nov. 8 along with his admission to having an extramarital affair. Huang, however, did not admit to an affair with Alice Hung, just that he had been "unfaithful to my wife." The Nvidia Board appointed Colette Kress, the company's CFO, to take over as interim CEO while a search for a permanent replacement is launched. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun denied reports that Alice Huang, a one-time executive at Megaspeed International, was an intelligence agent. He told reporters, "The claim regarding a so-called Chinese spy is completely groundless and pure slander." The Singaporean cloud-computing company released a statement saying Alice Huang "left Megaspeed effective Aug. 30, 2025, and currently has no role with the company." "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters," the company's statement said. The company, which is under scrutiny over alleged transfers of advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies, also announced an internal investigation led by outside lawyers. Megaspeed told The Associated Press that it runs a "legitimate and lawful business" and was aware of media reports containing claims about its business, supply chain and global operations "that are not supported by verifiable evidence.” The company did not address specific allegations. Jensen Huang, 63, has become a trusted ally of Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026, according to ABC News' reporting. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain. When asked Monday if Jensen Huang should be reinstated at Nvidia, Trump said, "I think having Jensen go back, a lot of people are asking Jensen... They think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn't a bad idea." Trump's comments on Monday came as ABC News has learned that Jensen Huang will likely testify before Congress during the first week of December, sources with knowledge of the negotiations to get Huang to testify told ABC News. Jensen Huang and House lawmakers are continuing to negotiate a joint, behind-closed-doors testimony with multiple House committees. Sources with knowledge of the negotiations told ABC News that Jensen Huang is expected to appear voluntarily and House lawmakers are not expected to subpoena him, although sources have made it clear they maintain the option. The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that both Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the panel. Both have expressed willingness to testify before the panel, but they have not yet settled on dates. A third committee, the House Intelligence Committee, has also asked Lutnick to testify. It's unclear where those talks stand. Lawmakers have raised concerns about national security implications of Jensen Huang's reported extramarital relationship given that he ran the world's largest computer chip manufacturer. "Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said last week. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department for dragging its feet on blacklisting Megaspeed as an alleged national security threat. "Many other departments were pushing for this and Commerce had the pen," Bessent told Fox News. Bessent said the real question is whether Nvidia’s chips were illegally being diverted to China. "I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings,” said Bessent, adding that he would like to see Nvidia’s next CEO come from outside the company. Meanwhile, Trump isn't the only one open to Jensen Huang making a comeback at Nvidia, whose stock has lost more than 30% of its value since early October. The Financial Times reported over the weekend that one of Jensen Huang's allies, whose name was not disclosed, is building a war room to lobby Nvidia's Board of Directors and the White House to reinstall Huang as Nvidia CEO. More than 177,000 supporters of Jensen Huang, including Elon Musk and nearly 93,000 Nvidia shareholders and more than 8,800 current Nvidia employees, have signed a letter addressed to Nvidia's Board of Directors demanding that Huang be reinstated as the company's CEO. "Bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts, unless and until you can provide compelling evidence that his removal is in NVIDIA's best interest," the letter says. The letter goes on to raise concerns that Jensen Huang was removed "without meaningful due process." "We have not been shown evidence substantiating the allegation that the woman at the center of this controversy was a spy," the letter says. "Suspicion or association alone is not a sufficient basis for ending Jensen's leadership. The inquiry must establish the facts, not merely justify an outcome already imposed." Organizers of the letter are encouraging Nvidia investors to dial in to Nvidia's earnings call on Tuesday, the first without Jensen Huang, to voice support for the demands in the letter. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Roku players are some of the most popular streaming devices on the market, and you won't go bankrupt buying one. Flagship products like the Roku Ultra and Roku Streambar SE usually don't cost more than $150, but even the company's $30 and $40 streaming devices are jam-packed with features. But what does it mean when your trusted Roku player starts displaying a red light? It could mean one of two things: If the light is solid red, it means your Roku device is starting to overheat; if it's a strobing red light, it means your hardware is underpowered. Most Roku hardware contains a white LED indicator to let you know your device is powered and able to receive commands — often located on the front or side of the set-top box or dongle. This is the same indicator that will turn red when overheating or power issues are detected. You should also see a warning at the top-right of Roku OS when the device is running too hot. Your best course of action? Disconnect the power cable from your Roku device and give it a solid 10-15 minutes to cool down. If the device is too hot to touch, unplug it from the wall outlet or USB port on your TV. Roku devices are designed to run indefinitely, but you'll want to match that performance with ideal room conditions. If it can be avoided, try to keep your Roku device out in the open; media cabinets with closed doors have a tendency to suffocate electronics. One of the conveniences of owning a Roku streaming dongle (such as the Roku Streaming Stick Plus) is that the HDMI connector is built into the device. Once connected to one of your TV's HDMI ports, you can connect the provided USB cable to an outlet adapter. You can also use one of your TV's USB ports to power the Roku, but doing so may trigger a red light or a message that indicates overheating or low power. The back of your TV isn't the coolest place either, and heat dissipation is even tougher if you're dealing with a wall-mounted setup. Maybe it's best to avoid making that Roku mistake if all signs point toward back-of-the-TV overheating. Fortunately, Roku makes an HDMI extender you can use to reposition your dongle or set-top box. Theoretically, you should be able to use third-party extenders, too, if that's the path you'd prefer; just be aware that you may run into issues with HDCP safeguards. If your Roku device is throwing low-power indicators and it's connected to one of your TV's USB ports, try using a different port; if that doesn't work, we'd recommend sticking with a USB power adapter. These AC-powered bricks are far more reliable than your TV's USB ports, which simply may not be outputting enough wattage to your Roku gear. Should you end up going this route for power, make sure your Roku device is also connected to a surge protector. Some of the best units on the market (like this Anker one) have built-in failsafes for overheating, voltage spikes, and other signal or power mishaps.

It’s often said that a monopoly can be bad for business. For years, two brands have had a monopoly of sorts in the intercom market: Cardo and Sena. Sure, there have been a few smaller players that've tried to muscle their way into the conversation now and then, but when it comes to premium helmet communication systems, these two have largely had the run of the place. And that's not necessarily a bad thing. Both brands have built solid reputations over the years, offering riders increasingly sophisticated ways to stay connected on the road. But a lack of serious competition can also mean established players have fewer reasons to shake things up. Enter RESO, a relatively new name looking to upset that comfortable little arrangement. Its Pilot Pro helmet intercom arrives with a rather ambitious feature list, promising everything from hybrid mesh connectivity and action camera integration to built-in GPS functionality and long battery life. I’ve had a couple of these intercom units for a few weeks, and boy, am I impressed? The first thing you'll notice about the intercom is that it doesn't look particularly interested in screaming for attention. I love that. Not in a million years would I want a hefty intercom with blingy colors and flashing lights stuck on the side of my helmet. The Pilot Pro is fairly sleek and compact. The styling has a bit of a DJI influence, which isn't entirely surprising given that RESO says its team includes former DJI engineers. The main unit weighs approximately 65 g (2.29 oz) without its mounting base, so it doesn't add a particularly cumbersome lump to the side of your helmet. The buttons and volume control are sensibly laid out. My favorite bit is the magnetic mounting arrangement, which makes it easy to detach the unit when you leave your helmet behind. It's also IP67-rated for dust and water resistance, too, so getting caught in an unexpected downpour shouldn't be a reason to panic. Installing a helmet intercom isn't exactly rocket science, especially in 2026 when there are tons of tutorial videos for those who still need guidance. You get 40-mm speakers, a wired microphone for full-face helmets, a boom microphone for open-face and modular helmets, Velcro pads, and the necessary mounting hardware, all in the box. The speakers are small enough to slot into the ear pockets of most helmets, and the wires are long enough to connect everything nice and tidy. There’s an adhesive mounting arrangement that you can use or a clip mount, which is what I ended up using. This is where things start getting interesting. The RESO Pilot Pro connects to your smartphone over Bluetooth 5.2, and you can manage most of its more advanced functions through the companion RESO Link app. Pairing the unit with your phone is relatively straightforward, while setting up a mesh group can be done through the physical controls, voice commands, or the phone app. Once the group is established, the system can automatically switch between hardware and software mesh connections through its DuoSync technology. The voice assistant is another useful addition – although a bit irritating if you’re not used to it. There were times when ordinary conversation with my wife on the other end occasionally triggered commands unintentionally. That’s because the system doesn't require a specific wake-up prompt. Something I think RESO can improve with an OTA update. But have to admit, for first-time users, there's a small learning curve here. The sheer number of functions and settings may make you spend some time getting familiar with the app before heading out. This is probably the Pilo Pro’s strongest suit. Traditional motorcycle intercoms rely on Bluetooth or proprietary mesh networking, with communication eventually dropping when you and your buddies move beyond the system's operating range. RESO tackles that with DuoSync, which combines two different communication technologies. Its hardware mesh offers a claimed point-to-point range of up to 1.5 miles (2.5 km), with a maximum group communication range of 7.5 miles (12 km). RESO makes it possible through the mesh network's multi-hop communication, where connected riders help relay the signal across the group. But when even that isn't enough, the system can switch to software mesh, which uses mobile internet connectivity to keep riders connected. In theory, this means your buddies could be several miles away and still carry on a conversation, provided everyone has a working internet connection. The automatic switching between the two modes is arguably the cleverest part. You don't have to manually switch networks every time someone drops out of hardware mesh range. There is, however, a rather obvious catch. Software mesh depends on mobile network coverage, so don't expect unlimited communication range when you're riding through remote mountain passes or deep into the wilderness without cellular connectivity. I haven’t had the unit long enough to test that in a no-internet area, but it’s worked flawlessly between my helmet and my wife’s helmet so far.  I'm a big believer in keeping motorcycle controls simple. You're already dealing with traffic, road conditions, navigation, and the occasional idiot trying to occupy the same piece of tarmac as you. The last thing you need is a complicated menu system attached to your helmet. Thankfully, RESO hasn't gone overboard here. The Pilot Pro uses three physical buttons and a rotary control, with the latter handling volume adjustments. The buttons are reasonably well spaced, making them easier to locate without having to take your eyes off the road. It took me barely a few minutes to get acquainted with the layout. The buttons feel reasonably clicky, and the rotary volume control is one of the best I’ve used on my helmets. A motorcycle intercom can have all the features in the world, but if the person on the other end can't understand what you're saying, you might as well throw the thing away and resort to hand signals. Thankfully, that’s not the case here. The Pilot Pro comes with 40-mm speakers and AI-assisted wind-noise reduction, with RESO claiming clear communication at speeds of up to 110 mph (180 km/h). I can only vouch for that claim up to 70 mph 110 km/h, though. The mic’s noise suppression is one of the stronger points of this intercom. I like its ability to filter out background wind noise, even with the visor open on my adventure-style helmet. Music playback is also more or less very good. Of course, it’s a subjective affair – some may want bigger drivers, some may want more bass, some more volume. But for a set of speakers on a helmet intercom, I had zero issues here. What’s particularly neat is that the Pilot Pro also supports direct action-camera connectivity, allowing you to record intercom conversations alongside your footage. For those who like to record their rides, that's a big win. Sadly, my DJI Osmo Action 5 is almost always connected to the brilliant Mic Mini, so I didn’t end up using this feature. Nevertheless, it’s still brilliant to have it for any days I might lose my mic or forget it back home. The Pilot Pro packs a 1,950-mAh battery, and RESO has clearly put some thought into making sure it doesn't run out of juice halfway through a long ride. The company quotes up to 13 hours of operation with dual mesh, music playback, and GNSS running simultaneously. That figure increases to approximately 18 hours with audio playback and GNSS, while Bluetooth-only operation in power-saving mode can stretch to a claimed 33 hours. There's also 15-W fast charging through USB-C. RESO says five minutes plugged in will provide up to two hours of additional use, while a 30-minute charge can replenish approximately 80% of the battery. Those are impressive numbers, although it's worth remembering that battery life varies considerably depending on which features you're using. Personally, I was very impressed with the battery. I completed two full riding days without needing to recharge. Now, usually, this is where the review would end for a regular intercom. But, the Pilot Pro features a few extras, starting with the built-in GNSS functionality that allows you to record ride routes without relying on your phone's GPS. You can access ride histories, monitor the real-time location of connected group members, and keep track of where everyone is during a ride through the RESO Link app. It also includes SOS support, allowing emergency contacts to be alerted when assistance is needed. Of course, availability of some safety functions depends on regional support, connectivity, and configuration. Then there's the aforementioned action-camera integration. The system supports selected DJI, GoPro, and Insta360 cameras through USB-C or direct Bluetooth connections, depending on the camera model. You also get music sharing, FM radio, cross-brand connectivity, and the ability to receive firmware updates wirelessly. The cross-brand feature deserves particular attention because it addresses one of the biggest frustrations with motorcycle intercoms: not everyone in your riding group necessarily owns the same brand of intercom. However, there's a distinction worth making. Connecting to another manufacturer's intercom over Bluetooth doesn't automatically mean you get to use its proprietary mesh networking features. The connection method and functionality available depend on the particular Cardo or Sena model you're pairing with. The pricing is actually one of the more interesting aspects of the RESO Pilot Pro. Currently at US$359, it sits right in the territory occupied by some fairly serious competition like the Cardo Packtalk Neo ($359.95) and the Sena 50S ($379). Step up a little further, and you're looking at the Cardo Packtalk Edge ($439.95) and the newer Sena 60S ($439). That's some pretty stiff competition for a relatively young player trying to muscle in the market.  I’ll finish how I started. For years, the motorcycle intercom business has felt like a private party hosted by Cardo and Sena. You could pick a side, argue about sound quality and mesh connectivity, and spend a small fortune making sure everyone in your riding group was on the same system. It’s clear RESO wants to crash that party – and, to its credit, it hasn't turned up empty-handed. The Pilot Pro brings a compelling mix of features, capable hardware, clever software, and a refreshingly straightforward approach to staying connected on the road. But there's a catch: all that clever connectivity is only as useful as the people you're riding with, and some of its biggest promises depend on having a data connection. But perhaps the biggest speed bump is convincing your buddies to switch ecosystems. While the likes of Cardo and Sena have spent years building their respective empires, getting an entire riding group to jump ship is no small feat. RESO definitely has the hardware to make a serious case, but building a community around it could be the bigger challenge. Still, the Pilot Pro is exactly the kind of disruption this market could use. It might not knock the established players off their thrones overnight. But I think it would have done its job if it made them look over their shoulders. Product page: RESO Sign up for our FREE daily New Atlas newsletter!

At least once a month, sometimes more, readers write in to ask how they can break into the field of computer security. Some of the emails are from people in jobs that have nothing to do with security, but who are fascinated enough by the field to contemplate a career change. Others are already in an information technology position but are itching to segue into security. I always respond with my own set of stock answers, but each time I do this, I can’t help but feel my advice is incomplete, or at least not terribly well-rounded. I decided to ask some of the brightest minds in the security industry today what advice they’d give. Almost everyone I asked said they, too, frequently get asked the very same question, but each had surprisingly different takes on the subject. Today is the first installment in a series of responses to this question. When the last of the advice columns have run, I’ll create an archive of them all that will be anchored somewhere prominently on the home page. That way, the next time someone asks how they can break into security, I’ll have more to offer than just my admittedly narrow perspectives on the matter. Last month, I interviewed Thomas Ptacek, founder of Matasano Security, about how companies could beef up password security in the wake of a week full of news about password leaks at LinkedIn and other online businesses. Ptacek’s provocative advice generated such a huge amount of reader interest and further discussion that I thought it made sense to begin this series with his thoughts: Ptacek: “Information security is one of the most interesting, challenging, and, if you do it carefully, rewarding fields in the technology industry. It’s one of the few technology jobs where the most fun roles are well compensated. If you grew up dreaming of developing games, the laws of supply and demand teach a harsh lesson early in your career: game development jobs are often tedious and usually pay badly. But if you watched “Sneakers” and ideated a life spent breaking or defending software, great news: infosec can be more fun in real life, and it’s fairly lucrative. I’m a software developer. I try to look at security through the lens of computer science. To me, the most attractive thing about the field is the opportunity it provides to work with lots of different concepts at lots of different levels. Computer security might be the best way to work professionally with compiler theory, or to spend time understanding computer microarchitecture, or to apply advanced mathematics. Other people get involved in security for different reasons, and those reasons are probably equally valid. Some people really like the “good guys / bad guys” narrative that comes with security. Some people see security as an opportunity to save the world. Other people are drawn to the competitive nature of the field: at the higher levels, it really is a cat-and-mouse game. It also comes closer to meritocracy than most of technology: you can either break in or you can’t; your defenses either work or they don’t. But for me, it’s just one of the best development jobs you can get, and with that in mind, here’s my advice for people interested in pursuing a career in it. First: I want you to learn how to program. Clearly, you can get through college and get a good-paying steady job without ever learning to love programming. But no one factor gives you as much control over your career, as much of an ability to write your own ticket, as the ability to solve problems using programming languages. A lot of very smart technology professionals have concluded that they just don’t enjoy writing software. Those people should reconsider. Try different languages, or different application domains, but find a way to make programming stick in your head. Second: the best jobs in our field are in application security. You can get good steady work designing firewall deployments, setting up desktop agents, or responding to incidents. But all those roles are fundamentally reacting to what’s happening in appsec. The next generation of security products — along with the org charts of security teams at the savviest companies — are being designed now, by accident, by application security practitioners. Appsec roles are roles that involve attacking software or devising fixes and countermeasures for those attacks. Two good ways to “come up” in appsec: become a penetration tester, or contribute to (or start) a secure software development practice in your company. A good way to move into penetration testing: grab some industry standard tools and use an Amazon EC2 account to set up a “shooting range” to attack. Some of the best-known tools are available for free: the Nessus scanner, for instance, while not an application security tool, is free and can land you a network penetration testing role that you can use as a springboard to breaking applications. When people reach out to Matasano asking how to get a foot in the door attacking software, we have a few simple steps to offer: 0. Learn to love programming in at least one language. The C Programming Language has the most cachet in application security, but for this step-by-step list, Java or Python or Ruby will do fine. 1. Grab a copy of  The Web Application Hacker’s Handbook. 2. Go to the “previous releases” archive at WordPress.org and grab very old versions of WordPress; install them at EC2. 3. Download OWASP WebScarab or Burp Suite Free Edition, both of which are free, and use them to find bugs in ancient WordPress. If you’re already in an IT role, and want to come up on the defensive side of appsec, try to position yourself near custom software development. Most large firms build “line of business” applications. As a rule, building “line of business” isn’t particularly fun. But defending those apps can be; sometimes, the most boring applications turn out to be surprisingly sensitive. And the good news for doing appsec in BigCo’s: most companies have very immature security programs. If you can get a role in QA, or in what the cool kids are calling “DevOps”, you can end up with a lot of influence in security. At Matasano, we’ve watched lots of ops people successfully transition to appsec and senior security management just by instituting basic security testing processes on their company’s software. To me, the whole field boils down to studying, understanding, and manipulating technology. Like most software security practices, we’ve gotten our hands dirty with a fascinating cross-section of the whole technology industry. We’ve written attack tools that target the control registers of device chipsets, we’ve done custom RF work, we’ve written low-level debuggers for different CPU architectures, and we’ve seen and beaten up on products built in almost every programming language and every platform you can imagine. If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. Spend a couple days Starbucks money on an EC2 account and deploy some broken apps to break. Find opportunities to practice in your job. And, uh, come talk to us? It allows you to get into the real low-level stuff.
