Like you pointed out, no system is 100% invulnerable to security issues. Until that happens, security will be around. I don’t believe it ever will happen. Security is a huge money making market and maybe that is why most security solutions are defensive based rather than offensive. If the problem goes away the jobs go away. We don’t go looking for trouble though, we defend against it. Even if we did fix all the hardware and software related security issues, you can’t download a patch to fill the gap in knowledge that everyday users have. Social Engineering and user error will ALWAYS be an issue. Companies will continue to adapt to make money the same way security adapts to new trends and technology. Simply from a social engineering standpoint, it will never be truly eliminated…  Once you can trick someone into installing a program onto their machine with admin rights (or bypass) then you can own that machine… Doesn’t matter what OS, what other features you have, 99% of the time if your CEO is dumb enough to click yes you lost the battle right there. But yes I do think a lot of the back end money would be better spent making sure the products being developed were more secure out of the gate.  I actually had a class on that in school, and what it boils down to is that the company designing the bad product rarely has to pay for the damages, and also faces pushback from the user base if they make it too restrictive.  Until the developer writing the code has some skin in the game, they are going to do keep doing the fastest and most profitable code they can. I was about to post your exact response. I’m currently in the process of working on a social engineering project that educates users about how it’s done and what they shouldn’t do. Essentially, I’m dumping some “encrypted images” with various interesting names on USB sticks, with a decryption program. Most people are curious, so run the program to look at the pictures. What the program actually does is open their browser to a page that explains the dangers of what they just did, and how they can avoid becoming targets of social engineering. They also get to keep the flash drive! 🙂 @Whats in a name: “Once you can trick someone into installing a program onto their machine with admin rights (or bypass) then you can own that machine… Doesn’t matter what OS, what other features you have, 99% of the time if your CEO is dumb enough to click yes you lost the battle right there.”   If we want computer security, we cannot wait for CEO’s to get smarter.  Nor can we depend upon user education to prevent inevitable human errors.  Instead, we need systems which minimize the consequences of error.  Current PC’s are peculiarly susceptible to infection, which is exactly why we need new designs for more secure equipment.   Any system which re-boots a clean OS immediately before banking is “99%” unlikely to be “owned” during that banking session.   There is, of course, no *perfect* security.  But a DVD-load OS is inherently and vastly *more* secure than the hard-drive-boot alternatives now in use.  DVD-load systems, without a hard-drive (or flash drive), are easily cleaned with a simple re-boot.   In contrast, there is no simple way to un-own a hard-drive-boot system.  There is not even a way to guarantee *detecting* when a conventional system is owned essentially forever.   Is the need to reboot a security hole?  Sure; somebody has to manually command a reboot.  But manual reboots could be unnecessary in new designs which automatically force a reboot before banking online.  With new custom hardware (and corresponding OS changes), such a design could even support hard drives and operate much like a conventional PC.  When lesser security guarantees are acceptable, automatically booting or loading a new virtual machine to do banking could be useful.   The hope of very secure online banking equipment is not a dream.  Non-ideal but working DVD-load systems exist now.  Which makes it only reasonable to ask why our equipment is still so insecure.   The business of selling anti-vi and other security add-on’s depends on failure.  If there were no failure, no “owned” equipment, and no consequences, there would be no continuing business.  How can we say that security companies want to solve the malware problem, when their very business depends on security failure? Ultimately, we have to decide which side we are on. Nothing is ever that simple.  BYOD changes the game.  Can you lock down an iPad? The  idealist says yes, but of course these devices are vulnerable.  Maybe Win 8 will better, probably not.  No technical solution can keep up with the user vulnerability. I would add as a base line get a certification, cheaper than a degree and more up to date.  CISSP and CEH require CPEs per year attempting to keep practictioners relevant, unlike a 4 yr degree.  While some think they prove nothing other than motivation and the ability to retain some information, they’re better than a criminal record.  120hrs/3 years means at least you are paying attention. Get involved with OWASP and ISSA.  Do community outreach, grade schools, high schools, retirement communities. Get the HACME apps for each language and hack away and learn SEVERAL languages, at least architectural and syntactically.  Code in one or 2 for your own programs, but I don’t know of any pure homogenous application. Get the OWASP testing guide, love it learn it, feel free to edit or add to it. OWASP needs volunteers to stay up to date. Even with a dvd boot live system you can still have people tricked into giving out info, emailing critical files, or memory based attacks.  I agree you can’t wait for CEOs to get smarter, but you can’t realistically lock them out of every single sensitive server, spreadsheet, or webpage either. Open/FreeBSD you can avoid this by easily locking down user /home areas and preventing root escalation. So the CEO can’t screw himself over. However, Social Engineers get around this by simply impersonating being a contractor and needing the root password at a time when nobody else is around, so they just convince whoever is on the phone during nightshift to give it to them ‘temporarily, change it afterwards’ then they install whatever they want and leave. 🙂 Some criminals here got jobs as night cleaners and just installed hardware keyloggers when nobody was around. All security meaningless when they have every password. “If crawling through the ventilation ducts of the world’s most important technology is something you think might make you tick like we do… well, appsec! Learn to code. ” ??? that makes no sense. i dont know a single “appsec” person doing that. I think he was referring to application security in the exploit-finding sense. I think “crawling through the ventilation ducts” very accurately sums up the feeling you get when you have WinDbg + Immunity + IDA + a dozen other windows open, digging through stack traces and virtual tomes of assembly. Or proxying http calls and replaying response/request interactions.  Web service hacking very much feels like crawling through ducts (especially on unpublished APIs). Other recommended reading: Mark Dowd, John McDonald, and Justin Schuh, The Art of Software Security Assessment: Identifying and Preventing Software Vulnerabilities Michal Zalewski, The Tangled Web: A Guide to Securing Modern Web Applications Bigger picture: Ross Anderson, Security Engineering: A Guide to Building Dependable Distributed Systems (2nd edition) — excellent book, deep on technical detail AND on economic and social aspects of security, with many handy references Bruce Schneier, Secrets and Lies: Digital Security in a Networked World Bruce Schneier, Liars and Outliars: Enabling Trust That Society Needs to Thrive In addition to programming, I recommend learning symbolic logic, critical thinking, social psychology, and epistemology.  (I got into security from a background in philosophy, cognitive science, and computer science.) A lot of pentesting is deemed ‘illegal’ by companies, primarily side-channel email attacks which almost always work. They claim this is ‘cheating’ or dangerous as you getting shell through the browser and not actually outside the network punching your way through with some sort of pen testing attack. Even government servers end up side channel attacked now and then and they sheepishly admit to the press how some low level employee clicked on a spear phishing link, was browser hijacked and now that guy is running all over the network because he’s impersonating a trusted local user, and companies and governments seem to love hooking up absolutely everything to a network.  Reminds me when the Cdn gov’t was side-channeled by presumaly Chinese state hackers who didn’t have access to the main database of secret info, so they just lay waiting in some unsecure printer for the documents to be printed off and caught them as they went past. Crucial, top secret documents that were encrypted but didn’t matter because you could just sniff the printer traffic and get everything you wanted. Comments are closed. Strategy bought 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 million and spent $228.1 million repurchasing STRC preferred shares, largely funded by new common stock sales. Michael Saylor’s Strategy bought 485 Bitcoin for $33.4 million last week while spending nearly seven times as much repurchasing STRC preferred shares. The company purchased the Bitcoin (BTC) at an average price of $68,887 between Monday and Sunday, bringing its holdings to 850,849 BTC, according to a Monday filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission. Strategy said it raised $244.7 million by selling 2.09 million common shares (MSTR), using $33.4 million to buy Bitcoin, $206.3 million to fund STRC repurchases and $5 million to its separate cash balance. It funded the remaining $21.8 million in buybacks with interest earned on its cash and short-term investments. The company repurchased 2.28 million STRC shares during the week. STRC is Strategy’s variable-rate preferred stock, which pays regular dividends to shareholders. Strategy reported a $4.75 billion US dollar reserve after using $18.9 million to pay preferred stock dividends. Its separate cash balance stood at $151.2 million as of Sunday. The company also maintained STRC’s annual dividend rate at 12% for December, saying it intends to keep the rate steady until the shares demonstrate sustained trading near $100. Strategy spent $188.3 million repurchasing STRC shares and $81.9 million buying Bitcoin the previous week. Strategy’s MSTR stock fell 8.45% to $102.2 in Monday’s premarket trading, while STRC declined 0.78% to $99.1, according to Yahoo Finance. The losses followed MSCI’s confirmation last week that it would remove Strategy from its global equity indexes after the Nov. 30 market close. Watch CBS News  November 16, 2026 / 1:03 PM EST             / CBS News            Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation as Nvidia's CEO last week dealt a hammer blow to the chipmaker's stock price, vaporizing more than $550 billion in its market value. If history is any guide, meanwhile, the company's shares could be in for a rough road. Other companies whose chief executives departed due to personal conduct reasons have underperformed the S&P 500's average return in the year following the executive's exit, according to financial services firm StoneX. For example, shares of HP (formerly Hewlett-Packard) tumbled nearly 29% in the 12 months after former CEO Mark Hurd resigned in 2010 for concealing a relationship with a former contractor, while the S&P 500 rose 9% over that period. "Removing a CEO over personal conduct has more often than not been followed by a difficult year for shareholders," StoneX said in a recent report that analyzed the stock performance of 12 major companies, including Boeing, CNN and McDonald's, after their CEO exited under a cloud. Huang stepped down on Nov. 12 after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies identified as a Chinese spy. Nvidia shares plunged the following day and are now down more than 30% from a recent peak on Oct. 6. Of the companies StoneX analyzed, seven lagged the average S&P 500 returns the year after their CEO left. Cody Acree, an equity research analyst at StoneX, thinks Nvidia shares could also struggle as the chip giant searches for a new leader and amid uncertainty over the AI sector. Already, several Wall Street analysts have downgraded their price forecasts for Nvidia's stock, citing the leadership vacuum left by Huang's departure and questions about Nvidia's future. Truist, an American bank holding company, lowered its price target last week from $346 per share to $174. Yorkville Ives and Co., led by noted tech analyst Dan Ives, also reduced its estimate from $300 to $225. In morning activity on Wall Street, Nvidia shares were down 2.1% to $159.31. Of the companies StoneX analyzed, five outperformed the S&P 500, according to StoneX. However, those examples may offer "little comfort" to Nvidia, given that those companies had a successor lined up to replace the departing CEO. "They had heirs apparent," Acree told CBS News. "They had people that were kind of ready to take the position." In Nvidia's case, Huang's sudden departure has made for a more chaotic succession plan. The company's board tapped Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Wall Street analysts said the company's board will be eager to find someone with the dealmaking prowess and technical know-how to lead the world's leading chipmaker.  In the meantime, Nvidia will have to reassure investors about who will handle responsibilities that once rested with Huang, including engaging with officials in Washington and managing relationships with Nvidia's customers and partners, StoneX said in its report. Nvidia will also have to assuage concerns about possible restructuring efforts, Acree added. Huang had more than 60 direct reports, a structure that kept him at the center of Nvidia's decision-making. "If you come in with a more standard CEO, does he try to implement that structure that he's maybe more used to, or does he try to reproduce what Jensen already had in place?" Acree said. Already, some are calling for Huang's return, with a petition to reinstate him garnering more than 170,000 signatures. Nvidia also faces other challenges, including heightened competition in the chip industry and the possibility that the U.S. could tighten export controls on AI chips, according to Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli. Still, Nvidia retains powerful competitive advantages. The company already has a roadmap for chip production over the next two years created by Huang, Acree noted. Demand for Nvidia chips and related equipment is also expected to remain robust, given the rapid growth of AI services. "There's still going to be demand that outstrips even that ability to supply for the next couple of years," Acree said. The next major test for Nvidia will come on Tuesday, when the company is scheduled to announce its quarterly earnings.         Edited by                                                                            Alain  Sherter  In:        © 2026 CBS Interactive Inc. Read the latest issue of Dazed for free Campbell Gulbrandsen, a fashion assistant living in New York City, says she was on the creatine wave “before it got super popular” online. The 24-year-old first heard about creatine on social media, where it was being promoted by fitness influencers doing highly demanding sports, like bodybuilding and marathon training. But it wasn’t until she saw it being taken by more casual exercisers – the Pilates princesses – that she decided to give it a try. The brand she opted for was Arrae, which sells creatine in gummy form. “The branding definitely roped me in,” says Gulbrandsen. “They’re cute flavours and the whole thing is that it tastes good … It’s very female-oriented.” Once primarily advertised with blocky typefaces and images of men with bulging muscles, creatine supplements, which have existed since the 90s, have recently shifted their focus to female consumers. That’s been made obvious through a shift in the supplement’s visual identity, with Goop-esque, pastel-coloured options like Midi, Flo and Cymbiotika entering the market. Alongside the sleek new branding, the nature of the products has changed too. Not a fan of giant tubs of powder? You can now chew your creatine in the form of gummies, drink it from squeezable packets, or slap it on via topical patches. Within the past year, the supplement’s aesthetic facelift has been accompanied by a swell of social media content, in which UGC wellness creators rattle off everything creatine has done for them, from toning their muscles to alleviating their brain fog.  The rebrand isn’t subtle. New female-centred brands, like Fit Git Creatine, are continuing to enter the market. “What we wanted women to feel when they first saw it was that it was something they could see themselves using right away,” says creative director Olivia Vlachos, whose agency has led the new product’s marketing and design. The supplement, which launches early next year, comes in hot pink sachets and flavours like pink lemonade. “Branding is how someone encounters a product,” says Vlachos. “If you’re walking down the aisle at Erewhon, are you going to pick it up?” The marketing efforts are working. Searches for “creatine monohydrate for women” are up 190 per cent compared to this time last year, according to Google Trends, and on Amazon, sales within the creatine subcategory have surged 90 per cent over the last 12 months, according to SmartScout marketplace data. With creatine market size projected to reach $8.7 billion by 2033, growing at nearly three times the rate of the global dietary supplements market, the numbers are clear – the boom is real. But what exactly is behind it? Answering that question requires an understanding of where creatine comes from, and what it can and can’t do. Creatine is a compound that comes from amino acids and supplies energy to the muscles. “[It’s] something that our bodies naturally make from three amino acids, and it’s mainly created in our liver and kidneys,” says Yasi Ansari, a sports dietitian based in California. “Having more creatine in our muscles can allow us to do more short and intense work in the gym, on the field, on the court, and over time, this results in more gains in our strength and our muscle,” she adds.  While creatine has long been taken to build muscle, more and more people are now reaching for the supplement to promote brain health. But is there any validity to these claims? Experts believe it’s too soon to say. Although a few small studies have shown that large doses of creatine can slightly increase brain activity, the research isn’t conclusive, and, as Ansari says, “the jury’s still out” on the supplement’s cognitive benefits.  On social media, however, the concept of creatine’s brain-boosting abilities has gained traction, making it one popular reason people are clicking “add to cart”. Hana El Sherif, a 25-year-old finance associate, for example, began taking creatine after a friend told her it could help with sleep and cognitive function. “One thing I liked about creatine is that it almost felt like a multivitamin,” says El Sherif. “It ticks so many boxes, and you get all these benefits you otherwise would have to get from four or five supplements.”  Grace McHugh, a 24-year-old living in New York City, also started taking creatine because of its potential cognitive benefits. Her primary reason, though, was for marathon training. Though her college boyfriend took creatine every day, it was female influencers who got her to start – she decided on the brand Promix after reading a profile on the brand’s founder, an extreme athlete turned wellness entrepreneur. “I do think there’s an increased interest among women,” says McHugh.  “In the 2010s, it was all about women trying to lose as much weight as possible. Then, we saw a complete shift in how women think about workouts, as muscle mass became something that people started to value more”  There is clearly a connection between the rise of creatine and the fact that, in recent years, more women have taken an interest in building strength. “In the 2010s, it was all about women trying to lose as much weight as possible,” says brand strategist Katie Klencheski, whose marketing agency SMAKK Studios specialises in health and wellness. “Then, we saw a complete shift in how women think about workouts, as muscle mass became something that people started to value more.”  It’s true that the popularity of strength training, which can be especially beneficial as we enter menopause and lose bone density, has been on the rise among women. But aside from increased awareness about menopause, Klencheski also points to the explosion of GLP-1s, which can cause muscle loss, as a reason for the current preoccupation with strength. “You have a lot of people on GLP-1s who are barely eating any food, and the muscle wasting thing is a very real concern,” says Klencheski. “A lot of people are looking for ways to stop that.”  Aside from eye-catching packaging, brands are partnering with influencers and UGC creators to spread the good news of creatine to the masses. As with other supplements, though, this can get murky because, as Klencheski notes, the regulatory system around this content is “a little bit like the Wild West”. In the US, supplement companies can make certain claims about how a product affects the structure or function of the body, provided those claims are substantiated and not misleading, but they cannot market supplements as diagnosing, treating, curing or preventing disease.  The lack of regulation of the supplement market is especially important to keep in mind when it comes to creatine, given that much of its current online buzz is being fuelled by creators using language like “body-changing” to promote its powers. “Everyone thinks they’re going to take creatine and magically transform their body solely from the supplement,” says Anna Hellickson, a 23-year-old living in Los Angeles. Hellickson started taking creatine in March, but, sceptical of the gummies and drinks she saw marketed towards women online, opted for an old-school unflavoured version. “I don’t need the fun version, just the benefits,” she says. Though the irresponsible claims by influencers don’t negate the fact that creatine has legitimate, science-backed benefits, Ansari says that it “cannot be a substitute for good nutrition”. While some of the online commentary has veered into problematic territory, many women feel that the overall movement is still about getting stronger rather than shrinking, which is a step in the right direction. “We’ve been in this skinny trend for a good amount of time now, and I think that creatine is helping propel this next stage of body image norms,” says Hellickson. “Strength is coming back.” Still, it's not exactly the case that the creatine boom is the antithesis of diet culture. While creatine may have once been viewed as something for more extreme fitness enthusiasts, in a health landscape where DIY peptide stacking has become normalised, it’s perhaps not surprising that there’s a new sense of openness around the supplement. And with that openness, or “white space,” as a marketer would call it, comes a readiness for the wellness industry to do what it’s always done: sell, sell, sell.  Get must-see stories direct to your inbox every weekday. About this rating    In mid-November, an alleged Truth Social post by U.S. President Donald Trump claiming that disruptions to food and banking services were imminent spread on social media.  A screenshot of the alleged post circulated on TikTok, Threads, and Facebook several days before customers at a handful of major U.S. banks experienced service outages on Nov. 16. JPMorgan Chase confirmed that a technical issue was behind the disruptions, according to the Associated Press. The purported screenshot read: URGENT: New intelligence and global developments indicate there could be serious disruptions to our food supply, banking system, and critical services in the coming weeks. To protect your family, I strongly recommend that Americans take the following steps immediately:  This is about being prepared, not panicking. The risks are real, and it's better to be ready now than to be caught off guard later.  I want to thank Diane Cavoto, who has been sounding the alarm on this for months. She has been right, and her guidance has helped many Americans get prepared.  Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J TRUMP. (Accessed via X) We found no evidence of Trump sharing the above post on any of his social media accounts. As such, we've rated the screenshot fake.  Searches for variations of the quote on Google, DuckDuckGo (archived) and Bing uncovered no reporting from reliable media outlets connecting it to the president, which would have been the case if it were authentic. We searched for various phrases within the purported post, including "New intelligence and global developments," "Stock up on at least 90 DAYS of food" and "This is about being prepared, not panicking," none of which returned any relevant results. Likewise, searches of Roll Call's archive of Trump's posts on X and Truth Social and Trump's Truth, a website dedicated to archiving his Truth Social posts, did not return any results for posts resembling the screenshot.  As of this writing, we were unable to determine who originally shared the fake post. Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit CEOs have never cared much for holdcos. Enterprise solutions, on the other hand, get a meeting. Which makes Deloitte Digital’s new operating system for marketers an awkward one for the rest of the industry. It’s sold as a license, though not the kind a CMO can approve alone. Designed eventually to stretch across sales, marketing, service and commerce, it’s the kind of deal Deloitte Digital’s U.S. CMO Mark Singer called a “more executive conversation.” That conversation happens in the C-suite, well above the marketing department where holdcos usually pitch.  The product is called Converge Front Office. It strings together AI agents, some built by Deloitte and others a client already runs elsewhere, to handle marketing and sales work from research and briefs through to campaign deployment and deal tracking. Two parts are live, a marketing operating system and a sales one, with a commerce version on the way. Singer pitched them as pieces of one front office system built around an idea the consulting firm calls “brand to cash” — every step of marketing and sales, from building a brand to closing a deal, should be traceable back to revenue.  “It’s not just about the agents, it’s about the task orchestration among them,” said Singer.  If that sounds familiar, it’s because holdcos have spent the better part of two years saying much the same. It carries more weight from a consulting firm, though, and Singer made a point of setting Deloitte’s version apart. The market is full of AI tools, he said, and “everybody’s doing a press release every 20 minutes on them.” Some exist to make an agency more efficient for its cleints. Others sell smarter work off the back of an owner’s media insights. Deloitte wants to build tools “that we hand off to our clients,” said Singer. From there, they can run them in-house or use them as a way of “rethinking their agency infrastructure,” he added. A demo showed how that could play out. Umberto Castaldo, Deloitte Digital’s Converge marketing go-to-market lead, ran a campaign for a dummy sneaker brand. Agents passed the work along from market research and media modelling to the brief, the content, quality assurance and finally deployment into the brand’s existing mar tech. All those agents are routed into the consulting firm’s wider tech stack. Some of them draw on Deloitte’s own asset along the way. The research agent, for instance, can tap Deloitte’s own third-party data spine alongside client data. Of those steps, content is doing a fair share of the selling, at least in the system’s current form. In the consulting firm’s view, brands have already paid for far more content than they’ve used. Big brands have spent hundreds of millions, if not billions, on content over the past five years, Castaldo argued, and little of it has run recently. The system’s answer is to put that back catalog to work. Tagging agents can first relabel what sits in a brand’s asset library so other agents can find it. In the demo, those agents then built email and display ads for three audiences out of images and headlines the sneaker brand already had on file. Each asset is tracked from there, so the brand can see how it performs from one campaign to the next. The sales side runs in parallel. Abe Awasthi, Deloitte Digital’s AI sales transformation leader, showed how its built around a seller’s day: the gap to quote, which deals need attention and where new demand might come from. That last job falls to an agent called Scout, which reads campaign results from the marketing side and matches them to a rep’s target customers. Administrators decide how far each agent can go, from suggesting to drafting to acting.  “Autonomy should be earned,” said Awasthi. For now, most early clients are using the two halves separately, though Singer said some are starting to take both. Joint marketing and sales deals remain early, with one or two pitches in the past year, Singer said. As clients mature, he expects them to see the value in the “white space in between.” The consulting firm shared one result. A client gave half of its 300 business development reps the sales operating system. Over a three-month pilot, the response rate on their outbound emails went from 17% to around 56%. Once the rollout scaled, that settled in the 30s — roughly double the starting point. Quotas for the team up 20%, said Awasthi, and the client is hiring more reps. Marketing teams are similarly seeing early gains in throughput, said Castaldo, who didn’t share any specifics. Like everything the consulting firm has tried in advertising, Converge is designed to sit above it all, and Singer was blunt about where that leads. He expects “everything will be disrupted” across marketing services and said the shift is already underway. Four large clients he wouldn’t name are pulling their marketing into global capability centers, which he said is now possible without losing the personalization each market and language needs. Deloitte Digital already runs centralized functions like these for clients. They cover most of the marketing work, though brand advertising sits outside them. Setting up a function on that scale. Singer added, means building what he called “captive environments” for it. In outsourcing, a “captive” is an operation a company owns and runs for itself. The brand keeps the people and the budget. The system they all work inside is another matter, and that’s what the largest marketing services groups are now chasing. Consulting firms like Deloitte have the advantage of already being in the room where that gets decided. The holdcos have been trying to get there for a while. At CES in January, Omnicom, Stagwell, Havas and WPP each unveiled agentic platforms built to sit on top of a client’s existing tools and run the work between them. WPP has since gone further, recasting itself as a single company with four divisions: WPP Media, WPP Production, WPP Enterprise Solutions and the newly-created WPP Creative. Publicis started earlier, paying $3.5 billion for Sapient in 2015 and $4.4 billion for Epsilon in 2019. Software companies are doing the same. Adobe used its conference earlier this month to introduce its end-to-end content supply chain product. “One of the secret weapons of the management consultancy agencies in gaining market share during the past 10 years has been leveraging their established relationships with client CEOs, CIOs, and Boards of Directors,” said Gartner vp analyst Jay Wilson. “These relationships, and the credibility and sway those agencies have with those executives often allowed them to intercept opportunities before an agency review took place. Increasingly, we see and hear from clients and agencies that the CFO is the critical piece of the new business puzzle, as marketing budgets remain flat, and CMOs are pressured to prove the value of marketing, including agency investments.” Marketers use creator, influencer and tastemaker interchangeably, but the industry still hasn’t settled on what the labels mean. A new product manager role will explore ad-related monetization, suggesting the platform could make ads a bigger part of its business. Marketers expect their 2026 holiday revenue to increase 1% to 31% or more in comparison to their 2025 holiday revenue. By   	Jon Blistein   	Every year, countless artists have their hopes and dreams dashed when the Recording Academy reveals its nominees for the Grammy Awards. For the most part, the unfortunately snubbed choose to lick their wounds in private. Maybe they toss out an oblique or pithy quip on social media. Or maybe they make a video like Muna’s Katie Gavin, who copped to feeling disappointed, discussed the challenges of trying to shoehorn the band’s music into the Grammys’ sometimes overly-rigid genre categories, and still celebrated the artists who did get nominated.   	But few show the chutzpah of DJ-producer John Summit, who took to X to proclaim, “Never submitting to the Grammys again unless shit changes, it’s all a fucking joke.”  never submitting to the grammys again unless shit changes, it’s all a fucking joke. i’m not just talking about myself either there’s zero respect for real electronic dance music & dj’s. the whole dance category is just music industry fueled pop stars  	Summit — who dropped his second album, Ctrl Escape earlier this year and was recently seen performing on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (cool) — was specifically frustrated with how the dance and electronic music categories shook out. “The whole dance category is just music industry fueled pop stars,” he lamented, insisting that the choices showed “zero respect for real electronic music & dj’s.” (And, he swore, “i’m not just talking about myself.”)  	           	It is true that that the dance and EDM categories didn’t really feature any top-line DJs/producers besides Fred Again and Skrillex. And the categories were otherwise dominated by artists like Madonna, Robyn, Tinashe, Slayyyter, and Zara Larsson, who do present, at least on first glance, as pop musicians. But Summit went so far as to claim that these acts are “just not dance music, they’re pop,” and that “no DJ is playing that music in the clubs.”  not saying the artists nominated aren’t good, they’re just not dance music, they’re pop.no dj is playing that music in the clubs.  	Essays — perhaps even dissertations — could be written about how a person, let alone a professional DJ and producer, comes to think that, somehow, Madonna and Robyn do not make dance music. And that’s before you start to wonder if there’s maybe something telling about Summit’s focus on “pop stars,” “pop,” and the “lil teeny bopper pop stan accounts” flooding his replies, when noted psych rock band Tame Impala also got nominated in several dance and electronic music categories.   	            	 		Editor’s picks 	 	            	 	 		 					The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far		 	               	 	 		 					The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time		 	               	 	 		 					100 Best Movies of the 21st Century		 	         	On top of all that, Summit’s tweets also manage to erase all the work put into this music by producers just like him. Nightfeelings, who worked on Tinashe’s Grammy-nominated “Melatonin,” astutely pointed this out to Summit, writing, “I actually come from dance music, my first project released on the same labels as aphex twin … I’ve performed at Berghain .. Andy weatherall played my tune Cheaters in every set for a while, I made a song with Romanthony ..  just gonna leave it there.”  	He then added, “Not to mention Tinashe is literally a dj.”   	In vintage “im not mad. please dont put in the newspaper that i got mad” fashion, Summit ended his little polemic by trying to laugh off the whole thing. “Oh no i’m getting attacked hard on here. time to log off and continue my sold out arena tour for my real fans :)”       	 		Trending Stories 	 	       	 	 		 					Watch Buffalo Springfield Come Together for the First Time in Many Years		 	          	 	 		 					Jennifer Lopez Teases New Music on ‘Fallon’: ‘This Does Feel Like a Happy Era’		 	          	 	 		 					Miley Cyrus Shares Sweet Memory of Godmother Dolly Parton as They Earn a Grammy Nod Together		 	          	 	 		 					Cynthia Erivo, Travis Barker Honor Phil Collins With Big Vocals, Big Drums at Rock Hall Ceremony		 	         	Not being able to help himself, he later hopped back on to pen, “i realized i didn’t do a good job of making my point earlier. my intent was not to drag other artists down and i seriously congratulate everyone who was nominated they fully deserve the recognition. i just think there should be an extra category for more dance music djs & producers much love everyone.” Summit then promised, signing off from twitter now for a while.”  	Sure, man, whatever. A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London. The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico. Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.  Leisure and wellness projects win big again The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.  “It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added. The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.          Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi        The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico. A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners. Read more about all the winning architecture projects below: Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces. Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure. “Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” said the master jury. “It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.” House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast. This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island. “This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury said. “In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.” House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China. This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory. “This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” said the judges. “Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.” Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra. A deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces. The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”. “It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they said. Recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote. House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan. It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes. The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.  “It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added. House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran. It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life. Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home. The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.” “It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they said. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote. Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo. A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves The new building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose. “A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” said the master jury.  “It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.” Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States. A very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange. The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”. “It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added. Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China. The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public. “A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.  “The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.” Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London. Well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe. The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote. Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India. In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people “This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury. “In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.  “The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.” The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote. Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France. It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose. “It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” said the judges.  “The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.” Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson. There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.  The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.  “There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they said. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote. Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.  A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city. The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.” “A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.” Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland. A minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks. The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”. Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu Architecture studio Tonkin Liu won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in York, United Kingdom. The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral. “There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure,” said the judges.  “The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space,” they added. Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733 Mexican studio Colectivo C733 won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico. Despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism. It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals’ habitat while allowing people to explore the area. The judges praised the project as “rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists,” adding that, “despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.” Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio Rammed Earth house by Tuckey Design Studio in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year, sponsored by Michelmersh. Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.  As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as “a radical example of material innovation”.  “Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe,” they said. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote. Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo Dutch firm Mecanoo won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank in Amsterdam. An admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building. In 1969, the last spike of the Transcontinental Railroad was nailed into a rail line in Promontory, Utah, officially connecting the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads. The decade that followed was marked by extraordinary corruption and inequality in the United States, as entrepreneurs made fortunes off the shipping industry and the underpaid laborers who made it run.Â  The period is known as the Gilded Age today, a name taken from Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warnerâs satirical novel of the same name. But while political and economic corruption ran rampant at this time, those who benefitted most from it simultaneously followed strict behavioral standards and moral codes. Some of these behavioral imperatives might seem outlandishly strict today, but back then, they were key to upholding a complex social hierarchy. Women of all social classes faced a wide range of strict expectations during the Gilded Age, most centered on modesty. One particularly tricky balancing act women had to perform at this time was keeping their skirts away from mud, which was no small task given the amount of manure, dirt, and vehicle exhaust found on the average Gilded Age city street. At the same time, they were expected to avoid showing too much of their ankles. This body part was not always considered scandalous, and in fact, many Victorian-era dresses revealed womenâs ankles, but by the time the Gilded Age rolled around, long dresses were all the rage and members of polite society were expected to bury their ankles under silk, chiffon, velvet, and brocade. Table manners were a detailed business among the upper classes of the Gilded Age, and dinner party faux pas could easily reveal a personâs nouveau riche background. Knowing which utensil was to be used for which dish was of paramount importance, and one particular etiquette guide noted that green peas were only supposed to be eaten with forks, not knives, âno matter how dexterously the feat may be performed.â (Of course, all this occurred while 90% of families in the nation were living on less than $1,200 per year and often struggled to afford food.)Â  These days, itâs generally forgivableâif frowned uponâto shoot a quick message to your host letting them know youâll be a bit late. But this was not the case during the Gilded Age. Arriving early was considered slightly rude, but arriving late was absolutely taboo. Most dinner parties started between 7:30 and 8:30 p.m., at which time guests would be ferried into the drawing room, where drinks would be served. This was a critical moment for guests to examine one another, for young women to speak to suitors, and for all manner of networking to occur. According to some Gilded Age etiquette guides, being late by more than 15 minutes was absolutely unacceptable and could bring ruin to oneâs social status. Dressing was an intricate and loaded affair among the upper classes of the Gilded Age, and women would sometimes change up to four or five times a day. According to the 1891 guidebook Manners, Culture and Dress of the Best American Society, it was vitally important to dress properly for every mealâand part of that involved not dressing too well, depending on who you were. âNever dress above your station,â the book advised, claiming this could lead to âgreat evils, besides being proof of an utter want of taste.â It even suggested that hostesses should dress in subdued colors to avoid outshining their guests.Â  Today, making a new friend can be as simple as asking to meet for coffee, but things were a bit more complicated in the 1870s.  Calls, or home visits, were central to Gilded Age social systems. These visits generally lasted around 15 minutes and involved extremely strict rules that were different depending on the time, location, and reason for the call.Â The 1884 guidebook Our Department stated that hostesses were expected to meet callers immediately and stand when guests arrived, and that gentlemen should be presented to the hostess first during introductions. If two women were visiting, however, the younger ought to be presented first. If the person one was calling upon was not home, visitors would leave their personal cards in silver trays in the hall, and the person receiving the card would either send a card back or pay a visit of their ownâbut only if they wished to continue the relationship.Â If they did not wish to, they simply would not send a card or call, which could theoretically be seen as the Gilded Age version of ghosting. (Reuters: Ann Wang) No-one has ever seen it coming. A new technology, a spark of interest, a rush of blood, a flood of cash, a booming stock market and fabulous riches, culminating in the inevitable crash. It's a tale that's been on a permanent, high-rotation repeat throughout the course of history. Who could forget the Great Railway Crash of 1846 after the Bank of England brought an era of easy money to an end when it suddenly raised interest rates, devastating the vast speculative fortunes of the merchant class? Or the Great American Railroad Crash just 30 years later, after one of the banks behind a debt-fuelled track expansion collapsed, sending the New York Stock Exchange into a 10-day halt, the collapse of thousands of businesses and the onset of the "Long Depression". What about the Radio Boom of the 1920s, when an incredible new communications technology sent the market soaring before it all came to grief with the great 1929 Wall Street crash? Radio Corporation of America (RCA) shares surged from $US1.50 to $US568 before shedding 98 per cent of their value. And some of us were around when the dotcom bubble burst at the dawn of the new millennium. Wall Street indices nosedive as investor thinking about the rollout of AI infrastructure turns on its head. History doesn't always repeat. But it's a mighty powerful indicator of what may be to come. Which raises the question: Why should it be any different this time? An ocean of debt has been poured into artificial intelligence on a scale deemed unimaginable just five years ago. The investment boom behind AI is looking increasingly shaky just as it is about to revolutionise our lives. And like almost every other technology-driven investment boom, companies overburdened with debt are under scrutiny. Dario Amodei must be kicking himself. In a few days, the fate of the biggest initial public offering in history will be decided when Amodei's AI upstart, Anthropic, the outfit behind chatbot Claude, hopes to haul in $US90 billion ($134 billion). That should value the firm at $US1.5 trillion, substantially less than the $US2 trillion anticipated just weeks ago. Dario Amodei must be kicking himself right now. (AP: Markus Schreiber/File) It will be a crucial test for investors already concerned about the ability of these firms to generate enough returns in time to cover their extraordinary debts, the huge amounts already invested, not to mention their plans to tip vastly more cash into their ventures. If only he could have beaten Elon Musk, whose SpaceX encountered a turbulent lift-off midway through the year, not to mention the market wobbles that accompanied the failure of Australia's Firmus to raise cash two months ago. Even worse, did Jensen Huang, Nvidia's leather-jacketed AI kingmaker, have to get caught in a love tryst with an alleged Chinese spy just days before Anthropic's historic cash raising? Capping off the concerns, uppity residents of the world's biggest cities, and many smaller ones, suddenly are threatening to put a halt to the rollout of crucial AI infrastructure either physically in person or via the ballot box. Little wonder investors are edgy. This is an industry with a level of concentration rarely ever witnessed. The top 10 AI-exposed companies account for about 40 per cent of the American stock market. And their huge outperformance in recent years has attracted vast inflows of global capital to ride the boom. Almost everyone has a bet riding on the outcome. Jensen Huang's affair scandal was bad timing. Anthropic and its arch-rival OpenAI, the company that kicked off the entire AI scramble after it released ChatGPT four years ago, are the pair blazing away at the frontier of designing and teaching machines to out-think and outsmart humans. Anthropic has been lauded as having a vast cash reserve of more than $US130 billion, even before its stock market listing. But, according to its prospectus, the firm is looking to invest up to $US900 billion over the next five to 10 years. Much of that is expected to come from its own revenue, with investment bank Goldman Sachs predicting the firm will earn $US53 billion this year and as much as $US636 billion by the end of the decade. When it comes to risk, there has never been a stock float in history quite like Anthropic. Almost a quarter of the 300-page document is dedicated to the "existential threat" posed by AI. In a Yin and Yang balancing act, the authors point out that AI could solve all of humanity's problems from the profound to the mundane. Or it could hasten the end of civilisation. "AI can be misused by those who wish to do us harm, for example to conduct cyber attacks or design biological weapons," it reads. While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain. Or they may take control on their own, behaving "in unintended, misaligned or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no end user or third party directed". A devotee of a philosophy known as Effective Altruism, Amodei has long championed curbing the speed of AI development for the sake of humanity, even as he leads the push to push the boundaries. Some cynics have suggested his ulterior motive is to protect the lead Anthropic has on the rest of the industry, at least until the stock float is finalised. But for many, the real risk for Anthropic and the entire AI boom lies in the threat posed by the intensely concentrated structure within the AI ecosphere. AI is set to radically reshape the way we work and live. (Unsplash: Solen Feyissa) Unlike OpenAI, which relies heavily upon ordinary consumers, much of Anthropic's revenue comes from a handful of companies, most of which are engaged in software development. Any problems with those clients will have an immediate affect on Anthropic. Both, however, are terrified of threats from Chinese AI developers and, in particular, an outfit called Moonshot, which has developed a platform known as Kimi. Anthropic and its Claude platform have managed to maintain a lead over Kimi, but it is narrowing. A year ago, Anthropic was ahead by about nine months. Now, it's closer to four months and, in some instances, Kimi can outperform it. The biggest contest, however, won't be on performance; it will centre on price. While there is evidence it had connections with Alice Huang, the lover of Nvidia's hapless boss Jensen Huang, Moonshot was forced to develop its AI models without easy access to the premium chips. As a result, it has developed a system that is significantly cheaper than Claude and, if push comes to shove, buyers generally opt for the cheapest. That may undermine all the earnings projections within the Anthropic prospectus and poses a serious risk to the massive outlays already sunk by America's AI firms. Your correspondent caught the train to work today. Even though it was raining, it ran reasonably smoothly on a rail network that often throws the Sydney system into chaos. Early morning radio delivered a hit of news and the internet worked just fine on the way into the office. Each one of these technological innovations outlived the catastrophic market collapses at their birth, caused by the irrational mania that so often has accompanied the investment phase. The regulator that oversees Australia's banks, super funds and insurers will run "stress tests" to examine hypothetical doomsday scenarios linked to AI. Not all technologies are even profitable. Warren Buffett once joked that investors would have been better off if someone had shot down Orville Wright on his famous test flight at Kitty Hawk in 1903, given the patchy financial performance of airlines. Thrilling and terrifying in equal measure, AI is set to radically reshape the way we work and live. A mere handful of internet hopefuls survived the dotcom crash and some ended up enormously profitable. But there are never any guarantees that inventors are a great financial bet. It hasn’t even been a full week since Nvidia’s former CEO and founder, Jensen Huang, resigned after admitting to an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. And yet, major investors in the chipmaker are already talking about Huang making a comeback.Huang resigned last Thursday, but by Saturday, both Brad Gerstner, CEO of Altimeter Capital, and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker had written to Nvidia’s board to ask them to consider leaving “all options” on the table, “including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”Some speculators are inclined to agree. At the time of writing, Polymarket users assigned a 40% probability to Huang rejoining Nvidia by December 2027. 12% suspect he’ll be back before the end of this year. Over on Kalshi, the odds of Huang’s return as CEO are more muted. At the time of writing, 18% of users say Huang will be the next CEO of Nvidia, trailing only Rene Haas, the CEO of Arm Holdings. Haas, who leads the British semiconductor and software design company, has reportedly been approached for the role. A “Stand with Jensen” campaign has also been launched, with Elon Musk—CEO of SpaceX and Tesla—at the top of the petition. Of nearly 180,000 signatures, nearly 9,000 are reportedly “current Nvidians.” But while petitions and speculators online can be waved off, major Nvidia shareholders are harder to ignore. Altimeter holds approximately $1.9 billion in shares, and Atreides approximately $250 million. The letter did not call for Huang’s immediate reinstatement (the company is currently led by interim CEO Colette Kress, formerly CFO), but added: “If after all the facts are known the Board decides that it is not in shareholders’ best interest to have Jensen Huang back as CEO, that is the Board’s prerogative.” “But the founder and long time incredible leader of this extraordinary company has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known.”  The Financial Times reported over the weekend that Huang had discussed a return with close confidants, citing multiple sources familiar with the matter. This letter was sent to the Nvidia Board today which we believe outlines the minimum acceptable standards the Board owes shareholders as it manages this difficult situation.  Onward. 🫡 pic.twitter.com/fIsyXVQ5tR Nvidia’s stock continued to slide this weekend, and fell another 2% overnight, to just over $158 per share. Some market analysts see Huang’s return as impossible. The AI stock boom is “in its final stages,” Capital Economics wrote on Monday, and what does the U.S. economy really have to show for it?  Anthropic is going public, anyway, on Thursday, in a deal estimated to raise about $64.35 billion at the top of its range. That’s nearly twice what every U.S. IPO raised together last quarter, per Renaissance Capital. If Capital Economics is right, the timing is bad for more than Anthropic’s bankers. The AI boom has been carrying the growth half of what Goldman Sachs economists called “jobless growth.” The economy grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter while employers added an average of 48,000 jobs a month over the 12 months through September—before a massive 165,000 gain in October. AI spending drove more than half of business-investment growth in the first three quarters of the year, Goldman estimates. Take the boom away and you could be left with the jobless part. J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s David Kelly already sees real GDP growth slowing to 1.6% over the next four quarters, with hiring stuck near 50,000 a month. Capital Economics markets economist Joe Maher pointed to falling share issuance and “investors’ waning appetite for new shares of AI-firms at lofty valuations.” Anthropic, he wrote, is “a key test.”  By Kelly’s math, two years of 2.3% growth “should have led to a monthly gain of roughly 155,000 net new jobs.” Instead, the economy got just 48,000. Kelly mainly blames “a lack of available workers due to a sharp reversal of immigration policy.” The bar has dropped to match. Morgan Stanley’s research digest on Monday, summarizing chief U.S. economist Michael Gapen’s 2027 outlook, put the breakeven at about 50,000 jobs a month. That’s the hiring pace needed just to keep unemployment from rising. Federal Reserve economists Seth Murray and Ivan Vidangos think labor force growth “could be near-zero starting this year,” which would put the breakeven near zero, too. If so, growth in potential GDP “will need to come entirely from productivity growth.” In other words, the economy needs the AI boom to deliver. So far, a lot of this growth has gone overseas. Goldman estimates AI investment will add 0.6 percentage points to “true” GDP growth in 2027 and only 0.2 points to the GDP that actually gets counted. Chips are undercounted in the official data and most of the servers are imported, so they get netted out. Morgan Stanley is more upbeat. Gapen sees hyperscalers spending $1.6 trillion on capex in 2027, adding 0.9 points to growth. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the first two of 22 underwriters named on the cover of Anthropic’s prospectus. Even so, Gapen’s outlook says the AI money is mostly propping up upper-income households, while low- and middle-income consumers lead the slowdown. He expects AI disruption and tighter Fed policy to keep hiring subdued.  The banks roughly agree on jobs. On growth, they don’t: Morgan Stanley sees 2.5% in 2027 and Goldman 2.4%, against JPMAM’s 1.6% over the next four quarters. Wall Street’s appetite for Anthropic, at least, looks intact. Bloomberg reported Nov. 12 that the deal was about six times oversubscribed, just days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, threatening the entire AI ecosystem at a pivotal moment. Nvidia is still buying about $10 billion of Anthropic stock in a private placement alongside the offering. Goldman calls today’s job market “low-hire, low-fire,” repeating a phrase made famous by former Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell. That works out fine if you already have a job, but it’s dire if you’re young and trying to get one. Employers hired at a 3.4% rate in September, according to the Labor Department’s JOLTS report. The unemployment rate for 20- to 24-year-olds was 7.5% in October, against 4.1% overall. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found in August that employment of 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs was about 19% below where it would have been had it kept pace with peers in less-exposed work. Staying put doesn’t pay much in this economy, either. Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the 12 months through October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said. JPMAM points out that “despite a tight labor market, real year-over-year wage growth has been negative for seven consecutive months.” Workers are scarce, and they’re still losing ground. They’re also getting a smaller cut of what they produce. Productivity in the nonfarm business sector rose at a 3.6% annual rate in the third quarter, the BLS said Nov. 5, while labor’s share of output, the part paid out to workers as compensation, fell to 53.0%, the lowest since the series began in 1947. AI investment “appear[s] to be contributing” to the productivity gains, Indeed Hiring Lab’s Aubrey Woessner wrote. But “increased labor productivity has not yet translated into higher real pay.” The most direct evidence that AI is holding pay down comes from Apollo Global Management. Economists Sania Edlich and Torsten Slok sorted occupations by how heavily their tasks show up in Claude conversations, using Anthropic’s own Economic Index. After 2023, real wage growth in the most-exposed occupations has run about 6.7 percentage points behind less-exposed jobs, they found, with no statistically significant effect on employment.  Workers in the lowest wage quartile of those jobs took the biggest hit, about 10.7 points. “The first measurable labor market effect of AI adoption has been wage compression rather than employment displacement,” they wrote. Apollo estimates about 5.8 million workers are in the most-exposed occupations, and the authors caution that the period “may be partially confounded by post-pandemic labor market dynamics.” Not every measure points the same way. Advertised salaries in the most AI-exposed occupations have risen 46% since 2021, against 25% for the least exposed, according to Indeed data reported in September. That counts what employers offer new hires, not what people already in those jobs are earning. People can tell. The University of Michigan’s consumer sentiment index stood at 51.0 in its preliminary November reading. “About 57% spontaneously mentioned that their living standards have been eroded by high prices,” survey director Joanne Hsu wrote. Capital Economics says the boom is in its final stages. Goldman Sachs has a guess at the stage after that.
