A Wealth of Common Sense Posted November 15, 2026 by Ben Carlson This Jensen Huang situation is one of the craziest market stories I’ve ever seen. The most important CEO of the most important company in the most important technological innovation this century just resigned during the middle of an AI boom. Huang is quite possibly the most central figure in orchestrating the AI buildout. I don’t think we’ve even begun to figure out what all the ripple effects will be from the fallout of this scandal. There is so much going on here. I don’t want to get into the affairs, potential spy operation, importance of chip technology in the race for global AI world domination with China, etc. I want to look at this from a stock market perspective. The stock was down almost 14% last week alone. Nvidia is down more than 30% from the highs and it happened in a hurry. The market cap was $5.8 trillion a month ago. It’s shed nearly $2 trillion since then. In October Nvidia was almost 8% of the S&P 500. Even after the crash it still makes up more than 6% of the total and remains the second largest position in the index (for now). Now look at the difference in drawdowns between NVDA and the S&P 500 (via Exhibit A): One of the biggest, most influential stocks in the S&P 500 got marked down by one-third in five weeks and the market barely budged. This market is incredible. Nvidia’s stock price isn’t the only thing crashing at the moment for the company. The valuation has been in a freefall for some time now: For context, the S&P 500 currently trades at a little more than 18x its forward earnings estimates. That means Nvidia is trading at nearly a 40% discount to the market. The fundamentals are still there. Earnings are growing like crazy. Will they continue to grow in the future? I don’t know. A similar dynamic is playing out in semiconductor stocks. The sector is down almost 30%: This makes sense when you consider Nvidia is the biggest holding in this fund. However, a lot of other semiconductor stocks are getting creamed right now too: These companies had some massive gains earlier this year so it makes sense they would be volatile.1 Similar to Nvidia, the fundamentals are still there but the prices don’t care at the moment. Look at how the the relationship between estimated earnings and stock prices has broken down of late: It’s a huge divergence. Earnings estimated keep getting ratcheted up but prices are falling. Of course, semiconductors are known for extremely cyclical earnings growth. You can see it in the chart. There are a few interesting observations to be made about this divergence between prices and fundamentals going on in AI stocks right now: Maybe investors don’t want a bubble. Tech valuations keep falling even as the stock market keeps rising. It’s quite possible investors have learned their lesson and don’t want to take multiples to nosebleed levels during a boom. This could be a sign of sobriety in the market. The market is usually right. The market doesn’t seem to believe the high level of earnings will continue into the future. The market is not always right but it’s right most of the time. What if it’s wrong this time and earnings aren’t as cyclical as they were in the past? It can pay big time to be a contrarian when the market is wrong. You can also get run over since contrarians are wrong most of the time (by definition). That’s what makes this game so interesting in times like these. Picking AI winners and losers is nearly impossible. Who could have possibly predicted a few weeks ago the Nvidia would be crashing because their CEO got caught up in a scandal like this? Maybe the company will come back even stronger. Maybe the shareholders will get their way and Jensen will come back as CEO. Maybe there will be new winners that pick up the slack. Maybe this really is the end of the AI boom for now. Maybe this is all impossible to predict at any given time and being certain about anything will surely make you look foolish in a matter of days or weeks. Here are some questions to ponder when thinking about AI forecasts: What edge do you have that will allow you to understand who the winners and losers will be in this arms race? What are your guidelines for when to sell? When will you admit you were wrong? What is your position sizing if you are trying to pick the winners or avoid the losers? Do you need to pick the winners in order to achieve your financial goals? Every new AI story leads me to believe that the only certainty here is uncertainty. Trying to forecast when this boom will end, how it will end, who will win and who will lose is a game I don’t want to play. There’s no shame in admitting that most of the time the market is too hard to predict. Further Reading: This is Why You Need a Plan 1SMH is in a 28% drawdown but still up 35% on the year. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung) NSW Premier Chris Minns has shelved real estate underquoting laws which were due to come into effect on Tuesday. Under the laws, agents could be banned from lowering the advertised price of some properties, even in a falling market. The rules could be on hold for up to a year. Laws designed to protect buyers from real estate underquoting in New South Wales have been shelved amid fears they could backfire in the current housing downturn. The rules were due to take effect on Tuesday, but the ABC has learnt they will be paused for up to a year, following a last-minute intervention from NSW Premier Chris Minns. On Monday morning, the premier said he was concerned about agents being banned from lowering the advertised price of a property even if it was not generating buyer interest. "It's not the seller or the agent's fault if the price of real estate is dropping," he said. "The legislation, at least intuitively, believed that the prices would always rise. "Well, that may not be the case." By Monday evening, the premier had decided the controversial change should not proceed, just hours before it was due to come into force. The rules were due to take effect on Tuesday before a last-minute delay was flagged. (AAP: Darren England) Underquoting occurs when a property is advertised below the actual price that a real estate agent expects it to sell for. While advertising a lower price can generate market interest in a property, it frustrates potential buyers and is therefore already illegal. Under the next tranche of Labor's underquoting laws, which were due to begin on Tuesday, agents could be banned from advertising a price that was lower than a written offer rejected by the seller. The change was designed to protect buyers by preventing agents from advertising unrealistic prices that the seller would not be happy to accept. However, the market has turned. Cotality data shows Sydney house prices have fallen by close to 9.7 per cent since the end of January, with units falling 5.2 per cent. The market is experiencing downward pressure.  (AAP: Mick Tsikas) Under the now-scrapped rule, if a buyer believed their home was worth $1.5 million and rejected a written offer of $1.3 million, their agent could not advertise the property for anything less than $1.3 million. Even if the seller later realised their expectations were too high and wished to adjust their asking price, the agent would not be able to change the advertised price. Topic:Courts Topic:Courts Topic:Discrimination Topic:Terrorism Real Estate Institute of NSW CEO, Tim McKibbin, said the rule would mean buyers would not know that a property had become more affordable. "It misleads and disadvantages those purchasers and it certainly disadvantages the vendor," he said. He said real estate agents had been warning the government that the legislation could backfire. "We made clear that this wouldn't work out in the market [and] we were ignored," he said. Mr Minns has hit pause on the legislation. (ABC News) The premier said he had received negative feedback from real estate agents in his own electorate. "I do think it's unforeseen, but it is something we're going to have to deal with," Mr Minns said. "A deteriorating real estate market may mean that you rejected an earlier offer, but in actual fact, you'll take it a month later. "Particularly if it's a distressed sale." With just a few days of parliament left for the year, the government is not expected to make any legislative amendments to pause the controversial changes. Instead, it is expected to issue a regulation that would have the same effect. Also being put on hold will be the requirement for agents to advertise a selling price, or price range, for properties. Fines of up to $110,000 for underquoting will also be delayed, while the government reassesses the full suite of changes. The reversal of key reforms will be a significant blow to Fair Trading Minister Anoulack Chanthivong, who is facing a separate preselection battle in his seat of Macquarie Fields. Mr Chanthivong said the laws had been passed "at a different time and in a different economic and housing market". "People are already doing it tough, and the last thing we want is for laws designed to protect home buyers to inadvertently make it harder for them to buy a home," he said. Shadow Fair Trading Minister Tim James said the government should have designed laws that could withstand a property downturn. "Property prices move in cycles," he said. "The law needs to be able to meet the dynamics of the market at any given point in time." Stratechery Plus Learn MoreMember Forum Latest Podcast  Listen to Podcast  Listen to this post: Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called life.― Prince Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted. In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA, convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT. ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs. More than that, Huang had realized that the future of accelerated computing was not just chips, but rather systems; that drove the purchase of Mellanox in 2019, which provided the technology for Nvidia to scale out from chips, setting it down the road to being the best option for the sort of large scale training that made large language models possible. For this Nvidia charged very high prices, with margins exceeding 70%, because they could: they had the platform, the technology, and, over the past few years as others sought to make their own chips, the supply chain. Huang’s impact on the Asian supply chain in particular cannot be overstated. Byrne Hobart, in his book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation, notes that one of the benefits of bubbles is that they provide a coordination function, as the fear of missing out incentivizes multiple entities with interlocking dependencies to all commit to building at the same time; Huang was, in many respects, a one-person coordination function. Huang gave multiple keynotes a year, which he explained as how he communicated with the ecosystem broadly, and was famous for eating and drinking his way across Asia in particular, convincing reluctant suppliers that the AI boom was real, and locking up the lion’s share of their output for Nvidia and its stunning commitment to a yearly release cycle. Huang, who had toiled for decades in relative obscurity, known primarily to gamers, and only barely to the tech industry, became a rock star, swarmed wherever he went, always in his black leather jacket. He also, to his ultimate detriment, became a political figure. Nvidia had long had no presence in either Washington D.C. or Beijing, and was blindsided by the Biden administration’s imposition of chip controls in 2022. Nvidia’s immediate reaction to those initial controls, which restricted exports based on interconnect speed, was to immediately release the A800 in China, which was an A100 with a third of its interconnects disabled. That set the tone for the conflict that I believe was the true cause of Huang’s downfall: Huang strenuously disagreed with the various iterations of the chip ban, and Nvidia only bothered to do the bare minimum to abide by the letter of the law, never the spirit. That approach, in all likelihood, extended to Nvidia’s oversight (or lack thereof) of Singaporean entities that were alleged to be fronts for chips for China. Some of these were legal: Chinese companies are allowed to access cloud computing facilities outside of China that house leading edge Nvidia chips, although chip control advocates are seeking to close that loophole; some were not legal, in that the chips were ultimately ferried to China. Megaspeed, whose executive, Alice Huang, was the first person Huang was alleged to have an affair with, was officially in the former business, and alleged to actually be in the latter. There are whispers that Megaspeed’s ultimate customer was not, or not just, Alibaba, but also the Chinese military. These are whispers, to be clear; it was the affairs that were enough, at least publicly, to lead to Huang’s resignation. Nvidia’s durability — at least that of their margins — was already an open question. Start with CUDA: when the market was software written for GPUs, a platform — including not just an API but a huge set of libraries targeting every conceivable market for accelerated computing — was a nearly impenetrable moat. That is why LLMs like GPT were written using CUDA. LLMs, though, both brought Nvidia its incredible success, and also seeded its greatest risks. The first is that the vast majority of developer energy moved up the stack, using the LLM’s API as a platform; for most companies, CUDA didn’t matter. The second is that Anthropic, which found funding from Amazon and Google, originally also-rans to the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, had to learn how to use Trainium chips from Amazon and TPUs from Google; this was difficult, but ultimately meant that the leading LLM did not have any Nvidia dependency at all (Anthropic runs on Nvidia chips, because they learned how to run on anything). The third is the most devastating: LLMs are so effective at writing software that any software-based moat will inevitably dry up. Nvidia’s second moat, its networking and systems approach, is more durable, although challenged by Google (and by extension, Anthropic) in particular. Nvidia’s systems approach is also the easy answer for enterprises and governments seeking to own their own hardware, and neoclouds seeking to build data centers that are independent of the hyperscalers. The latter market rents chips to both hyperscalers and frontier labs, as well as individual companies, but is challenged as obvious sources of power and political permission disappear. They also need money to afford Nvidia’s systems, which has increasingly come from Nvidia itself. Nvidia’s third moat is its mastery of the supply chain, and this is the moat that suddenly looks much more tenuous. Huang has bragged about the fact that he has never signed a contract with TSMC over their three decades of partnership; it’s a relationship built on a handshake and mutual trust with Huang specifically. This is, per the point above, a very Asian way of doing business, and Huang was the master of that. It’s questionable whether or not that trust and willingness to commit will persist when the handshake is no longer there. Nvidia’s most important moat, however, was the degree to which it was not a normal company. Huang organized Nvidia as an exoskeleton around one man: himself. There is very little management at Nvidia — Huang famously has 60 direct reports — for the same reason that there was no succession plan: Nvidia could move so quickly and so aggressively because the company still behaved as if it were a startup. Indeed, lots of established companies — including those still led by founders — claim to still be a startup, but only one, Nvidia, really was organized that way. That paid off with all of those successful bets; it also created an environment where there were no checks on Huang. And, now that he is gone, the exoskeleton is much more poised to collapse than you might expect. The first part of the AI buildout was funded by free cash flow, particularly from the hyperscalers. Then, during the second half of last year, nearly everyone started turning to debt. Now — starting with Google this past summer — the primary funding mechanism is equity. In the long run, this should come full circle, and future build-outs will once again be funded by free cash flow, generated from the infrastructure that is being built now. The problem for Nvidia is that the companies most able to navigate this progression are the hyperscalers, which have the resources to challenge Nvidia’s hold on the chip market. To that end, Nvidia has been very eager to ensure that it is selling not only to the hyperscalers, but to other would-be competitors, like the neoclouds; there will likely, at some point, be serious questions raised about exactly how Nvidia went about allocating compute in pursuit of this goal. The neoclouds, however, are at a meaningful disadvantage when it comes to funding. First, their debt is significantly more expensive, given that their only business is renting GPUs (as opposed to, say, running the most valuable advertising businesses in the world, or the world’s largest e-commerce platform, or dominating enterprise software). Second, their equity is increasingly worthless, given the significant risks attached to that credit. If a neocloud can’t pay, it’s the equity holders that get wiped out first. This led to what I termed Nvidia’s Risky Business: Nvidia increasingly used its cash flow and credit rating to backstop and fund the companies who were buying its chips. Bears called this circular financing; bulls called it a necessary bridge to a future where AI revenue paid down these companies’ debt and drove massive upside. What is undoubtedly true is that this was the sort of risky business that is uniquely possible for a multi-trillion dollar company that is completely controlled by one man, who has made an entire career of pushing the limits and making risky bets — and seeing them pay off. It’s also a series of bets that are unlikely to continue. The neoclouds should be very nervous about losing their patron, along with their creditors and equity holders. The other problem is that the revenue necessary to make all of this build-out work is something on the order of a trillion dollars industry-wide, and it needs to materialize sooner rather than later; if it falls short, it’s the hyperscalers who will prioritize their own compute first, and they will likely be seen as a safe haven for everyone committing to spending. In that world, Nvidia’s neocloud hedge — absent Huang’s willingness to shore the ecosystem up — is liable to turn into a millstone, with their assets flooding the market even as the supply chain ramp-up brings ever more supply to market. Perhaps because he had been preaching the gospel of accelerated computing for so long, Huang was the leading figure pushing back against the doomer narrative surrounding AI. Yes, AI was a massive business opportunity, but it was still normal technology; the safety issues presented were engineering challenges to be solved. What required consideration was not just the next five years, but the next fifty. It’s a view that I am, in full disclosure, generally aligned with. Many others are not. On one hand there are the aforementioned doomers, certain that fast takeoff is imminent — or has already started — as AI increasingly builds better AI in a recursive loop. The end state is an AI that is massively more capable than humans, and uncontrollable by them; the only hope is to ensure that AI is aligned with humanity, by which adherents to this viewpoint mean aligned with them and their view of the world. This contingent is, broadly speaking, represented by Anthropic. And, in this view, actively working to enable and accelerate uncontrollable open weights models is a threat to humanity. On the other hand there are the China hawks, who view AI as a national security issue, and the key to U.S. military dominance in a world where China owns the means of production of most militarily relevant hardware. In this world giving China access to chips is effectively treason against the United States. For both of these groups, Huang was public enemy number one, because of his determination to do what was best for Nvidia’s business, which was to sell chips to China. This made sense for Nvidia for multiple reasons: This last point is worth dwelling on. The chief objection that China hawks in particular make to the idea that it is a good idea to sell China chips in order to prevent them from surpassing the U.S. is that China is already heavily invested in building their own ecosystem. This is certainly true, but I think it underplays the complexity of chips and what is necessary to actually compete with the West. Specifically, the Chinese government can only control the supply side, by spending money and making top-down imperatives; building an ecosystem, however, whether that be for AI specifically, or semiconductors broadly, requires demand as well. Progress in models and systems and chips depends on a feedback loop between the user and the developer, or the customer and the manufacturer. The demand side, however, is much more short-term oriented than the Chinese government might prefer. The model companies’ concern is the other model companies: that means if they are distilling, we must distill too. If they are using Nvidia chips, then we must too. This matters up and down the stack, just as it has always mattered in technology, which really is different in this regard from almost every other industry. A useful analogy is to consider the Internet. Why is it that country after country can profess a desire to have an indigenous alternative to the American tech giants, yet miserably fail in every attempt to generate it? It’s because the tech giants are only a click away! In this regard, China’s Great Firewall was one of the most brilliant geostrategic moves ever: by virtue of cutting off access to the American tech companies, China created the demand that pulled China’s own tech giants into existence. You need demand, not just desire. This is why China itself is currently banning the import of Nvidia’s two-generations-behind H20 chips, after the Trump administration foolishly banned their import, only to reverse themselves while bragging about the reason to do so — i.e. keep China addicted to Nvidia. China is replaying the Great Firewall playbook: force its internal demand to use its much worse alternatives, because that is the only way those alternatives become better. And, in the long run, those alternatives, and the entire ecosystem that supports them, will flood the world. Huang was, to be perfectly clear, talking his book when it came to his insistence on selling chips to China, or, in the case of the current controversy, allegedly turning a blind eye towards nominally legal buyers who were intent on violating the chip ban; that doesn’t mean, however, that he was wrong about the long-term effects, at least if AI is a normal technology (and I haven’t gotten to the risks this imposes on the Taiwan Strait). What is clear now, however, is that the doomers and the hawks have won: AI, at least in terms of policy, will be treated as anything but normal, and in the fullness of time, it is the U.S. chip ecosystem that will pay the ultimate price. The birth date for the last obituary was the invention of the transistor; the birth date for this one is the founding of Intel. Robert Noyce and co-founders had spent the last decade at Fairchild Semiconductor, but were constrained by their parent company’s fundamental conservatism and chafed at their lack of upside. Arthur Rock effectively created the venture capital industry in Silicon Valley through his financing of Intel; Noyce created the concept of the commercial-market-led technology company that made it up in volume. At that time the largest single purchaser of chips was the U.S. government; Noyce realized that the fastest way to progress was to make chips for everyone, including the government, and on his terms, not theirs. From that point on, tech as an industry operated with the assumption that the world was its customer, and that their own executives defined the route to progress. Government was free to buy their products, but not to define them, and if they wanted the best products, then they best not restrict who they could sell them to either. That’s how important volume was, and, over time, it became clear how powerful and essential ecosystems were. Other industries operate differently; I thought this article in the Financial Times was striking, and not just because of the headline: Bessent says Nvidia needs ‘shake-up’ with external CEO: Bessent said that it is important “to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions” and whether its top executives knew they were being skirted. “Was it a low-level fail? Was it in the middle, or was it up in the C-suite? And who knew? These shell companies were obvious, they were being investigated, and did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?” he said. “Were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” The Treasury secretary added that Nvidia needs to provide answers within a matter of days: “I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel”. He added that “we will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore”. Bessent has pointed the spotlight on Howard Lutnick’s commerce department for failing to ban exports of Nvidia’s chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean company linked to the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Huang. US authorities have been investigating whether Megaspeed, which builds AI data centres in Asia, has been involved in smuggling high-end Nvidia chips, which are powering the AI boom, into China. Bessent has blamed the commerce department more than once this week for failing to ban exports of Nvidia’s chips to Megaspeed. Commerce delayed efforts to add Megaspeed to Washington’s blacklist of companies the US considers a risk to national security. “Many other departments were pushing for this, and commerce had the pen,” Bessent repeated on Sunday. “We have all the rules we need. We just need them enforced.” Lutnick is under mounting pressure from within the administration and from Congress, which has demanded that he explain how he allowed chips to be exported to a company linked to an alleged Chinese spy. US lawmakers are also accelerating efforts to crack down on advanced AI chips reaching China. If Nvidia “were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the [Treasury’s Office of the Comptroller of the Currency] would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed”, Bessent said. Scott Bessent is the Treasury Secretary, which is to say that he operates an apparatus that is arguably just as, if not more, powerful than the U.S. military. Treasury controls the flow of money around the world, and its soldiers are the banks; if Treasury has sanctioned an entity, then it is up to banks to ensure those sanctions are enforced. They need to know their customers, and they need to analyze every dollar flowing through their systems; if they do not, they are breaking the law. Ignorance is not a defense. Ignorance, on the other hand, has been tech’s defense basically forever. Yes, there are bad people in the world, which means that if the whole world is using your products, they will be used to do bad things. That was considered an acceptable trade-off, however, because most people are good and the benefits that come from scale — and an avoidance of the friction that comes from trying to track the activities of billions of people — were worth the risk. This was certainly what Huang believed, and, to his detriment, he aggressively belittled anyone who dared disagree (the extent to which Huang is despised in Washington D.C., as evidenced by the giddiness and bloodlust online last week, is extraordinary). In Huang’s view, as long as the Commerce Department said that it was ok to sell to Megaspeed, then it was ok to sell to Megaspeed — and to sleep with one of its executives. Bessent views the matter entirely differently: he thinks that Nvidia should operate like a bank. It’s not just their job to abide by the letter of the law, but the spirit of it. It’s not the government’s job to enforce the chip ban, but the company’s. An attestation from a Singaporean customer that chips aren’t going to China isn’t worth anything; actually putting boots on the ground and ensuring compliance is the only way Nvidia cannot be in violation of the U.S. government’s dictates. Again, for tech, this is extraordinary, even if it is normal in banking. Extraordinary enough, in fact, that Huang is being labeled by many — not just in Washington, but also in the finance world — as a traitor. Huang, in my estimation, is just a businessman who cares about nothing else other than Nvidia; that worked out great when he made GPUs for gaming that no one in government cared about or understood. That’s just a normal technology; when AI was deemed to be anything but normal, however, business as usual wasn’t just over: it was a crime, and it cost Huang his job — and maybe more. It’s worth pointing out that while this episode was shocking, I should not, in retrospect, have been surprised. Earlier this year, when Anthropic faced off against the U.S. government, I wrote in Anthropic and Alignment: At the same time, what is the standard by which it should be decided what is allowed and not allowed if not laws, which are passed by an elected Congress? Anthropic’s position is that Amodei — who I am using as a stand-in for Anthropic’s management and its board — ought to decide what its models are used for, despite the fact that Amodei is not elected and not accountable to the public. And, on the second point, who decides when and in what way American military capabilities are used? That is the responsibility of the Department of War, which ultimately answers to the President, who also is elected. Once again, however, Anthropic’s position is that an unaccountable Amodei can unilaterally restrict what its models are used for. My point in that Article was that if AI is as exceptional as claimed, then the government will demand a say in how it is used, whether or not private company executives agree; moreover, that was a good thing, or at least a least-bad thing. The same analysis applies to Nvidia and Huang: Huang may have fundamentally disagreed with the chip ban, but at the end of the day, it was his duty to accept that it was the law of the land. To the extent he did not do so is ultimately his responsibility. Perhaps the most tragic aspect of the Huang affair is the extent to which he was the personification of The American Dream. Huang was sent to America as a nine year old who didn’t speak a lick of English, and somehow ended up at a boarding school in rural Kentucky for misbehaving youth, where he would trade help on homework for protection from bullies. From there he went to a state school in Oregon, became an engineer, before famously ending up at a Denny’s diner where he and his co-founders decided to start Nvidia. Then, over the following 33 years, he took risk after risk, created innovation after innovation, until he became a hero not just in the United States, but across the world. And then, you might say, he flew too close to the sun. Certainly he did so in his private life: it’s not just the affairs, which may be par for the course for rich and powerful men; rather, it’s notable just how reckless the affairs were. The ones that were revealed last week were with a customer and potential Chinese spy, and two of his own employees; both are fireable offenses. Meanwhile, the way in which Huang treated his opponents — including actively seeking to get people fired who he felt stood in the way of getting his way — bore the marks of a man who has constructed a life, and a company, where no one can or will stand up to him. That is a recipe for disaster, and here we are. At the same time, it really does bum me out that what ultimately doomed Huang was a set of rules that really are a big departure from the status quo — and, in my opinion, misguided. Huang’s actions — or lack of actions, in terms of enforcing compliance with the chip ban — are treated as if they are an obvious crime, when in fact this is a dramatic shift in expectations from a short time ago (although there is certainly a callback to previous controversies around selling advanced computing to adversaries). Huang should have adjusted and accepted the new reality, make no mistake; I’m sympathetic to the fact he couldn’t, and recognize the failure in not having structures in place that could have warned him about the dangerous road he was embarking on, even as I realize Huang’s willingness to navigate dangerous roads is precisely why he was an American success story. Beyond Huang, however, there is the question of how we compete with China, and I am disappointed, although not surprised, that we are pursuing the route of bans and forced compliance, instead of innovation and openness. Make no mistake, I am no China dove, and I have been very early to the argument that we erred greatly in willingly exporting entire industries to the communist state. That, however, makes it even more imperative that we sprint in the opposite direction of China, towards more freedom in a bet on inventing new industries, not more control and a focus on gatekeeping what we have. I get the logic, particularly in the case of AI, which is extraordinary; I lament the implications of what it says about our belief in ourselves and our ability to stay ahead. Presented by As AI models improve, you might expect the market will consolidate around a handful of providers. But user data tells a different story. Among OpenRouter customers spending at least $100 a month, the median number of AI model families in use has doubled over the past year, from three to six. Even as AI models become more capable, businesses are using more models, not fewer. This makes sense when you consider that intelligence isn’t one-dimensional. A model that’s exceptional at writing code may not be the fastest at answering customer questions, or the most economical at processing millions of documents. The question is shifting from “which AI model should we build on?” to “which model should handle each task?” The answer, increasingly, is ‘it depends.’ Which is great for flexibility, less great for simplicity. Their strategies look suspiciously similar. Reading time: 2 minutes Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile Samsung logo Samsung and two other memory chip manufacturers were sued this past summer. A group of 17 plaintiffs, including small businesses and individual consumers, alleged that Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron engaged in price-fixing practices in the memory market.  Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron filed a joint motion to dismiss. However, on November 14, the U.S. District Court Judge handling the case dismissed the filing.  In the original lawsuit, filed on June 14, the plaintiffs alleged that the three companies formed an oligopoly and intentionally bottlenecked the DRAM supply to force higher prices. Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron have allegedly focused on expanding HBM (high-bandwidth memory) production while halting DDR4 manufacturing, knowing the side effects.  The court observed that all three memory giants announced plans to scale back DDR4 production in mid-2025. More importantly, all three companies adopted similar review procedures to verify end-customer demand starting in January 2026. That was a red flag.  In response, Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron said there was no collusion. Instead, their actions reflected what each other competitor was doing.  That, however, wasn't enough. According to Korean media, the Judge was not convinced and said the companies' conduct went beyond observation and resembled a flock of hawks flying in formation.  A final decision as to whether or not Samsung and the other companies colluded on price-fixing has yet to be reached, but the court determined that the allegations are plausible enough for the lawsuit to proceed.  Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron were ordered to file their answers by December 7.     [email protected]  First Samsung device: SGH-A800 Mihai is a blogger and column writer at SamMobile. Amazon Prime Video is one of the most popular streaming services on the planet, second only to Netflix. They have old stuff, new stuff, good stuff, bad stuff, glad stuff, sad stuff. In November, Amazon has added over 100 films to the Prime Video library, and counting. As the holidays approach, you might want some guidance as to which to watch during your free time. Gods Don't Give Gifts will be the first big AI-generated film to play in movie theaters.  Thanksgiving isn't quite here yet, but Prime Video is already bringing out the big Christmas guns. One of the most powerful is Elf, the comedy about a human being (Will Ferrell) who's raised in Santa's workshop as an elf. Once he finds out the truth, he ventures to New York City is search of his birth parents, and makes everyone vaguely uncomfortable with his relentless positivity. Naturally, they eventually come to appreciate it and learn the true meaning of Christmas. Elf became a classic pretty much immediately after it opened in theaters in 2003. Good Christmas movies tend to have long shelf lives; there's always a market for them, which is maybe why Prime Video is so eager to get a jump on the holiday season. Other Christmas movies already available to watch on the service include Bad Santa, Jingle All the Way, Scrooged, A Very Harold & Kumar Christmas, and the 1999 version of A Christmas Carol starring Patrick Stewart as Ebenezer Scrooge, which could be a nice way to honor the actor's legacy after his passing. Good Will Hunting feels like more of a movie for the fall. Matt Damon plays Will, a 20-year-old janitor at the prestigious Massachusetts Institute of Technology who also happens to be a self-taught genius in mathematics. When he anonymously solves a complex mathematical problem meant for graduate students, faculty members take interest, and it looks like Will could have a bright future. But first he has to overcome trauma left over from his childhood, which is where psychology professor Dr. Sean Maguire (Robin Williams) comes in. Good Will Hunting was the breakout movie for both Matt Damon and Ben Affleck, who wrote the screenplay together, and has one of Robin Williams' most iconic roles. The drama still works nearly 30 years later, and it's a great, cozy movie to watch on a chilly day. Prime Video also added a bunch of classic films to its lineup in November. One of the most famous is Some Like It Hot, a 1959 comedy about a pair of jazz musicians (Tony Curtis and Jack Lemmon) who witness a mob hit and are forced to go on the run. Naturally, they decide the best way to avoid detection is to dress up like women and go on the road with an all-female band, but things get complicated when one of the men falls for Sugar Kane, the band's singer, played by Marilyn Monroe. Some LIke It Hot is considered one of the great screwball comedies. The jokes come fast and furious, the performances are all iconic, and the movie pushed boundaries for the time with its gender-bending plot. Other classics in Prime Video this month include Duck Soup, Imitation of Life, The Manchurian Candidate, The Pink Panther, In the Heat of the Night, Last Tango in Paris, and Annie Hall.  A lot of these films are pretty old, so let's highlight one that came out more recently. Blink Twice slipped largely under the radar, but got good reviews when it came out in 2024. This thriller stars Channing Tatum as a tech billionaire with the unlikely name of Slater King. Naomi Ackie and Alia Shawkat sneak into a high-profile fundraiser where they meet King and get invited to his lavish private island. It sounds like fun, and it is...for a while. As the movie goes on, the girls realize that something is wrong on the island, and that King and his compatriots may be taking advantage of people like them in some very scary ways. With all the talk about Jeffrey Epstein's behavior in the news lately, the movie feels pretty relevant, and is much better than you'd expect given that it got very little press. Maybe it can find a following now that it's on Prime Video.  Let's end with something lighter and older. Mean Girls is a 2004 classic about a high schooler (Lindsay Lohan) trying to fit in at her new school, even as she's torn between different social groups. Written by Saturday Night Live alum Tina Fey, the movie bristles with quotable lines and memorable bits. It's a great one to revisit and show to the next generation of up-and-comers. Prime Video seems to be on a 2000s kick this month. Other entrants include the Agent Cody Banks movies (best of luck to Frankie Muniz), the Hot Tub Time Machine films, and the Jeepers Creepers horror flicks. Enjoy the nostalgia bomb, millennial readers. November isn't over, and Prime Video still has a couple of things on the way. One of the biggest is Madden, a biographical drama where Nicolas Cage plays football coach and commentator John Madden. That one will drop on November 18. On the TV side, the third season of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is currently airing, and there's a new Blade Runner TV show coming on November 25. We want to hear from you. Meta          Shop Meta Quest 3 Shop Meta Quest 3s   Takeaways:  Today, Meta brought over 180 small businesses, heartland merchants and creator-entrepreneurs together at Meta Upskill Day 2026 in Singapore, part of its Small Business Growth Academy, with Guest of Honor Ms Low Yen Ling, Senior Minister of State, Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth & Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry, in attendance. The Academy helps owners use Meta’s digital and AI-enabled tools to find customers, improve productivity and grow. Through hands-on Business Agent training, demonstrations and discussions with Meta experts, participants explored how to apply these tools to their everyday business needs.  In Singapore, this focus on practical skills aligns with the National AI Strategy’s emphasis on broadening AI adoption and building the capabilities to use it effectively. It also complements the National AI Impact Programme’s objective of helping enterprises deepen their use of AI. By combining hands-on training with outreach through Enterprise Singapore’s (EnterpriseSG) partnership with the Heartland Enterprise Centre Singapore’s (HECS) business advisors and heartland merchant network, the Academy equips business advisors with AI knowledge and practical tools that can support local businesses in exploring AI applications for customer engagement and everyday operations. YouGov Research  New YouGov research commissioned by Meta found that 94% of small business owners surveyed in Singapore agree that small businesses need more guidance to gain the full benefits of AI. The same research found that 82% of Singapore small business owners surveyed whose business has used AI report a positive impact on productivity over the past 12 months. Among Singapore small business owners who report a positive impact on productivity, 62% use time saved through AI to improve the quality of existing work. “Our focus is helping Singapore’s small businesses find customers, improve productivity and grow by pairing practical digital and AI tools with training. Honeymill uses WhatsApp Business to build customer relationships, while SpeakEasy Lab uses Meta Business Agent to handle routine enquiries and give its founders more time for personal conversations. These examples show how digital tools can help small teams serve customers and compete more effectively,” said Nicole Tan, Managing Director of Meta Singapore. Putting Meta Business Agent to Work Customer engagement is one area where owners see opportunities for AI. In Singapore, 52% of small business owners surveyed have used or would be interested in using AI-powered customer responses. The Business Agent masterclass gave participants hands-on experience alongside demonstrations and guidance from Meta’s Business Messaging experts. The sessions explored how businesses can use agents to support customer enquiries through WhatsApp and Messenger, giving their teams more time to focus on other parts of the business. For Singapore communication training business SpeakEasy Lab, that support helps a two-person team manage routine enquiries while its founders step in when customers need personalised advice. According to the business, routine questions that previously took around an hour or longer to answer now receive almost immediate responses. The founders estimate that Meta Business Agent saves their team 10 to 15 working hours each week. “For a small business like ours, every enquiry matters. Meta Business Agent helps us respond to customers quickly, even when we’re teaching or away, while saving us 10 to 15 hours every week. That means we can spend less time answering routine questions and more time understanding and connecting with our learners as we grow,” said Mervyn Ye, Co-founder of SpeakEasy Lab. Helping Businesses Create More Video With Dream Render Creating content is another practical area for support. In Singapore, 46% of small business owners surveyed say AI training for marketing and content creation would be useful. That’s why alongside practical training on Meta Business Agent, Meta is also introducing Dream Render, an AI-powered web app for small businesses and creators who need to produce product videos regularly. It turns a short product description or photo into a first draft in minutes. Users can adjust individual shots, framing, pacing, voiceover and on-screen text, then preview and approve before the final video is produced. They download and publish the video themselves as social content or ads, with a label showing it was made with AI. “Dream Render gives small businesses a quick starting point for product video, with the controls to shape it for their products and customers. Through Meta Upskill Day and partners such as Enterprise Singapore, we’re helping owners build the skills and confidence to put AI to work,” added Tan. The tool runs in a browser at dreamrender.com, giving businesses and creators another way to develop product content while managing the everyday demands of running a business. People can sign in with the Facebook profile page or Instagram professional account they already use, with nothing to download or install. Singaporean startup Haldy, which makes sugar-free turmeric mints, has been using Dream Render for their video needs. “Dream Render has been a game changer for accelerating Haldy’s social media presence in a short span of time. We love how effortless it is to produce high-quality content that resonates with our consumers in Singapore and beyond,” said Push Sharma, Founder & CEO of Haldy. Supporting Singapore’s Small Business Community Since its launch in Singapore in 2021, Upskill with Meta has trained more than 500+ small businesses and upskilled over 4,500 entrepreneurs. Meta has worked with government partners including Digital Industry Singapore, AI Singapore, EnterpriseSG and the Singapore Economic Development Board to help local businesses transform their operations with digital and AI tools.  About the Research The research was commissioned by Meta and conducted online by YouGov among 3,983 small business owners across Australia, Singapore, Vietnam, Indonesia, Taiwan, India, Thailand, Japan and Hong Kong. Data was collected between 6 August and 2 September 2026.  Within each market, quotas were applied by business size to achieve a broad and balanced spread across businesses with 1–9, 10–19 and 20–49 employees. The findings provide insights across a diverse cross-section of small businesses in each market, rather than being nationally representative of the small business population. Reported adoption and impact differ across the nine markets surveyed.
